modules.title: Foundations & Table Math
modules.sub: EV, pot odds, equity, combos & the numbers you carry
modules.recap:
The bedrock.
- EV = your edge over the long run; grade decisions, not results.
- Pot odds, the Rule of 2 & 4, combos & blockers, MDF & alpha - the math you run at the table.

steps.title: You are paid for decisions, not sessions
steps.feel: Play to make the right decision, not to win tonight. A great call still loses sometimes and a bad one still wins - the money only shows up over months. So judge the choice, not the result.
steps.formula: Your results = your decisions + variance. Only the decisions are yours to control, so those are what you grade.
steps.proof:
Poker is a long-run expected-value game. Every action wins or loses chips on average if the exact spot were repeated many times. Your job is to choose the higher-EV action and ignore how one hand happens to land.

A great decision often loses and a bad one often wins in the moment. Over a large sample only EV survives.

Module 1 stays light on proofs; from here on I will show the full derivation, then the intuitive form, then the one line worth memorizing.
steps.memorize: Grade the decision, not the scoreboard.

steps.title: Expected value and the call formula
steps.feel: Every choice is a bet on the future. Expected value asks one thing: if I made this exact play a thousand times, would I come out ahead? If yes, do it and forget how this one hand lands.
steps.formula: EV = (chance you win) × (what you win) − (chance you lose) × (what you risk). Pick the action with the bigger number.
steps.memorize: Would I make this exact play 1,000 times?

steps.prompt: Pot $100. Villain shoves $50 (you are all-in if you call) and you have 40% equity. EV of calling?
Pot $200. Villain bets $100 all-in, you have 30% equity. EV of calling?
Pot $60. Villain bets $40 all-in, you have 25% equity. EV of calling?
options: -$5 (fold)
+$5 (call)

steps.title: One-line EV of a call
steps.feel: Sometimes you want the actual dollars, not just a percent. Take how often you win times the money you'd win, then subtract how often you lose times the money you're putting in. Positive number, call it.
steps.formula: EV = equity × (pot you win) − (1 − equity) × (your call). Break-even is exactly when this hits 0, which recovers the pot-odds rule.
steps.proof: Expected value averages outcomes by probability: win branch pays the final pot minus your call (net gain = pot-you-win), loss branch costs your call. EV = eq×gain − (1−eq)×call. Solve EV=0 and you land back on eq = call ÷ (pot + call).
steps.memorize: EV = equity × win − (1 − equity) × call.

steps.prompt: You have 30% equity. You can call $30 to win a final pot of $120. What is the EV of the call?
steps.explain: Winning nets the pot minus your call: 120 − 30 = $90. EV = 0.30 × 90 − 0.70 × 30 = 27 − 21 = +$6. Profitable call.

steps.prompt: You're all-in on the flop with a flush draw (9 outs, use 4/2 rule → 36%). Pot after your call is $73 and you had to call $24. What is the EV of the call?
steps.explain: Total-pot method (Gaines): 0.36 × $73 − $24 = $26.28 − $24 = $2.28. The 4/2 rule gives 9 × 4 = 36% equity on the flop, and the call is clearly +EV.

steps.title: The only calling formula you need
steps.feel: When someone bets, compare risk to reward. Paying $25 to win $90 means you only need to be right about 1 in 4 times. Think you're better than that here? Call.
steps.formula: Required equity = call ÷ (pot after your call). Anchors: ½-pot → 25%, ¾ → 30%, pot → 33%, 1.5× → 37.5%.
steps.memorize: Risk / (pot after your call) = the % you need.

steps.prompt: Villain bets three-quarters of the pot. Required equity to call?
Pot is $150 and villain bets $50. What equity do you need to call?
Villain bets the full pot. Required equity?
Villain overbets 1.5x the pot. Required equity?
Pot is $60, villain bets $30. What equity do you need to call?
steps.explain: You call $30 to win a final pot of $60 + $30 + $30 = $120. 30 ÷ 120 = 25%.

steps.prompt: Pot is $45, villain bets $15. What equity do you need to call?
steps.explain: Call $15 into a final pot of 45 + 15 + 15 = $75. 15 ÷ 75 = 20%. (A third-pot bet lays you 20%.)

steps.prompt: You're being offered 3-to-1 on a call. What equity do you need?

steps.title: The "% you must win" bet-size chart
steps.feel: When villain bets, you don't need to reduce anything to a ratio in your head. You already know how much you must win, just from how big the bet looks compared to the pot. A shove-into-a-small-pot needs you to win rarely; a big overbet needs you to win a lot. Memorize the handful of sizes you actually face and the number just pops out.
steps.formula: Break-even % to call = bet ÷ (pot-after-call). Gaines' shortcut table for common sizes: Villain bets 2× pot → win > 40% Pot-size bet → > 33% 2⁄​3 pot → > 28% ½ pot → > 25% 1⁄​3 pot → > 20% 1⁄​4 pot → > 16%
steps.proof: Take a ½-pot bet into $10. You call $5, and the pot after your call is $5 + $10 + $5 = $20. You must win 5 ÷ 20 = 25%. A 1⁄4-pot bet ($2.50 into $10): 2.5 ÷ (2.5 + 10 + 2.5) = 2.5 ÷ 15 ≈ 16%. Every row is just that same call ÷ final-pot arithmetic, precomputed so you never do it at the table.
steps.memorize: Pot bet = 33%, half-pot = 25%, third-pot = 20%, quarter-pot = 16%.

steps.prompt: Pot is $30. Villain bets $30 (a pot-size bet). What is your break-even calling %?
steps.explain: You call $30 and the pot after your call is $30 (his bet) + $30 (pot) + $30 (your call) = $90. Break-even = 30 ÷ 90 = 33%. That's the pot-size-bet row of Gaines' must-win chart.

steps.prompt: Pot is $40. Villain bets $10 (1⁄4 pot). Roughly what % must you win to call?
steps.explain: Call $10, final pot = 10 + 40 + 10 = $60. 10 ÷ 60 ≈ 16%. A 1⁄4-pot bet only needs ~16% equity — the cheapest call on the chart.

steps.title: Outs to equity: why the Rule of 4 and 2 works
steps.feel: Counting your chances is easy: each card that helps you is worth about 2%. Two cards are coming on the flop, so double it - roughly 4% an out. Nine cards to a flush is about 36%.
steps.formula: Flop (2 to come): outs × 4. Turn (1 to come): outs × 2. Shade down for "dirty" outs that might hand someone a better hand.
steps.memorize: Flop: outs x 4. Turn: outs x 2.

steps.prompt: How many outs to the flush, and your rough equity on the flop?
options: 9 outs, ~36%
4 outs, ~16%
9 outs, ~18%
8 outs, ~32%

steps.prompt: Open-ended straight draw on the turn. Equity to the river?
You need a Queen for Broadway (gutshot). Flop equity?
Flush draw AND open-ender (15 outs). Your quick Rule-of-4 estimate?
options: 60% (rule of 4; true ~54%)

steps.prompt: Flop, you have a flush draw (9 outs). Rough equity to the river?
steps.explain: Rule of 4 on the flop: 4 × 9 = 36%. (True figure is about 35%, so this is spot on.)

steps.prompt: Turn, you have an open-ended straight draw (8 outs). Rough equity to the river?
steps.explain: Rule of 2 on the turn: 2 × 8 = 16%. One card to come.

steps.prompt: Flop, you have a gutshot (4 outs). Rough equity to the river?

steps.title: Memorize the common draw counts
steps.feel: You shouldn't be counting cards one by one at the table — memorize the handful of shapes. A flush draw, a two-way straight, a gutshot, two overcards. Recognize the picture and the number pops out instantly.
steps.formula: Flush draw = 9 outs. Open-ended straight (OESD) = 8. Gutshot (inside) = 4. Two overcards = 6. Flush + open-ended combo ≈ 15. Set→boat/quads = 7. Pair→trips = 2.
steps.proof: Flush: 13 of a suit − 2 in hand − 2 on board = 9. OESD: two ranks complete it, 4 each = 8. Gutshot: one rank, 4 cards = 4. Overcards: 3 each of two ranks = 6. Combo: 9 flush + 8 straight − 2 shared = 15.
steps.memorize: Flush 9, OESD 8, gutshot 4, overcards 6.

steps.prompt: How many outs is a combo draw with a flush draw AND an open-ended straight draw (no shared cards double-counted)?
options: 17 outs
15 outs
12 outs
9 outs
steps.explain: 9 flush + 8 straight = 17, but 2 of the straight cards are your own suit and already counted in the flush, so 17 − 2 = 15 outs. Monster draw — often a coinflip or better.

steps.title: Discount the dirty outs
steps.feel: Not every out is real gold. Some outs pair the board and hand a bigger boat to your opponent, or complete a flush that beats you. A 'dirty' out looks like an out but often loses anyway. Shave a couple off before you multiply.
steps.formula: Effective outs = clean outs. Rough discounts: a card that also makes an obvious flush/straight for villain, or pairs a scary board, counts as roughly half an out. Then apply ×4 / ×2.
steps.proof: Equity from the Rule of 2/4 assumes hitting an out actually wins. If some fraction of the time hitting still loses, expected win-value per out drops by that fraction. Weighting a suspect out at ½ is just baking that loss probability straight into the count.
steps.memorize: If an out can lose, count it as half.

steps.prompt: You have 8 straight outs, but 2 of them also complete an obvious flush for villain (count each as half). Effective outs?
steps.explain: 6 clean outs + 2 dirty outs at ½ each = 6 + 1 = 7 effective outs. Discount before you multiply.

steps.title: Continue or fold = equity vs price
steps.feel: Two quick checks: how likely am I to hit, and what's the price? If your chance to improve beats the price, keep going. Big draws can chase; weak ones can't.
steps.formula: Continue if (draw equity from the Rule of 2 & 4) ≥ (the pot-odds price). Nut draws add implied odds; a bare draw on the turn usually can't chase.
steps.memorize: Equity beats the price -> continue.

steps.prompt: Flush draw (~36%). Villain bets half pot (you need 25%). Best play?
options: Fold - draws are behind
Call - equity clears the price
Check it back

steps.prompt: Turn: bare nut flush draw (~20%). Villain bets half pot (you need 25%). On raw odds?
options: Call - you have the nut flush draw
Fold - below the price
Raise as a pure bluff
Call - already priced in

steps.prompt: Turn gutshot (~9%). Villain bets three-quarters pot (you need 30%). Play?
options: Fold - far below the price
Call - you could hit Broadway
Raise
Call - implied odds cover it

steps.title: Count combinations
steps.feel: Stop guessing his one hand. Picture all the hands he'd play this way - he almost always has far more weak ones than monsters, so don't fold to the monster in your head.
steps.formula: Combos: pair = 6, suited = 4, offsuit = 12, any unpaired = 16. Every visible card removes some (a set with one card already out = 3 combos).
steps.memorize: Count the range in combos - monsters are rare.

steps.prompt: How many combos of A-K remain when one ace is already on the board?
A 7 is on the board. How many combos of the set 77 can villain have?
How many combinations of a specific suited hand, say A-K suited?
How many combinations of a specific offsuit hand, say A-J offsuit?
Before any cards are seen, how many combos of pocket aces (AA) are there?
steps.explain: A pair is C(4,2) = 6 combos. Every pocket pair starts with 6.

steps.prompt: Before any cards are seen, how many combos of ace-king (AK, any suits) are there?
steps.explain: An unpaired hand is 4 × 4 = 16 combos (4 suited + 12 offsuit).

steps.prompt: You hold the ace of spades. How many combos of AA can villain have?
steps.explain: Only 3 aces remain, so C(3,2) = 3 combos. Holding one card of a pair halves it from 6 to 3.

steps.prompt: Flop is K♠A♥3♦ (you hold neither an A nor a K). How many combos of AK does villain have?
steps.explain: AK is normally 4 × 4 = 16. But one Ace and one King are on the board, leaving 3 Aces and 3 Kings: 3 × 3 = 9 combos. Each exposed card of a rank knocks the unpaired-combo count down by multiplying the smaller remaining totals.

steps.prompt: Flop is K♣A♥3♦. How many combos of a set of 3s (33) can villain have?
steps.explain: A pocket pair is 6 combos, but one 3 is on the board. With three 3s left, the combos are 2 + 1 = 3. Removing one card of a paired rank always drops it from 6 to 3.

steps.title: Blockers are just subtraction
steps.feel: The cards in your hand are spies. If you're holding the ace of spades, he can't have the nut flush - so his big bet is more likely a bluff. Lean toward calling.
steps.formula: Holding a card from his value range subtracts those combos, so his bluff-share rises and your call (and your own bluff) improve.
steps.proof:
Holding a card that lives in villain's range deletes those combos. This swings close spots.

Hold the A♠ on a three-spade board: he cannot have the nut flush, so his value shrinks while his bluffs do not - both your call and your own bluff improve.
steps.memorize: Your cards block his - the nut-flush ace kills his nut flush.

steps.prompt: You hold the A-spades on this three-spade board when villain bets big. Effect on your decision?
options: Nothing - your cards do not matter
Lean fold - he has the flush
Lean call - you block his nut flushes
Always raise
steps.explain: Removing the A♠ cuts his nut-flush combos while leaving his bluffs untouched, so the bluff share of his range rises and your call moves toward +EV.

steps.title: How long until you know you are winning?
steps.feel: A losing night proves nothing. Poker is a tiny skill edge buried under huge luck each hand - it takes tens of thousands of hands for the skill to surface. Judge your decisions, never the scoreboard.
steps.formula: Hands to trust a win rate ≈ 400 × (SD ÷ win-rate)². At SD 100 and a 10 bb/100 edge, about 40,000 hands.
steps.memorize: A few sessions = noise; ~40k hands to know you're a winner.

steps.prompt: Win rate 10 bb/100, SD 100. Roughly how many hands before you can trust you are a winner?
You have lost 4 sessions in a row (~400 hands). What should you conclude about your play?
options: Drop down in stakes
Overhaul your preflop ranges
Almost nothing - it is well inside variance
You are a losing player

steps.prompt: Same SD of 100, but your edge is only 5 bb/100. Hands needed now?

steps.title: Coin Flips and Crushes: Living With Variance
steps.feel: Even when you get it in great, you lose sometimes. An 80/20 favorite still loses one hand in five. A coin flip is exactly what it sounds like — you will lose half. Getting it in as an 88% favorite still means one bad beat every eight or nine times. If losing a flip or an 80/20 tilts you, the game will grind you down before your edge ever shows up. Your job is to get the money in ahead; the cards decide the rest.
steps.formula:
How often the favorite still LOSES:
• Coin flip (52/48) → loses ≈ 1 in 2
• 80/20 (pair vs two unders, pair vs pair) → loses ≈ 1 in 5
• 88/12 (AA vs AK) → loses ≈ 1 in 8
steps.proof: Probability of losing is just 100% minus your equity. An 82% favorite loses 18% of the time = about 1 in 5.5. Run that spot 5 times and expecting to win all 5 is (0.82)⁵ ≈ 37% — so more than 6 times out of 10 you lose at least one. Over a session you will string flips and 80/20s together; the short-run outcomes are noisy even though the long-run edge is real. Variance is the price of admission — bankroll and mindset absorb it so your edge can compound.
steps.memorize: 80/20 loses 1 in 5. Flips lose half. Get it in ahead and let the math pay off over volume.

steps.prompt: You get it in as an 80/20 favorite five times in one session. Roughly how likely is it that you lose at least one?
options: About 5%
About 18%
About 40%
About 63%
steps.explain: Winning all five is (0.82)⁵ ≈ 0.37, so losing at least one is about 1 − 0.37 ≈ 63%. An 80/20 still loses ~1 in 5 individually, so across five spots a loss is more likely than not. Variance is normal — get the money in ahead and trust the volume.

steps.title: Risk of Ruin: your real chance of going broke, and how bankroll kills it
steps.feel:
You can be a long-term winner and still go broke, because winnings arrive in a jagged, streaky line, not a smooth ramp. 'Risk of ruin' is the probability that a run of bad luck wipes out your whole bankroll before your edge saves you — assuming you keep playing the same game forever. Two facts anchor everything: if the game is a loser, your risk of ruin is 100% no matter how much money you have; if the game is a winner, more bankroll drives the risk down fast — but never all the way to zero, because there is always some nightmare losing streak lurking.

The most important practical warning: risk of ruin assumes you leave all your winnings in the bankroll. The moment you start skimming profit off the top and keeping the bankroll flat, your true risk of ruin climbs back toward 100%. A bankroll you constantly draw down is a bankroll that will eventually break.
steps.formula: For roughly normal results (limit and no-limit ring games): R(b) = e^(−2μb ÷ σ²), where b is bankroll, μ is your win rate per hand/hour, and σ is the standard deviation of that same unit. More bankroll b, more edge μ → exponentially lower risk. Handy shorthand — the 'half-bankroll' (the size that gives exactly a 50% risk of ruin): b½ = (ln 2) ÷ α ≈ 0.693 ÷ α. Stack N half-bankrolls and your risk drops to (½)^N: one half-bankroll = 50%, two = 25%, three = 12.5%, and so on.
steps.proof: The whole model rests on one elegant property: the risk of ruin of a combined bankroll equals the product of the pieces, R(a+b) = R(a)·R(b). (Losing a 1000-unit roll means losing one 500-unit roll and then another independent 500-unit roll — so R(1000) = R(500)².) Taking logs turns the product into a sum, forcing R(x) to be a clean exponential R(x) = e^(−αx) for some constant α set by the game. Solving the master equation ⟨e^(−αx)⟩ = 1 for a normal distribution yields α = 2μ/σ², giving the boxed formula. One caution the authors stress: tournaments are heavily skewed (you can win 99 buy-ins but only ever lose 1), so the normal-distribution formula badly OVERstates their risk of ruin — for tournaments you must solve the master equation directly rather than plug into e^(−2μb/σ²).
steps.memorize: R(b) = e^(−2μb/σ²). Skim profits and risk → 100%. Half-bankroll = (ln2)/α; each one halves your ruin chance.

steps.prompt: A winning player computes that a $2,000 bankroll gives him a 50% risk of ruin in his game (so $2,000 is his 'half-bankroll'). Assuming roughly normal results, what is his risk of ruin with $6,000 — three half-bankrolls?
options: About 50% divided by 3 ≈ 17%
About 12.5% — (½)³
About 0%, since $6,000 is a huge cushion
Still 50% — bankroll size doesn't change the percentage
steps.explain: Because R(a+b) = R(a)·R(b), stacking N half-bankrolls gives risk (½)^N. Three half-bankrolls → (½)³ = 12.5%. The relationship is exponential, not linear — each additional half-bankroll HALVES your ruin chance rather than subtracting a fixed amount.

steps.prompt: A player keeps his bankroll fixed at $10,000, withdrawing every dollar of profit above that level to pay living expenses. Over an infinite horizon, what is his risk of ruin?
options: Lower than if he reinvested, because he's locking in profit
Roughly 5%, a comfortable safety margin
100% — a bankroll held flat by skimming will eventually break
It depends only on his win rate, not the withdrawals
steps.explain: Chen & Ankenman are emphatic here: risk of ruin assumes you leave winnings in to weather future downswings. If you skim all profit and hold the roll flat, some path of bad variance eventually exhausts it — the risk of ruin of a bankroll maintained at a fixed level is 1 (100%). Any withdrawal, even from profit, raises risk.

steps.title: Kelly betting and choosing which stakes to play
steps.feel:
You have an edge and a bankroll and you want it to grow as fast as possible. Betting your whole roll on every +EV spot maximizes dollar-EV but guarantees you go broke the first time you lose. Betting a trickle grows too slowly. Kelly is the size in between that grows a bankroll the fastest over the long run. The trick is that you should not care about maximizing dollars won on one bet — you should maximize the logarithm of your bankroll, because a dollar matters more when you are poor than when you are rich (losing half your roll hurts as much as doubling it helps).

The clean result for an even-money bet: wager the same percentage of your bankroll as your percentage edge. A 3% edge → bet 3% of your roll. This scales automatically: win and your next bet is bigger, lose and it shrinks, so pure Kelly can never fully bust. Chen & Ankenman also use this to answer a practical grinder's question — when should I move up to a bigger, swingier game?
steps.formula: Kelly utility: U(x) = ln x (maximize the log of the bankroll, not raw dollars). For an even-money bet, bet fraction = your edge (3% edge → bet 3% of bankroll). Game-selection cutoff (game 1 = bigger/swingier, game 2 = smaller): play the bigger game once your bankroll exceeds c ≈ (σ₁² − σ₂²) ÷ [2(μ₁ − μ₂)]. Above c the extra win rate is worth the extra variance; below c, stay small.
steps.proof: For a 3% edge at even money with bankroll B, maximize ⟨U⟩ = 0.515·ln(B+x) + 0.485·ln(B−x) over the bet x. Setting the derivative to zero gives 0.515/(B+x) = 0.485/(B−x), which solves to x = 0.03B — exactly 3% of the roll. For game selection, the change in log-utility from playing a game is approximately μ/B − (μ²+σ²)/(2B²); dropping the tiny μ² term (win rates are minuscule next to variance in poker) and setting the two games' utilities equal gives the cutoff c ≈ (σ₁²−σ₂²)/(2(μ₁−μ₂)). Example from the book: $20-40 holdem ($35/hr, σ=$400) vs $40-80 ($60/hr, σ=$800) → move up once your bankroll passes about $19,295. The caution: because tournaments have outcomes as big as the whole bankroll, this Taylor-series shortcut breaks down there — use it only for ring games.
steps.memorize: Kelly = maximize ln(bankroll). Even-money: bet your edge% of your roll. Move up once bankroll > (σ₁²−σ₂²)/(2Δμ).

steps.prompt: A sports bettor has a genuine 3% edge on even-money bets and a $5,000 bankroll. Under the Kelly criterion, what should he bet?
options: His whole $5,000, since every bet is +EV
$150 — 3% of his bankroll, matching his edge
A flat $50 to stay safe
$2,500 — half his roll, to grow fast without busting
steps.explain: For even-money bets, Kelly says bet the same fraction of your bankroll as your percentage edge: a 3% edge → 3% of $5,000 = $150. Betting the whole roll maximizes single-bet dollar-EV but guarantees eventual ruin; Kelly maximizes long-run growth rate by maximizing ln(bankroll), and it rescales after every win or loss.

steps.title: You profit from their mistakes
steps.feel: You don't make money from good cards - you make it from other people's bad decisions. The most profitable choice you make all night is which table you sit at.
steps.formula: Win rate = (their mistakes) − (your mistakes) − rake. Maximize the first, minimize the rest, and pick soft tables.
steps.memorize: Money = their mistakes. Game-select ruthlessly.

steps.prompt: Bankroll aside: tight regs at $1/$2, or drunk recreationals at $2/$5 playing deep. Higher EV?
options: $1/$2 regs - safer
Identical - it cancels out
Whichever has more players
$2/$5 recs - bigger stakes AND bigger mistakes
steps.explain: Bigger blinds, worse opponents, and deep stacks all scale the same profit source. Game quality beats stake level.

steps.title: The Matchup Map: Flips vs. Crushes
steps.feel: When your money goes in preflop, you are almost always in one of two worlds: a coin flip or a crush. AK against a small pair is a flip — you win about half the time. But AK against a bigger pair like aces? You are drowning. Learn to feel the difference the instant the chips go in: are you flipping, or are you crushed?
steps.formula:
Memorize these seven:
• AK vs a smaller pair (88) ≈ 52% / 48% — a flip
• AK vs QQ or JJ ≈ 43% / 57% — still close to a flip
• AK vs AA or KK ≈ 12% — crushed
• Dominated ace (A9 vs AK) ≈ 25–30%
• Pair vs two lower cards (88 vs 76) ≈ 82% / 18%
• Pair vs pair (QQ vs 88) ≈ 82% / 18% — the 80/20
• Flop a set with a pocket pair ≈ 11.8% (≈ 1 in 8.5)
steps.proof: Two unpaired overcards (AK) versus a pair get roughly 6 outs — three aces and three kings — hitting on the flop, turn, or river. Six outs over five cards lands near 50%, which is why overcards vs. a pair is essentially a flip. Against QQ/JJ your outs are the same six, but villain has two extra live cards to make a set or a straight, dragging you to ≈ 43%. Against AA/KK you are dominated: your ace or king outs are half-dead (villain holds some of them) and you rely on runner-runner or a lucky pair, collapsing you to ≈ 12%. Domination — sharing a card with a stronger holding — is what turns a flip into a crush.
steps.memorize: Overcards vs. a pair = a flip (52%). Overcards vs. a BIGGER pair = crushed (12%).

steps.prompt: You get all-in preflop with A♠K♦ against 8♣8♥. Roughly what is your equity?
options: About 12%
About 30%
About 52%
About 75%
steps.explain: Two overcards vs. a smaller pair is the classic coin flip. AK has about six outs (three aces, three kings) across five cards, landing near 50%. Actual equity is ≈ 52% / 48% in AK's favor — call it a flip.

steps.prompt: You shove A♥K♥ and get snapped by K♠K♣. How bad is it?
options: You're a slight favorite, ~55%
It's a flip, ~50%
You're crushed, ~12%
You're a small dog, ~40%
steps.explain: This is domination. One of your king outs is dead (villain holds two kings), leaving mainly your three aces plus runner-runner help. That collapses your equity to about 12%. AKs vs AA is ≈ 13% — same crushed neighborhood. Overcards vs. a BIGGER pair is a crush, not a flip.

steps.prompt: Q♦Q♠ is all-in against 8♥8♦. What are the approximate equities?
options: About 82% / 18%
About 65% / 35%
About 95% / 5%
steps.explain: Pair over pair is the famous 80/20. QQ wins about 82%, 88 about 18%. The smaller pair essentially needs to flop its set (~12%) or catch a lucky straight/backdoor. Same 82/18 shape as a pair vs. two lower cards.

steps.prompt: 8♠8♣ is all-in against 7♥6♥ (two lower, connected cards). Approximate equity for the pair?
options: About 55%
About 68%
About 82%
About 95%
steps.explain: A pair vs. two lower unpaired cards is ≈ 82% / 18%. The suited connector adds a little live equity (straights and flushes), but the made pair is a massive favorite. Same neighborhood as pair-vs-pair 80/20.

steps.prompt: You raise A♦K♦ and a tight player calls off with only QQ. What's your equity in that spot?
options: About 12%
About 43%
About 57%
About 70%
steps.explain: AK vs QQ (or JJ) is ≈ 43% / 57% — close to a flip but you're the slight dog. Your six overcard outs are all live, but villain can also improve to a set. This is the 'equity when called' lesson: against a tight range you're often a small underdog, not the favorite AK feels like.

steps.title: Equity When Called
steps.feel: The number that actually matters is not your equity against a random hand — it is your equity against the hands that call you. When you shove AK and a tight player snaps, ask: what does he have? If it is only QQ+ and AK, you are often a small dog or crushed, not the favorite you imagined. Hand selection is really the question: when I get called, what am I up against?
steps.formula:
Against a typical QQ+ / AK calling range you are roughly a coin flip at best and crushed at worst:
• vs AA/KK ≈ 12%
• vs QQ ≈ 43%
• vs AK ≈ split (tie)
Blend those and AK is a slight dog to a tight snap-call — good equity, but not the lock it feels like.
steps.proof: Equity-when-called weights each outcome by how often villain shows up with it. If a player calls with AA, KK, QQ, and AK, then two of those four crush you (AA, KK ≈ 12%), one is a near-flip (QQ ≈ 43%), and one is a tie (AK, split). Average over that range and AK sits below 50% — you are calling off as the underdog. The lesson: a hand's raw strength is meaningless until you fix it against the specific range that continues. Fold equity (folds you generate) is what makes shoving AK profitable, not the showdown equity.
steps.memorize: Your real equity = equity vs. the hands that CALL, not vs. a random hand.

steps.title: Set-Mining Probability and Price
steps.feel: You call a raise with a small pocket pair hoping to flop a set — three of a kind — and stack someone. It works, but not often. You flop your set only about one time in eight and a half. So set-mining is cheap-lottery-ticket poker: the ticket must be cheap and the jackpot must be huge, or you are lighting money on fire.
steps.formula:
Flop a set with a pocket pair ≈ 11.8% (about 1 in 8.5).
Rule of thumb: you need roughly 15× implied odds — the pot you can win should be about 15 times the price to call — before set-mining pays.
steps.proof: You hold two of the four cards of your rank, so 2 of the 50 unseen cards complete your set. The chance you miss all three flop cards is (48/50)(47/49)(46/48) ≈ 0.882, so you hit ≈ 11.8%. That is close to 1 in 8.5. Because you win the big pot only ~12% of the time, the ~7 losing attempts must be paid for by the one that hits — hence the ~15× implied-odds guideline. If the effective stacks are shallow, the jackpot is too small and the call loses.
steps.memorize: Flop a set ≈ 12% (1 in 8.5) → only call to set-mine with ~15× the price behind.

steps.prompt: You call with 5♣5♦ purely to flop a set. How often do you flop it?
options: About 4%
About 12%
About 20%
About 33%
steps.explain: Only 2 of the 50 unseen cards give you a set. Missing all three flop cards is (48/50)(47/49)(46/48) ≈ 88.2%, so you hit ≈ 11.8% — about 1 in 8.5. That is why you want roughly 15× implied odds before set-mining.

steps.title: Weighted equity vs a range + the mental-slider shortcut
steps.feel: Your equity against a single hand is easy. Against a range it's a weighted average — the hands villain has more combos of pull the number toward their equity. Do it exactly away from the table; at the table, picture a slider between your worst-case and best-case equity and drag it toward whichever group has more combos.
steps.formula:
Exact (4 steps, Gaines): 1) your equity vs each hand, 2) × that hand's combos, 3) sum, 4) ÷ total combos.
Slider shortcut: place the answer between the low and high equity, weighted by combo count. To go ¾ of the way from A to B: A + (B − A) ÷ 4 ... actually B − (B − A)÷4.
steps.proof: You're all-in vs 78 (16 combos, you have 66%), 55 (3 combos, 9%) and 66 (3 combos, 9%). Weighted: (0.66×16 + 0.09×3 + 0.09×3) ÷ 22 = (10.56 + 0.27 + 0.27) ÷ 22 = 11.1 ÷ 22 ≈ 50%. Sets are 6 ÷ 22 ≈ 25% of his range, so ¾ of the time you have 66% and ¼ you have 9%. Slider check: 66 − 9 = 57, 57 ÷ 4 ≈ 14, 66 − 14 = 52. About 50% either way — an easy call needing only 33%.
steps.memorize: Weight each hand's equity by its combos; slide toward the group with more combos.

steps.prompt: You have 60% equity vs one hand (16 combos) and 20% equity vs another (4 combos). What is your weighted equity vs the whole range?
steps.explain: (0.60 × 16 + 0.20 × 4) ÷ 20 = (9.6 + 0.8) ÷ 20 = 10.4 ÷ 20 = 52%. The 16-combo hand dominates the average, so you land near its equity.

steps.title: Break-even bluff frequency
steps.feel: When you fire a bluff you're risking your bet to steal the pot. The question is simple: how often does villain have to fold for this to just break even? Bigger bets risk more, so they need to work more often.
steps.formula: Fold% needed = risk ÷ (risk + reward) = bet ÷ (bet + pot). For a bet of size s×pot: alpha = s ÷ (1 + s). Half-pot needs 33%, pot-size needs 50%, 2× pot needs 67%.
steps.proof: Bluff EV = fold%×(pot) − (1−fold%)×(bet), taking villain's fold as an automatic win of the current pot and a called bluff as losing your bet. Set to zero: fold% = bet ÷ (bet + pot). Substituting bet = s×pot gives s ÷ (1+s).
steps.memorize: Bluff must work bet ÷ (bet + pot) of the time.

steps.prompt: You bet $50 into a $100 pot as a bluff. How often must villain fold to break even?
steps.explain: Fold% = bet ÷ (bet + pot) = 50 ÷ (50 + 100) = 50 ÷ 150 = 33%. A half-pot bluff needs to work 1 in 3.

steps.prompt: You bet $100 into a $100 pot as a bluff. How often must villain fold to break even?
steps.explain: 100 ÷ (100 + 100) = 50%. A pot-size bluff needs to work half the time.

steps.prompt: You shove $200 into a $100 pot (2× pot) as a bluff. Break-even fold frequency?
steps.explain: alpha = s ÷ (1+s) with s = 2: 2 ÷ 3 = 67%. Big overbets must work often.

steps.title: One reward:risk table for bluffing AND calling (Gaines)
steps.feel: Bluffing and calling are the same math wearing different clothes: both are risking some chips to win some chips. When you bluff, you ask "how often must villain fold?" When you call, you ask "how often must I win?" The percentage comes from the exact same reward-to-risk ratio, so you only have to learn one thing.
steps.formula:
Both use x ÷ (x + y). Gaines' unified table (x = your risk):
Risk x to win 0.5x (pot-size raise) → need 67%
Risk x to win 0.8x (½-pot raise) → need 55%
Risk x to win x (pot bet as bluff) → need 50%
Risk x to win 1.5x (call a 2× pot bet) → need 40%
Risk x to win 2x (pot bet / call a pot bet) → need 33%
Risk x to win 3x (1⁄3 pot bet / call a ½ pot) → need 25%
steps.proof: A pot-size bluff into $10: you risk $10 to win the $10 pot, so x = y, and 10 ÷ 20 = 50% — villain must fold more than half the time. Now flip it: villain bets that same pot and you're the caller. You risk $10 to win $20 (his bet plus the pot), so 10 ÷ 30 = 33%. The caller always needs a lower % because by the time action reaches him the pot is bigger. In hold'em you never risk x to win x as a caller — the posted blinds guarantee the pot is always bigger than your call.
steps.memorize: Same x÷(x+y): bluffer's fold% and caller's win% are the same coin, different side.

steps.prompt: Pot is $20 and you fire a pot-size bluff of $20. How often must villain fold for your bluff to break even?
steps.explain: Bluff uses x ÷ (x + y) with x = your bet: 20 ÷ (20 + 20) = 50%. Risking x to win x always needs a 50% fold. Anything more than 50% and the bluff prints.

steps.prompt: You make a pot-size RAISE (not bet) — risking x to win about 0.5x. How often must villain fold to break even?
steps.explain: A pot-size raise puts far more in than a pot-size bet, so you win only ~0.5x for your x risked: x ÷ (x + 0.5x) = 1 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 67%. That's why raise-bluffs need villain to fold much more often than bet-bluffs.

steps.title: MDF and Alpha: One Coin, Two Sides
steps.feel: If you fold too much when facing a bet, a thinking opponent can print money betting any two cards. To stop that, you must defend a minimum share of your range. The flip side is how often a balanced bettor is bluffing. These aren't two rules to memorize — they're the same indifference point seen from each seat.
steps.formula:
Facing a bet of size s (= bet ÷ pot): you must defend 1/(1+s) of your range — that's MDF (half-pot s=½ → defend ⅔; pot s=1 → defend ½). The share you may fold is alpha = s/(1+s) = 1 − MDF (half-pot → fold ⅓; pot → fold ½).

A different number: the bettor's balanced bluff share of a betting range = s/(1+2s) — half-pot → ¼ bluffs (3:1 value:bluff), pot → ⅓ bluffs (2:1).
steps.proof:
MDF: the bettor risks s to win the pot (1 unit). A pure bluff profits if you fold more than fold-equity break-even: bluff EV = fold% × 1 − call% × s = 0 → fold% = s/(1+s), so defend% = 1/(1+s). Alpha: for you to be indifferent to calling with a bluff-catcher, the bettor's value-to-bluff mix must make your call worth 0. Their bluff frequency that achieves this is s/(1+s) of their betting range. Same s, same fraction — the defender's fold% equals the bettor's bluff%.

The live edge: real players fold far more (nits) or far less (stations) than MDF demands — that gap is your profit.
Correction. MDF is a benchmark against an opponent whose bluffing you cannot read, not a rule. Live players under-bluff big bets and rivers, so against most of them you should fold more than MDF says (Acevedo, Modern Poker Theory p. 603). Against a maniac, defend more.
steps.memorize: MDF = 1/(1+s) defend; alpha = s/(1+s) fold. Bluff share of your bets = s/(1+2s): ¼ at half-pot, ⅓ at pot.

steps.prompt: Villain bets $50 into a $100 pot. What is your Minimum Defense Frequency (how much of your range to continue)?
steps.explain: MDF = pot ÷ (pot + bet) = 100 ÷ (100 + 50) = 100 ÷ 150 = 67%. Fold more than a third and a pure bluff prints.

steps.prompt: Villain bets $100 into a $100 pot. What is your MDF?
steps.explain: MDF = 100 ÷ (100 + 100) = 50%. Against a pot-size bet you defend half your range in theory.

steps.prompt: Villain makes a pot-sized bet on the river. What fraction of your range must you defend (call or raise) to avoid being exploited by any-two-card bluffs?
options: ⅓
½
⅔
All of it
steps.explain: MDF = 1/(1+s) with s = 1 for a pot-sized bet. 1/(1+1) = ½. Defend at least half your range. Fold more and a bluff of any two cards profits: fold ≥ s/(1+s) = ½ makes pure bluffing free money.

steps.prompt: A perfectly balanced player bets half-pot on the river. Of the hands in that betting range, what share should be bluffs?
options: ¼
⅓
½
⅔
steps.explain: Alpha = s/(1+s) with s = ½. (½)/(1 + ½) = (½)/(1½) = ⅓. So one third bluffs, two thirds value. That mix makes your bluff-catcher exactly indifferent — calling and folding both break even against it.

steps.prompt: A known nit bets $50 into $100. Theory says defend 67%, but he only bluffs 5% of the time. Best live adjustment?
options: Defend exactly 67% to stay balanced
Overfold — fold weak hands, he almost never bluffs
Raise all your bluff-catchers
Call every single hand
steps.explain: MDF assumes a balanced bluffer. A nit who never bluffs makes your bluff-catchers worthless — overfold and only continue with real hands. Ignoring MDF here is the exploit.

steps.title: Indifference in One Breath
steps.feel: A balanced strategy doesn't try to win every hand — it tries to make your opponent's decision not matter. You bluff and value-bet in a ratio, or defend and fold in a ratio, so precisely that their alternative choice earns exactly zero. When they're indifferent, they can't exploit you no matter which button they push.
steps.formula: Set the frequency so opponent EV(action A) = EV(action B). Bettor picks a bluff/value mix that makes your bluff-catcher break even; defender folds/calls at a rate that makes opponent's bluff break even.
steps.proof: Two options for the opponent have EVs that depend on your frequency f. Balance means choosing f so EV_A(f) = EV_B(f). At that f the opponent is indifferent — every mixed response yields the same value, so no deviation gains. This is a Nash equilibrium property: your mixing rate is tuned to the payoffs of their choices, not to your own hand. That's why the same s produces both MDF and alpha — both come from setting an opponent's option to zero EV.
steps.memorize: Balance = pick a frequency that makes the opponent's other option worth 0.

steps.title: Combos and pot odds are one tool
steps.feel: You don't need to read souls. A bluff-catcher only beats bluffs, so ask one thing: does this guy bluff more often than my price? Live players almost never bluff enough - so against big bets, when in doubt, fold.
steps.formula: Call if his bluff-share ≥ bet ÷ (pot + 2×bet). Defend at least MDF = pot ÷ (pot + bet) of your range so he can't profit by bluffing any two cards.
steps.memorize: Call only if he bluffs more than your price. Live: he doesn't - fold more.

steps.prompt: River, flush came in. Villain bets half pot (need 25%). You count 12 value combos and 8 bluffs. Call?
options: Fold - he usually has it
Call - the bluff share beats the price
Fold - you need 50%
Cannot tell

steps.prompt: Same board, villain bets three-quarters pot (need 30%), you read 15 value combos and 5 bluffs. Call?
options: Call - 25% is plenty
Fold - the bluff share is under the price
Call - you block him
Raise

steps.prompt: On the river you're value-betting. Villain will call with 12 combos that you beat and 10 combos that beat you. Is betting for value correct?
options: Yes — worse hands call more than half the time
No — too many better hands call
It's exactly break-even
Only if you have the nuts
steps.explain: Worse-hand calls = 12 ÷ 22 ≈ 55%, which is over the 50% threshold, so the value bet is +EV. Per $1: 2(0.55) − 1 = +$0.10. Count his CALLING range, not his whole range.

steps.title: Semi-bluff shove: the 3-step fold-equity shortcut (Gaines)
steps.feel: A semi-bluff shove wins two ways: villain folds, or he calls and you hit. Because you have real equity when called, you aren't truly risking your whole shove — you get some of it back. Discount your bet by your share of the final pot, then just read the reward:risk ratio like any bluff.
steps.formula:
Step 1: final all-in pot × your equity when called.
Step 2: your shove − that number = what you're truly risking.
Step 3: compare true-risk : pot with the reward:risk table for the fold% needed.
steps.proof: Pot is $39, you shove $27, your equity when called ≈ 24%. Final pot if called ≈ $81, and 81 × 0.24 ≈ $20 comes back to you. True risk = $27 − $20 = $7, to win the $39 pot. That's 7 ÷ 46 ≈ 15% — villain only needs to fold about 15% for the shove to profit, vs a raw 40% if you ignored your equity. That's the whole power of a semi-bluff: showdown equity slashes the fold% you need.
steps.memorize: Subtract (final pot × your equity) from your bet — that's your real risk before reading the ratio.

steps.prompt: Pot is $40, you shove $28, and your equity when called is 25%. Final all-in pot is $96. Using Gaines' shortcut, how much are you truly risking?
steps.explain: Step 1: 96 × 0.25 = $24 comes back to you when called. Step 2: 28 − 24 = $4 true risk. You're really risking just $4 to win the $40 pot, so villain barely needs to fold for the semi-bluff to profit.

steps.title: At $1/$2 the action is face-up
steps.feel: Low-stakes players hand you their cards through their bets. A limp or a flat means "not strong." A sudden big bet or raise from a quiet player means "I've got it" - believe them and fold.
steps.formula: Limps/flats = capped (rarely the nuts). Passive player + big bet = value. So value-bet them thin and bluff them rarely.
steps.proof:
Live players do not balance, so the line leaks the bucket:

Limp or flat-call = capped (rarely AA-QQ). A passive player suddenly betting or raising big = nutted; believe it.

Exploit: value-bet them relentlessly and fold to their rare aggression - the opposite of the balanced play MDF assumes.
steps.memorize: Their line leaks their hand - believe the big bets.

steps.prompt: A passive rec who limp-called preflop now bets big into three players on the river. His range?
options: A wide bluffing range - call light
Exactly a flush draw
Random - no read
Nutted - fold everything but a monster
steps.explain: A face-up passive player does not fire big into a crowd without the goods. Believe it and fold your one pair.

steps.title: Always a Repeated Game; Never Play Dominated
steps.feel: "I'll never see this guy again, so who cares if I'm balanced" is a trap. Every stranger is a fresh sample from the same player pool, and unbalanced lines get punished across thousands of hands even if not this one. Two rules follow: don't get sloppy against one-offs, and never take a dominated action — one that is always at least as bad as a different choice you had.
steps.formula: Dominated = for every opponent response, action X earns ≤ action Y (and sometimes less). Then X is never correct. Examples: open-limping (raising or folding dominates it); bluff-raising a hand you could just call as a bluff; calling a spot that is a clear raise-or-fold.
steps.proof: Formally, strategy X is weakly dominated by Y if payoff(Y, o) ≥ payoff(X, o) for all opponent strategies o, strict for some o. A rational solution never uses a strictly dominated action, and equilibrium play discards weakly dominated ones too. Open-limping the SB is the classic case: raising builds a pot when ahead and can win it now, folding cuts losses — limping captures neither the fold equity of a raise nor the discipline of a fold, so some better action exists against every opponent. Over a repeated game these tiny leaks compound into a measurable loss rate.
steps.memorize: One-offs are pool samples — stay balanced; and never pick an action beaten by another for free.

steps.prompt: You're first to act preflop in the small blind, folded to you, holding a marginal hand. Which of these is a DOMINATED action you should essentially never take?
options: Raising to build a pot and take the blinds now
Folding to cut losses
Open-limping (just calling the big blind)
Choosing between raise and fold based on the hand
steps.explain: Open-limping is dominated: against every opponent response, either raising (adds fold equity and initiative) or folding (avoids a bad spot out of position) does at least as well. Limping captures neither, so a better action always exists — that's the definition of dominated. Raise-or-fold is the correct SB framework.

steps.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Poker
steps.feel: The whole game in one sentence: you profit from what your opponents don't know.
steps.formula: Sklansky / The Theory of Poker (Ch. 3): “Every time you play a hand differently from the way you would have played it if you could see all your opponents’ cards, they gain; and every time you play your hand the same way you would have played it if you could see all their cards, they lose. Conversely, every time opponents play their hands differently from the way they would have if they could see all your cards, you gain; and every time they play their hands the same way they would have played if they could see all your cards, you lose.”
steps.proof: Poker is a game of incomplete information — that’s the only reason it’s a game at all. If everyone’s cards were face up, there’d be one mathematically correct play every street and no edge to be had. Your entire long-run win comes from inducing your opponents to deviate from the play they’d make with full information, while you play as close to the full-information line as you can. Sklansky’s two goals fall out of this directly: (1) read hands accurately so YOU make fewer theorem mistakes, and (2) play deceptively so THEY make more. A subtle point he stresses: an opponent who ‘correctly’ calls with a pair of aces against your revealed pat flush is still making a theorem mistake — not playing badly, but playing differently than he would with X-ray vision. That gain is real even on hands you lose.
steps.memorize: You get paid for their mistakes, not your cards. Every chip you win long-term traces to a spot where an opponent played differently than they would with your cards face up.

callouts.text: Reframe every losing pot: if the opponent would have folded seeing your cards but called anyway, you WON that decision even though you lost the chips. Sklansky says derive satisfaction from it — those calls are your edge.

steps.prompt: Sklansky's Fundamental Theorem of Poker (Ch. 3): you bet, an opponent who is a 5-to-1 underdog CALLS getting only 3-to-1 pot odds, and then draws out to beat you. According to Sklansky, what happened on that hand?
options: You got unlucky and made a bad bet — the result proves it
You gained on the decision (his call was a theorem mistake) even though you lost the pot
It was neutral EV since he ended up winning the chips
You should have checked to avoid giving him the chance to draw out
steps.explain: Sklansky is explicit: any time an opponent plays differently than he would seeing your cards — here, calling with the worst of it at 3-to-1 as a 5-to-1 dog — you GAIN, regardless of the actual card that falls. ‘His play is incorrect because it has negative expectation, and you gain any time he makes it.’ You should be happy when it happens. Grading by the chips (option A/C) is the tilt error the theorem exists to cure.

steps.title: Effective Odds (and Implied / Reverse Implied)
steps.feel: Your draw's true price isn't the bet in front of you — it's every bet you'll pay to see it through.
steps.formula: Sklansky / The Theory of Poker (Ch. 6–7). Effective odds = total you win if you make your hand : total you must invest across all remaining streets to get there — not just the current bet. Implied odds = (total expected win when your card hits) : (present cost of the call), counting money you’ll extract on later streets. Reverse implied odds = the mirror: when you likely have the best hand now but can only be beaten, you win little more if ahead yet pay off more if behind, so your true odds are much WORSE than the pot shows.
steps.proof: Sklansky’s example: $10-$20 hold’em, you flop a flush draw (≈1¾-to-1 over two cards) with $20 in the pot and one $10 bet to you. Naive pot odds say 3-to-1, easy call. But to see BOTH cards you’ll call $10 now and likely $20 on the turn — $30 total to win the $30 there now plus maybe $20 more = $50. That’s 50-to-30 ≈ 1⅔-to-1, and your draw is worse than that. It’s a losing call. Compute effective odds by adding every call you’ll make to the river, then compare to the total you’ll win. Implied odds swing it the other way: a small pair in the hole is ≈8-to-1 to flop a set but worth playing even at 5-to-1 pot odds because the set wins big future bets (he cites ≈150-to-10). Reverse implied odds (his AA on a 7♦-8♦-T♦ flop): “you’re not getting 70-to-20, you’re getting closer to 70-to-60” because a worse hand won’t pay you and a better hand will keep betting.
steps.memorize: Price your draw over the WHOLE hand: effective odds = total win ÷ total to invest. Draws to the nuts get implied-odds discounts; marginal made hands that can only be beaten pay the reverse-implied tax.

callouts.text: The classic mistake Sklansky names: comparing your multi-street draw percentage to the pot odds RIGHT NOW. You’ll owe more money on later streets — the pot odds worsen as you go, so use effective odds.

steps.prompt: $10-$20 hold'em. You flop a bare flush draw (about 1¾-to-1 to hit over two cards), there's $20 in the pot, and your single opponent bets $10. You intend to draw all the way to the river if needed. Per Sklansky's effective-odds analysis, is calling the flop bet correct?
options: Yes — you're getting 3-to-1 pot odds and you're only 1¾-to-1, easy call
Yes — flush draws are always worth one card at these prices
No — counting the $20 you'll also owe on the turn, you're really getting about 1⅔-to-1 to make a hand you're worse than that to complete
No — you can never call a bet as an underdog to the current best hand
steps.explain: This is Sklansky's exact effective-odds example. The 3-to-1 ‘pot odds’ are an illusion because you must call $10 now AND ~$20 on the turn to see the river — $30 invested to win the $30 there plus maybe $20 later = 50-to-30 ≈ 1⅔-to-1. Since your draw is worse than 1⅔-to-1, it's a negative-expectation call. The naive comparison in option A is precisely ‘the classic mistake’ he warns against. (A semi-bluff raise, or a fold, beats calling here.)

steps.prompt: Sklansky's semi-bluff arithmetic (Ch. 11): $60 pot, one card to come, you hold a hand worth ~30% to win. You compare checking-and-hoping to betting $20. He shows betting is correct. What is the SPECIFIC reason a $20 semi-bluff beats both a pure bluff and a pure value bet here?
options: Because a $20 pure bluff alone is +EV at these pot odds
Because you're a favorite to win the pot at showdown
Because neither the fold equity alone nor the pot-equity alone is enough, but combined (win now when they fold, or outdraw them when called) it clears +EV
Because betting always beats checking when you have any draw
steps.explain: Sklansky's point: a pure bluff getting 3-to-1 with one win in five is bad, and value-betting a 30% hand (‘betting only for value’ as a 7-to-3 dog) is also bad — but the COMBINATION makes it profitable. His 100-hand math: checking wins $1,800; semi-bluffing wins ~$2,000 (fold 20% for $1,200, plus +$800 net when called). ‘The combination of the two possibilities... makes a semi-bluff bet not just a good play but a mandatory one.’

steps.prompt: You flop the probable best hand in a MEDIUM-sized pot with more cards to come, and you're fairly sure a worse hand will fold if you bet. By Sklansky's free-card logic (Ch. 8/10), what's the general rule and why?
options: Check to induce action later, since betting only folds out worse hands
Bet anyway — giving a free card risks the whole pot, and that catastrophe outweighs the one bet you might save
Check because you gain more through deception in every medium pot
Bet only if you're certain to be called by a worse hand
steps.explain: Sklansky's ranking of mistakes: losing the pot is a catastrophe, losing one bet is not. Giving a free card hands opponents 'infinite odds' to outdraw you and can cost the whole pot; betting into a better hand costs at most one bet. So with the probable best hand you almost always bet. Checking (deception) is right only with a tiny pot, a planned check-raise, or a hand so strong it's barely outdrawable — not routinely in a medium pot.

steps.prompt: Sklansky's 'Analyzing the Cost of a Mistake' (Ch. 24), razz version: probability says calling your opponent's river bet is the correct play 55% of the time and raising is correct only 45% of the time. Sklansky says the best play is to RAISE. Why would you choose the play that's right LESS often?
options: Because raising is more aggressive and aggression is always best
Because when calling is wrong (45%) the cost is severe, while when raising is wrong (55%) the cost is only slight — weight the downside, not just the frequency
Because you're actually a favorite when you raise
Because the pot odds force a raise regardless of hand strength
steps.explain: This is Sklansky's cost-of-a-mistake principle: when one alternative has only slightly bad consequences when wrong and the other has terrible consequences when wrong, you may correctly choose the first even if it's slightly less often 'right.' Here a mistaken call (opponent made his 8,7) barely hurts because you still outdraw him often, while a mistaken fold-to... rather a wrong raise is only slightly wrong — so raise. Grade by expected COST, echoing the Sklansky-bucks idea of judging decisions by EV, not results.

steps.title: The Gap Concept
steps.feel: You need a stronger hand to CALL a raise than you'd need to OPEN one yourself.
steps.formula: Sklansky, The Gap Concept (from Tournament Poker for Advanced Players — not The Theory of Poker, though it’s pure Sklansky): there is a ‘gap’ between the hand strength required to open the pot with a raise and the (greater) strength required to call someone else’s raise. A raiser has already announced strength; to call you must beat that range, so you need more.
steps.proof: When you open first-in, you can win the pot two ways — everyone folds, or you win the showdown — so marginal hands like KJ or a small pair are fine as opens. When someone has already raised, the fold-equity path is largely gone and you’re facing a hand that voluntarily represented strength; a call with that same KJ is now dominated too often. Hence the gap: raise-first hands ≠ call-a-raise hands, and the tougher/more-solid the raiser, the wider the gap. Practically it means (1) being the aggressor (opening) is worth far more than calling, and (2) if your hand isn’t strong enough to reraise or comfortably call, folding to a raise is routine even with hands you’d happily have opened. This is the tournament-era companion to the FTOP: seize first-in aggression, respect declared strength.
steps.memorize: Open-raising range > calling-a-raise range. The gap is your reason to be the raiser, not the caller — and to fold decent hands to strength.

callouts.text: ‘But I’d have raised this hand’ is not a reason to call a raise with it. That’s exactly the gap — losing your fold-equity and running into a hand that chose to bet means you need more, not the same.

steps.prompt: The Gap Concept (Sklansky, Tournament Poker for Advanced Players): you'd happily OPEN-raise with a hand like KJ from your seat. A solid player in front of you raises first. By the Gap Concept, should you call the raise with that same KJ?
options: Yes — if it's good enough to raise, it's good enough to call a raise
No — you need a stronger hand to call a raise than to open one, because the raiser has declared strength and your fold-equity path is gone
Yes — position makes any raise-worthy hand a call
Only if you're getting better than 3-to-1 pot odds
steps.explain: The Gap Concept: there's a gap between the strength needed to OPEN a raise and the greater strength needed to CALL one. Opening, you can win by fold equity OR at showdown; calling a raise, the fold-equity path is largely gone and you're up against a hand that chose to represent strength, so KJ is dominated too often. 'I would have raised it' is not a reason to call a raise — that IS the gap. (This is Sklansky's concept, from Tournament Poker, not The Theory of Poker.)

modules.title: Preflop
modules.recap:
Win the pot before the flop.
- Raise or fold, wider in late position.
- Facing a raise: 3-bet, flat, or fold. Defend the big blind wide; small blind is 3-bet-or-fold.

steps.title: MIT 15.S50, Kevin Desmond: why position IS information
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 3 (Basic Strategy), Kevin Desmond: "the later position is better because you get more information. You get to see people acting before you. And as a result, the money flows, in general, to the late positions." His diagnostic for cash: "if you're losing money on the button, you should seriously reevaluate how you're playing that, because that's when you make the most amount of money."

His blinds warning cuts the 'cheap flop' myth: the big blind gets a discount "and entry into a hand where you're almost certainly going to be at a major informational disadvantage" — first to act every street after the flop.
steps.formula: Position = extra information every postflop street → money flows to the button. Losing on the button = a leak.
steps.proof: Desmond notes one exception: in short-stack all-in spots early position can be better, because you get to be the aggressor and keep fold equity — "like a game of chicken" where you throw your steering wheel out the window. But at deep cash stacks, information dominates and late position wins.
steps.memorize: MIT/Desmond: position = information; a losing button is a red flag, not variance.

steps.title: Why you open wider in later position
steps.feel: The later you act, the fewer players are left who might wake up with a monster, and the more often you'll have position for the rest of the hand. Both make stealing cheaper and the hand easier to play - so open more hands the closer you sit to the button.
steps.formula: Open range widens as players-behind shrinks: UTG ≈ 15% of hands, Cutoff ≈ 25-30%, Button ≈ 45%+. Fewer players to fold through → higher steal success, and you act last after the flop.
steps.memorize: Fewer players behind → wider you open.

steps.title: Raise or fold - never limp
steps.feel: When everyone folds to you, there are two ways to win the pot: they fold right now, or you take the betting lead and win it later. Limping throws away both - you can't win it uncontested, and you're playing with no initiative. So make it a raise or a fold, never a call.
steps.formula: First-in decision = raise or fold. A raise wins the blinds outright some of the time (free money) and makes you the aggressor when called. A limp wins the pot uncontested 0% of the time.
steps.proof:
When it folds to you, choose raise or fold - never open-limp. Raising wins the blinds outright some of the time (fold equity), builds a pot while your range is strong, and denies the blinds a cheap flop. Limping caps your range and drags you into multiway pots where your equity realizes poorly.

If a hand is not good enough to raise, it is a fold - not a limp.
steps.memorize: First in, you raise or you pass - never limp.

steps.title: Simplified opening rules (no 169-hand charts)
steps.feel: You don't need a 169-hand grid memorized at the table. A few simple buckets - pairs, suited aces, suited Broadways, suited connectors, plus the strong offsuit hands - get you 95% of the way there. Widen the buckets as you move toward the button.
steps.formula: Open if it's any of: a pocket pair (77+ up front), a suited ace, a suited Broadway, a suited connector (54s+), or a strong offsuit Broadway. Widen toward the button, tighten UTG.
steps.proof:
Open a hand if it is one of these:

• any pocket pair (from middle position on; 77+ up front)
• a suited ace (nut potential plus blockers)
• two Broadway cards - offsuit ones tighten up early
• suited connectors and suited gappers (from middle position on)

Fold offsuit junk. Widen as you approach the button.
steps.memorize: Pairs, suited aces, suited Broadways/connectors, strong offsuit - widen on the button.

steps.title: Opening from up front (~15%)
steps.feel: From early position you open a tight, top-heavy sliver of hands. Almost everything is a pair, a big broadway, or a strong suited ace. No junky offsuit stuff, no baby suited connectors. If it isn't clearly strong, you fold it and wait.
steps.formula: ~15% of hands: pairs 77+, suited aces ATs+, suited broadways (KTs+, QTs+, JTs, T9s), and offsuit AJo+/KQo. That's it.
steps.proof: You have 7-8 players still to act behind you. Any one of them can wake up with a monster and 3-bet, and you'll be out of position for the rest of the hand. So you only enter with hands that hold up when called and can flop top pair with a good kicker. Weak hands can't survive that many players and that much positional disadvantage.
steps.memorize: Up front: pairs, big aces, big broadways. When in doubt, fold.

steps.prompt: You watch a solid reg open the same tight sliver every time from up front: pairs like 88, big suited aces, KQ, AQ, and little else. Roughly what percentage of all hands is that?
steps.explain: A tight early-position opening range is about 15% of hands: pairs 77+, suited aces ATs+, suited broadways, and AJo+/KQo. That's the correct up-front frequency with a full table behind you. 5% would be only premiums; 30-50% are late-position (cutoff/button) numbers.

steps.prompt: You're first to act at a full $2/$5 table with 76s. Open or fold?
options: Open, suited connectors are great
Fold, it's not in your up-front range
Limp to see a cheap flop
Open, but only for the minimum
steps.explain:
76s is a fine hand, but not from up front. Your early-position opening range (~15%) is pairs, big aces, and big broadways, not baby suited connectors, because 7-8 players behind can punish you and you'll be out of position. Fold it here. The exact same 76s is a clear open from the cutoff or button. You play the seat, not just the cards.

Suited connectors are not universally openable. They need position and fewer players behind to realize their equity.

steps.title: Opening from the cutoff (~27%)
steps.feel: One seat off the button you nearly double your range. Now every pocket pair plays, every suited ace, more suited broadways, and the suited connectors (98s, 87s, 76s, 65s) come in as bluff-y hands that flop big equity. Offsuit widens to A9o+ and KTo+ too.
steps.formula: ~27%: 22+, A2s+, K9s+, Q9s+, J9s+, T8s+, 98s-65s, plus A9o+/KTo+/QTo+/JTo.
steps.proof: Only two players sit behind you (button + blinds are next), so the chance someone behind has a real hand drops sharply. Fewer players to get through means more of your steals go uncontested, and the ones that get called still have position or equity working for you. Position postflop lets these medium hands realize equity they couldn't from up front.
steps.memorize: Cutoff: all pairs, all suited aces, connectors join. Roughly double UTG.

steps.title: Opening on the button (~45%)
steps.feel: On the button you're opening close to half of all hands. Only the two blinds are left, and you'll have position on both for the entire hand. Almost any suited hand, most offsuit broadways, any pair, and a wide swath of connectors and gappers all become profitable steals.
steps.proof: Only two players sit behind you, and both are forced-money blinds who will fold a huge chunk of the time. Positional advantage postflop is largest here, so even weak hands realize enough equity and steal enough dead money to show a profit. The later the seat, the fewer players behind and the better your position, so the wider you open.
steps.memorize: Button: ~half of hands. Fewest players behind + position = widest steal.

steps.prompt: It folds to you on the button with 54s. Both blinds are still to act. Open or fold?
options: Fold, it's too weak
Open, position and fewest players behind make it profitable
Limp to keep the pot small
Open only if the blinds are tight
steps.explain: Open. On the button your range stretches to ~45% of hands, including 54s. Only two forced-money blinds are behind you, they fold often, and you'll have position for the whole hand, so the dead money plus your positional edge makes even a hand like 54s a profitable steal. The later the seat, the fewer players behind and the wider you open. This same 54s would be a snap-fold from up front.

steps.title: Percentile Anchors on the Grid
steps.feel: Forget memorizing a 169-hand chart. Picture the range grid and learn a handful of landmarks, then eyeball everything else. When you hear "he opens 20% from the cutoff," you should see a region light up, not recall a list. Ranges are shapes, not lists.
steps.formula: Anchors to burn in: top ~5% ≈ TT+ and AQ+. ~20% ≈ all pairs plus most suited aces (and strong Broadways). ~30% ≈ the "Broadway corner" — roughly any two Broadway cards. The ~50% "diagonal" ≈ hands whose two ranks sum to about 15 (A-2, K-3, Q-4, J-5, T-6…). Anything looser than the diagonal is a very wide range.
steps.proof: These come from combinatorics of the 1326 starting combos collapsed to 169 grid cells (13 pairs, 78 suited, 78 offsuit). TT+ (5 pairs) plus AQ+ (AK, AQ suited and offsuit) totals roughly 62 combos ≈ 4.7% of 1326 ≈ 5%. All 13 pairs (78 combos) plus suited aces (48 combos) already clears ~10%; adding strong Broadways pushes the shape to ~20%. The rank-sum-15 diagonal (A=14 down to 2, so A+2, K+3, Q+4…) traces the boundary where about half of all combos sit above it — a fast visual for the median hand. Exact percentages shift a point or two by source, but the landmarks are stable enough to read a table in real time.
steps.memorize: 5% = TT+/AQ+; 20% = pairs + suited aces; 30% = Broadway corner; 50% = ranks sum to ~15.

steps.prompt: A player tells you they only open "TT+ and AQ+" from early position. Roughly what percentage of all starting hands is that?
steps.explain: TT+ (five pairs) plus AQ+ (AK and AQ, suited and offsuit) is about 62 combos out of 1326 ≈ 4.7%, i.e. the top ~5% anchor. That's an extremely tight, value-heavy range — proceed with caution.

steps.prompt: Which is the WIDER range?
options: All pocket pairs plus most suited aces (~20%)
TT+ and AQ+ (~5%)
They're the same width
Impossible to compare without a chart
steps.explain: All pairs plus suited aces is the ~20% anchor; TT+/AQ+ is the ~5% anchor. Twenty percent covers four times as many hands, so it's much wider. Reading these as grid regions makes the comparison instant — no chart needed.

steps.prompt: Under the Gun with A-9 offsuit. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Weak offsuit aces are dominated by bigger aces up front. Fold UTG - it opens from the cutoff and button, not first in.

steps.prompt: Under the Gun with K-J offsuit. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Offsuit K-J is dominated by a tight early range (AK, AQ, KQ, AJ). Fold up front - it opens fine from late position.

steps.prompt: Under the Gun with Q-J offsuit. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Another dominated offsuit Broadway. Fold from up front - it plays fine as a late-position open, not first to act.

steps.prompt: Under the Gun with pocket eights. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Pairs 77+ open from any position - set value plus a hand that often flops an overpair. Raise.

steps.prompt: Hijack with A-10 offsuit. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: By middle position A-10 offsuit is a standard open - enough players have folded that domination is less likely.

steps.prompt: Cutoff with A-2 suited. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Suited aces open widely from late position - nut-flush potential, an ace blocker, and wheel straights. Also your best future 3-bet-bluff material.

steps.prompt: Folded to you on the Button with Q-7 suited. Your move?
options: Raise
Fold
Limp
steps.explain: A suited hand on the button with only the blinds behind - a fine open. Position and fold equity carry it; never limp.

steps.prompt: Button with J-8 suited. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Suited one-gapper on the button - great equity realization in position and disguised straights and flushes. Open it.

steps.prompt: Button with 7-2 offsuit. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
steps.explain: Even the button has a bottom. 7-2 offsuit is the worst hand in poker - fold it and open your other ~45%.

steps.prompt: Folded to you in the Small Blind with K-9 offsuit. Play?
options: Raise
Fold
Limp
steps.explain: Heads-up against just the big blind, K-9 offsuit is well ahead of a random hand - raise. Never limp and give a free flop.

steps.title: How big to open
steps.feel: Live $1/$2 players call too much and don't respect small raises, so open bigger than you would online. A larger raise thins the field and charges the sticky callers - exactly what you want when nobody folds.
steps.formula: Live $1/$2: open to ≈ $10-15 (5-7bb), and add about $1 per limper. Online: 2.2-2.5x. Go bigger on limpy, sticky tables to thin the field.
steps.proof:
Online: 2.2 to 2.5x. Live $1/$2: bigger - open to $10 to $15 (about 5 to 7 big blinds), because callers are sticky and you want to thin the field and charge them. Add about one big blind per limper.

Min-raising is a leak: it gives the blinds a cheap look and denies you fold equity.
steps.memorize: Live tables are sticky - open 5-7bb, add one per limper.

steps.prompt: Live $1/$2, folded to you on the Button with A-K. Best open size?
options: Min-raise to $4
Raise to $6 (3bb)
Raise to $12 to $15
Just limp
steps.explain: Live players are sticky, so open bigger - about 6 to 7 big blinds - to thin the field and charge callers. 3bb is an online size; min-raise and limp are leaks.

steps.prompt: One limper (UTG), you have A-J suited in the Cutoff. Best play?
options: Raise to isolate (~$12-15)
Limp behind
Fold
Min-raise to $4
steps.explain: Raise to isolate the limper and play a heads-up pot in position with the better hand. Limping behind squanders your edge; min-raising invites a crowd.

steps.prompt: Two limpers (UTG and HJ), you have A-K offsuit on the Button. Best size?
options: Raise to about $18 to $20
Raise to $6
Limp behind
Min-raise to $4
steps.explain:
About 3 to 4bb plus one big blind per limper, then a touch more to isolate - roughly $18 to $20. Multiway you especially want the field thinned; never just call A-K behind limpers.

Correction. The Course: $15–20 (7.5–10bb) over two or more limpers in live games.

steps.prompt: Best reason to raise rather than limp your A-J suited in the Cutoff?
options: To see a cheap flop
To build a pot with a range and positional edge, plus fold equity
To disguise your hand
To keep the pot small
steps.explain: Raising builds a pot while you are ahead and in position, and sometimes wins it preflop. Limping surrenders all of that.

steps.title: The gap: you need more to continue than to open
steps.feel: Someone already raised, so they've announced strength. To keep playing you need a better hand than you'd need to open yourself - because now there's a real range fighting back, not just two blinds waiting to fold.
steps.formula: Your continue range is tighter than your open range. Facing a raise, drop the weakest and most dominated hands you'd happily open first-in but can't profitably continue against a raiser.
steps.proof:
Someone has raised, so you are now against a range that has already shown strength. You need a stronger hand to continue than you would to open. Your three choices: fold, call, or 3-bet.

Continue tighter than you open - the "gap" - because the raiser's range is stronger than a random hand.
steps.memorize: It takes a stronger hand to call a raise than to make one.

steps.title: Call vs 3-bet vs fold
steps.feel: Three doors when someone raises: re-raise your best hands (and a few bluffs), just call the hands that play well but hate a re-raise, and fold everything else. Pick the door by asking how your hand does when the money goes in.
steps.formula: 3-bet: premiums for value + a few blocker bluffs. Call: playable hands with implied odds that don't want a 4-bet (suited connectors, suited Broadways, pairs to set-mine). Fold: dominated and weak offsuit hands.
steps.proof:
3-bet your value hands (premiums) and a few bluffs. Call hands that play well but do not want to face a 4-bet - suited connectors, suited Broadways, medium pairs - mostly in position. Out of position, especially from the blinds, prefer 3-bet-or-fold.

In position you can flat wide against a weak opener; out of position, tighten and polarize.
steps.memorize: 3-bet the best, flat the playable, fold the rest.

steps.prompt: An Under-the-Gun player opens to $12. You are in the Cutoff with K-J offsuit. Action?
options: Call
3-bet
Fold
steps.explain: K-J offsuit is dominated by a tight UTG range (AK, AQ, KQ, AJ). Cold-calling is a classic leak. Fold.

steps.prompt: An Under-the-Gun player opens to $12. You have Q-J offsuit. Action?
options: Call
3-bet
Fold
steps.explain: Another dominated offsuit Broadway against an early open. Fold - it flats in position vs a late open, not here.

steps.prompt: A cutoff player opens to $12, you are on the Button, deep. You have 8-7 suited. Action?
options: Fold
Call
3-bet for value
steps.explain: Suited connector, in position, great implied odds - flat and realize equity. Too weak to value-3-bet.

steps.prompt: A cutoff player opens, you are on the Button with K-10 suited. Action?
options: 3-bet
Call
Fold
steps.explain: K-10 suited flats well in position - not strong enough to value-3-bet, too good to fold against a wide cutoff range.

steps.prompt: An Under-the-Gun player opens to $12. You have A-K suited. Action?
options: Fold
Call
3-bet for value
steps.explain: A-K is a premium - 3-bet for value, especially live where worse aces and kings call, and you can get it in against a nit's QQ+/AK.

steps.prompt: A hijack player opens, you are on the Button with pocket nines, $250 effective. Action?
options: Fold
Call
3-bet or fold only
steps.explain: Pocket nines in position is a comfortable call - often the best hand vs a wide range, deep enough to set-mine, easy to play postflop.

steps.title: Set-mining, derived
steps.feel: With a small pair against a raise you're paying a small price hoping to flop a set and stack them. It only works if they have enough money left to pay you off when you hit - so you need deep stacks and a payoff-happy opponent, not just the right price.
steps.formula: You flop a set ≈ 12% (about 1 in 8.5). Only set-mine when implied odds ≥ ~10-15× the call - i.e. deep stacks + a villain who'll pay. Rough rule: 'call $12 to potentially win $150+'.
steps.memorize: Set-mine only when the money behind pays you 10-15×.

steps.prompt: Villain opens to $12. You have 3-3 with $200 effective. Set-mine?
options: Yes - $200 is about 17x the raise
No - small pairs are always folds
No - you need $400
Only if suited

steps.prompt: Same $12 open, but now only $80 effective with 3-3. Set-mine?
options: Yes
No - about 7x the raise, below 15x
Yes, always call pairs
Only from the blinds

steps.prompt: You call to set-mine with a pocket pair. Chance you flop a set or better?

steps.title: Call, don't reraise, with your good-not-great hands
steps.feel: Keep the tough decisions after the flop, where you're better.
steps.formula: 7-7 vs an EP raiser (AK/AQ/JJ+): reraising is 'rarely correct' — flatting in position is
steps.proof: Negreanu: 'I seldom reraise before the flop no matter what my hand is.' With 7-7 on the button vs an early raiser, a 3bet only gets called by a bigger pair or flips vs A-K — and lets him blow you off the hand. Flatting lets you flop a set to stack him, or take it when a ragged 9-4-2 rolls off. He even flats A-A to trap. Especially vs players who overplay preflop (reraise 9-9/A-K/A-Q): 'a good player doesn't want to race, but they do' — so don't neutralize your postflop edge by racing.
steps.memorize: Pocket 7s are a 'bust 'em' hand — goal is to see the flop as cheaply as possible, not to bloat a race. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.prompt: Blinds $1,500/$3,000. You have $88,000, open the button to $8,000 with 7♥8♥. The SB ($112,000) reraises to $30,000. Compare to the early-tourney version where the same 3bet was only to $500 with $10k stacks. Now?
options: Call both times — suited connectors love a reraise
Fold now (no implied odds, ~25% of stack), but the early version is a clear call
Shove both times
Fold both — 7-8s can't continue vs a 3bet
steps.explain: Negreanu's stack-size lesson: 7♥8♥ is a 'bust 'em' hand that needs deep stacks. Early, calling $500 more into a $10k stack is trivial — home-run potential intact. Here calling $22k more commits ~25%+ with no room to get paid; 'there is no home run to hit.' Don't jeopardize more than ~10% of your stack on a bust-'em hand. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.title: Live adjustments
steps.feel: At $1/$2 opens are wide and 3-bets are rare, so you can profitably chase more suited, connected hands in position - the implied odds are huge when you hit and they pay off. Just stop calling with dominated offsuit junk that keeps making second-best hands.
steps.formula: Live adjust: flat more speculative suited hands in position (big implied odds); drop dominated offsuit (reverse-implied); 3-bet more for value since they don't fold enough.
steps.proof: At $1/$2 opens are wide and 3-bets are rare, so flat more speculative suited hands in position (implied odds are huge), stop cold-calling dominated offsuit Broadways (K-J, Q-J, A-J vs an early open), and 3-bet premiums for value while bluffing far less than a chart says.
steps.memorize: Chase suited & connected in position; ditch dominated offsuit.

steps.prompt: A pure calling station opens. You have Q-10 offsuit. 3-bet it as a bluff?
options: Yes - pressure him
No - he never folds, so a bluff-3-bet burns money
Yes - Q-10 has good equity
Only in position
steps.explain: Stations do not fold, so a bluff-3-bet has no fold equity. 3-bet them only for value and value-bet postflop.

steps.title: What a 3-bet is for
steps.feel: A 3-bet (re-raise) does exactly one of two jobs: get money in with a hand that beats what they'll continue with (value), or fold out something better than your hand (bluff). If it's doing neither, don't 3-bet - just call or fold.
steps.formula: Every 3-bet = value (gets called by worse) OR bluff (folds out better). If your hand does neither job, it's a call or a fold, not a 3-bet.
steps.proof: A 3-bet re-raises an open. It has two jobs: value (get money in with hands that beat the opener's continuing range) and bluff (fold out better hands, using holdings a touch too weak to call that carry useful blockers). Everything else calls or folds.
steps.memorize: Every 3-bet is value or a bluff - never 'just because'.

steps.prompt: A hijack player opens to $12. You have pocket aces. Best play?
options: Flat to trap
3-bet for value
Fold
3-bet as a bluff
steps.explain: 3-bet aces for value: build the pot while crushing his range and avoid a cheap multiway flop that erodes your equity.

steps.prompt: An Under-the-Gun player opens to $12. You have pocket kings. Play?
options: Call to keep his bluffs in
3-bet for value
Fold to a tight range
