3-bet as a bluff
steps.explain: Kings 3-bet for value every time - only aces beat you, and flatting or folding a hand this strong leaves money on the table.

steps.title: Linear vs polarized - and the live default
steps.feel: Against a good player who folds a lot, mix premiums and bluffs (polarized). Against the typical sticky $1/$2 caller who never folds, drop the bluffs and just 3-bet a fat range of strong hands for value - they'll pay you off, so make them.
steps.formula: Vs a folding reg → polarized (premiums + blocker bluffs). Vs a sticky caller → linear/value-heavy (all your strong hands), bluffs ≈ 0.
steps.proof:
Against a tough opener who folds a lot, 3-bet polarized: premiums plus bluffs. Against a wide, sticky opener who calls too much - your $1/$2 default - 3-bet linear for value, because worse hands pay you off and you do not need bluffs.

Live baseline: 3-bet mostly for VALUE; add bluffs only against players who actually fold.
steps.memorize: They fold → polarize. They call → value only.

steps.prompt: Against a nitty reg who folds too much to 3-bets, your 3-betting range should be...
options: Linear - all your best hands
Polarized - premiums plus bluffs
Only AA/KK
Only suited connectors
steps.explain: Against a folder, polarize: value hands to get paid by his strong continues, plus bluffs to punish the folds. Linear is for sticky callers.

steps.title: Bluff 3-bets: pick your blockers
steps.feel: If you do bluff-3-bet, pick hands that make it less likely they hold something to continue with. Suited aces like A5s and A4s are ideal - the ace blocks their aces and strong ace-hands, and you still make nut flushes and wheels when you get called.
steps.formula: Best bluff-3-bets block their continues: A5s-A4s (the ace removes AA/AK combos) plus playability (nut flush, wheel). Avoid offsuit trash that blocks nothing.
steps.memorize: Bluff-3-bet the hands that block their calls - suited aces.

steps.prompt: A cutoff reg who folds a lot to 3-bets opens. You have A-5 suited. Best play?
options: Fold
3-bet as a bluff - great blockers
Call
3-bet for thin value
steps.explain: A-5 suited blocks AA, AK, AQ, makes the nut flush and wheel, and folds cheaply - a top-tier bluff 3-bet against a folder.

steps.prompt: Best 3-bet bluff against a folding opener?
options: K-7 offsuit
A-4 suited
J-9 offsuit
7-2 offsuit

steps.prompt: You hold one ace. How many combos of AA can the opener still have?

steps.title: The bluff-3-bet breakeven, derived
steps.feel: A bluff 3-bet risks your raise to win what's already in the middle. If they fold often enough it prints even when you have nothing; below that fold rate it loses money. Most live players simply don't fold enough - which is why you cut the bluffs against them.
steps.formula: Breakeven fold% = risk ÷ (risk + dead money). Risk $40 to win $15 dead → need ≥ 40/55 ≈ 73% folds. A typical $1/$2 opener folds ~40%, so the pure bluff loses.
steps.memorize: A bluff needs risk ÷ (risk + pot) folds - live players don't fold that often.

steps.prompt: He opens to $12 ($3 in blinds, so $15 dead). You 3-bet to $40 as a pure bluff. Minimum fold % to profit immediately?
Your bluff-3-bet needs ~73% folds, but a typical $1/$2 opener folds about 40%. Implication?
options: Bluff-3-bet relentlessly
Value-3-bet and bluff sparingly - they do not fold enough
3-bets never work
Only 3-bet suited hands

steps.title: How big, and what to do when re-raised
steps.feel: Size your 3-bet bigger out of position - you play worse without position, so charge more and win more folds - and a touch smaller in position. If a nit 4-bets you, believe them and fold everything but the very top of your range.
steps.formula: 3-bet ≈ 3× the open in position, ~4× out of position. Facing a nit's 4-bet: continue only with roughly AA/KK/AK, fold the rest.
steps.memorize: Bigger out of position; fold to a nit's 4-bet.

steps.prompt: You 3-bet from the big blind (out of position) over a $12 open. Best size?
options: To about $48 (~4x)
To $14 (min)
Just call

steps.prompt: You 3-bet A-Q and a nitty regular 4-bets big. Action?
options: Call
5-bet shove
Fold
Always call A-Q
steps.explain: Nits 4-bet only QQ+/AK, and A-Q is crushed by that range. Face-up - fold.

steps.title: Facing a 4-bet with AK (deep cash)
steps.feel: You open, someone 3-bets, you 4-bet or they 4-bet you, and now big money is going in preflop with AK. In deep cash this is a genuine decision, not an automatic stack-off. Against most small-stakes 4-bet ranges AK is in real trouble.
steps.formula: vs AA/KK you're crushed (~12%). vs QQ/JJ it's a flip (~43/57). At $1/$2, most opponents only 4-bet AA/KK/AK, so folding AK to a small 4-bet is often correct.
steps.proof: Do the range math. If a typical low-stakes reg 4-bets only AA, KK, and AK, then your AK is either crushed by the pairs or chopping/behind vs their AK. There's almost no worse hand in their 4-betting range, so you're never a favorite and often a huge dog. In deep 100bb+ cash you keep your whole stack rather than commit it as a small underdog. This is different from a short tournament shove, where fold equity and stack pressure can make AK a stack-off.
steps.memorize: vs a small-stakes 4-bet, AK is often a fold. Don't stack off 100bb light.

steps.prompt: Deep $1/$2, 100bb+. You open AK, a straightforward reg 3-bets, you 4-bet, and he cold 5-bets big. You've never seen him do this light. What's your play?
options: Stack off, it's AK
Fold, his range crushes you
Call and see a flop
Min-raise again to bluff
steps.explain:
Fold. A straightforward small-stakes player putting in a huge preflop reraise has AA/KK/AK almost every time. Against that range AK is either crushed by the pairs (~12%) or flipping/behind vs his own AK, never a favorite. In deep cash you keep your stack rather than jam it in as a big dog. This is not a tournament shove where stack pressure and fold equity rescue AK.

Don't stack off 100bb light just because "it's AK." AK is a drawing hand against a capped premium 4-bet range.

steps.title: Why the big blind defends wide
steps.feel: You've already got a blind in the pot and you act last before the flop, so you're getting a bargain price to see a flop from the big blind. That discount lets you defend a much wider range than you'd play from any other seat.
steps.formula: BB has 1bb already in + closes the action → great pot odds. Vs a 2.5x open you risk ~1.5bb to win ~4bb, so you defend very wide.
steps.memorize: You already paid and you close the action - defend wide.

steps.prompt: MIT's Kevin Desmond calls the big blind a bad position despite the 'discounted flop.' Why?
options: The discount is offset by the rake
You act first on every postflop street, at a major information disadvantage
You can never win the hand from the blinds
The ante makes it unprofitable
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L3, Desmond: the discount buys you "entry into a hand where you're almost certainly going to be at a major informational disadvantage" — the blinds "are the first to act in every single situation" postflop. Cheap entry, expensive position.

steps.prompt: Button opens to $6, small blind folds. You are in the Big Blind with 9-6 suited. Action?
options: Fold - too weak
Call - the price is great and it plays well
3-bet for value

steps.prompt: Button opens to $6, you are in the Big Blind with Q-4 offsuit. Action?
options: Call - you get a price
Fold - weak and out of position
3-bet as a bluff
steps.explain: Even at a price, disconnected offsuit junk realizes its equity terribly out of position and floats into second-best hands. Fold - price is not the only factor.

steps.prompt: Button opens to $6, you are in the Big Blind with pocket twos. Action?
options: Fold - tiny pair
Call - set-mine at a great price
3-bet for value
steps.explain: Any pair defends the big blind: you get a price now and can stack him when you flop a set. Call.

steps.prompt: Button opens to $6, you are in the Big Blind with T-9 suited. Action?
options: Fold
Call - connected, suited, priced in
3-bet or fold only
steps.explain: Suited connectors are premium big-blind defends - great equity realization for a hand that makes disguised straights and flushes. Call.

steps.prompt: Button opens to $6, you are in the Big Blind with A-Q offsuit. Best play?
options: Flat call
3-bet for value
Fold
steps.explain: A-Q dominates a wide steal range. 3-bet for value to build the pot and avoid a tricky out-of-position flop with a strong-but-not-monster hand.

steps.title: Minimum defense frequency
steps.feel: If you fold your big blind too often, anyone can raise any two cards and profit for free. To shut that down you have to keep fighting for the pot often enough that pure stealing stops being automatic money.
steps.formula: MDF = pot ÷ (pot + bet) = 1 − s/(1+s). Vs a min-ish steal, defend ~⅔. But vs a nit who only opens premiums, ignore MDF and just fold - there's nothing to punish.
steps.memorize: Defend enough that pure steals don't profit - unless they only raise premiums.

steps.prompt: A balanced button steals every hand. Which is the bigger mistake in the big blind?
options: Defending a bit too wide
Folding far below MDF, so he prints by auto-stealing
Calling with suited hands
3-betting your aces

steps.prompt: A tight, passive UTG player (raises only premiums) opens to $12. You are in the Big Blind with K-9 offsuit. Action?
options: Call - MDF says defend wide
Fold - his range crushes yours and MDF does not apply
3-bet as a bluff
steps.explain: MDF assumes a wide, balanced opener. Against a face-up premium range, K-9 offsuit is dominated and plays badly OOP. Over-fold - exploit the honesty.

steps.title: Big-blind defending range
steps.feel: From the big blind you can call with a lot of playable stuff - suited aces, connectors, any pair to set-mine, most suited Broadways - because the price is right and you'll often see the flop cheaply. Just don't get carried away with offsuit garbage against early raisers.
steps.formula: BB flat: suited aces, suited connectors/gappers, any pair, suited Broadways, offsuit Broadways vs late opens. 3-bet a value+bluff mix on top. Tighten vs UTG, widen vs CO/BTN.
steps.proof: Flat a wide, playable range: suited aces, suited connectors and gappers, any pair (set-mine), suited Broadways, most offsuit Broadways vs late opens. 3-bet a polarized range: premiums for value, and blocker hands (A5s-A2s, some suited connectors) as bluffs. Fold offsuit trash that flops badly out of position.
steps.memorize: Flat wide & playable; 3-bet a value+bluff mix on top.

steps.prompt: Why should you defend WIDE from the big blind but still not overvalue the discount?
options: You get a price to close the action, but you're out of position on every later street
The discount means you're a favorite in the hand
Wide defense guarantees you'll flop well
There's no downside — the discount is free equity
steps.explain: The BB has already posted, so closing the action is cheap — that justifies a wide defending range. But you act first postflop for the rest of the hand, a permanent informational disadvantage that raises the equity you actually need. So defend wide, yet favor hands that flop well (suited, connected, pairs) over raw high cards, and don't let the cheap call talk you into trouble.

steps.title: The small blind is 3-bet or fold
steps.feel: From the small blind you're stuck out of position with the big blind still waiting behind you, and just calling invites a squeeze. So take a clear stance: re-raise your good hands and fold the rest - skip the messy flat-call.
steps.formula: SB vs an open → 3-bet or fold (no flatting). 3-bet value + some blocker bluffs; fold everything else. Flatting out of position just invites the BB to squeeze.
steps.proof: From the small blind you are out of position with the big blind still behind, and flatting invites a squeeze. Default to 3-bet or fold: 3-bet your value and good blocker hands, fold the rest. Flat only a small, strong range against weak opens.
steps.memorize: Small blind: 3-bet or fold - never flat.

steps.prompt: A button player opens to $6. You are in the Small Blind with A-J suited. Best default?
options: Flat call
3-bet or fold
Limp along
steps.explain: From the small blind you are out of position with the big blind behind. Flatting is worst - 3-bet A-J suited for value, or fold weaker holdings.

steps.prompt: A cutoff player opens to $12. You are in the Small Blind with A-5 suited. Best play?
options: Flat call
3-bet or fold
Limp
steps.explain: From the small blind, play 3-bet-or-fold. A-5 suited is an ideal 3-bet - great blockers and a nut-flush/wheel hand - so 3-bet it rather than flat out of position.

steps.prompt: MIT's Desmond shows a small-blind vs an all-in big blind: you put in 100 to win a 400 pot. Your break-even equity, and how does his 'any two cards' point apply in a cash blind-vs-blind?
options: 50%; only play premiums
25%; you're almost always ahead of a random big-blind range, so folding donates EV
33%; fold everything but pairs
40%; call only suited cards
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L3, Desmond: 100 into a 400 final pot = 25% break-even. "You're virtually always ahead of 25% here" — worst heads-up hand vs any two is still 32%, and you're ~40% vs a random range. Folding is a ~60-chip mistake. In a live blind-vs-blind steal the same logic makes very wide shoves/defends correct.

steps.title: Equity when called, not "is it pretty"
steps.feel: The right question for hand selection isn't "does this look nice" or "can I hit a big flop." It's: when I get called, how much equity do I still have? You want hands that keep outs, overcards and draws after your bet gets called, so you win a big share of the pots that go to showdown.
steps.formula: Judge a hand by its equity-when-called. Suited connectors and suited aces keep equity across many boards; offsuit junk (72o, A4o offsuit) collapses to near-nothing when called.
steps.proof: Everyone flops top pair equally often, there's no "hitting flops" skill. The money comes from the hands that still have equity after a call, because those win the showdowns and the barrels. Concrete matchups: AK vs a pair like 88 is a near coin-flip (~52/48). AK vs QQ/JJ is about 43/57, still very live. But AK vs AA/KK is only ~12%, and a dominated ace like A9 vs AK wins just ~25-30%. Choose hands whose worst-case matchups aren't disasters.
steps.memorize: Pick hands by equity WHEN CALLED, not by looks. 87s beats A4o here.

steps.prompt: You get all-in preflop with AK against a hand you're sure is a pocket pair like 88. How does the matchup run?
options: AK is crushed, ~12%
Roughly a coin-flip, ~52/48
AK is a big favorite, ~70%
AK loses badly, ~25%
steps.explain:
AK vs a smaller pair like 88 is the classic "flip": about 52/48. Two live overcards racing against a made pair. That's why AK plays well when your opponent's range is pairs. Contrast: AK vs AA/KK is only ~12% (crushed), and a dominated ace like A9 vs AK wins just ~25-30%. Knowing your equity-when-called is exactly how you pick hands and size your stack-offs.

"Live" doesn't mean "ahead." A flip is still only 52%. Don't treat AK as a made hand.

steps.title: Small suited connectors over big offsuit paint
steps.feel: Counterintuitive: 5♣6♣ is a dream, K-J is a trap.
steps.formula: want: hands that make straights/flushes & fold easily | avoid: hands that make second-best one-pair (KJ, KQ, AQ, AK offsuit)
steps.proof: Negreanu on deep stacks: K-J is 'the rookie hand' — it flops top pair and can't lay it down, running into sets, K-Q, A-K, A-A. A-Q is 'much worse in every way,' A-K wins small pots but is a dog when money goes in. The ideal small-ball holdings are small suited connectors (5♣6♣, 6♠7♠, 6♥8♥): straight + flush + two-pair + trips potential, and easy to muck when you brick. J♠T♠ calling a tight raise on 5♥6♠7♥ is the dream — steal it when he has A-K, or draw at a hidden straight to stack an overpair.
steps.memorize: The best small-ball hands make big hands cheaply or fold cheaply. One-pair hands cost you big pots. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.title: Raw equity is a lie you tell yourself
steps.feel: The hand has "enough equity to call" and you still can't call — because you'll never get to cash it in.
steps.formula: %EV = Eq × EqR · so EqR = %EV ÷ Eq · break-even EqR = pot-odds% ÷ Eq
steps.proof: 9♣5♦ in the BB has 29.5% equity vs a 16% UTG open — well above the ~24% pot odds. But you're not all-in. Post-flop you get barreled off the best hand, dominated when you pair, and paid off rarely. The EqR factor (fraction of raw equity you actually bank as EV) is ~58% here; you'd need ~61% to break even, so it's a fold despite the raw-equity green light.
steps.memorize: %EV = Eq × EqR. High raw equity forgives a bad EqR; medium hands OOP get slaughtered by it.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: "my equity beats the pot odds" only settles it when you're all-in. Not all-in? Multiply by realization or you'll bleed.

steps.prompt: Which factor MOST hurts a hand's equity realization, forcing you to fold hands that have "enough raw equity" to continue?
options: Being suited
Being out of position with a medium-strength hand
Holding a high pocket pair
Having a nut flush draw
steps.explain: OOP you can't guarantee a free card — after you check you often face a bet and fold, forfeiting equity. Medium hands are worst: they crave showdown but can't take heat. High equity hands over-realize (happy to build pots); trash is easy (just fold); suited hands realize ~16% MORE via backdoor draws. Position + hand class drive EqR.

steps.title: You Play Against a Range
steps.feel: Stop asking "what does he have?" as if it's one holding — you'll almost always be wrong and you'll tilt yourself trying. Ask instead: "what's the whole set of hands he'd play this exact way, and how does my hand do against that set?" Your equity is never against one hand; it's the average against everything they'd take this line with.
steps.formula: Equity vs range = average of your equity against each hand in their range, weighted by how likely each is. Widen their range → your strong hand's equity drops toward a coin flip; tighten it → your equity swings hard one way. Judge decisions on the weighted average, not the scariest single combo.
steps.proof: If villain holds hand hᵢ with probability pᵢ (Σpᵢ = 1), your equity is E = Σ pᵢ · equity(you vs hᵢ). Fixating on the single worst hᵢ overweights a low-probability branch and leads to over-folding; assuming the best hᵢ leads to over-calling. The correct object is the full distribution. This is why a "strong" hand can be a fold against a range that's polarized to nutted value, and a "weak" hand can be a call against a range stuffed with bluffs — the same cards, different range, opposite decision.
steps.memorize: Compute equity against their whole likely range, weighted — never against one guessed hand.

steps.prompt: You hold JJ. Against which opponent range does JJ have HIGHER equity?
options: A wide ~40% opening range (many weak aces, small pairs, suited junk)
A tight ~5% range (TT+/AQ+ only)
Equity is identical against both
JJ is a favorite only against the tight range
steps.explain: JJ dominates most of a wide 40% range — it beats every smaller pair and every unpaired hand not yet improved, so its equity is well above 50%. Against a tight TT+/AQ+ range, JJ is roughly a coin flip or worse (behind QQ+, flipping vs AK/AQ). Same cards, opposite outlook — that's playing the range, not the hand.

steps.prompt: Villain shoves the river and you're deciding whether to call with a bluff-catcher. What is the RIGHT question to ask?
options: What is the full set of hands he'd shove this way, and how does my hand fare against that whole set?
What single hand does he most likely have right now?
Is my hand strong in absolute terms?
Would I be embarrassed to lose to a bluff?
steps.explain: You play against a range, so estimate every hand he'd take this line with — value shoves and bluffs — and weigh your equity against that whole distribution. Fixating on one guessed hand overweights a single low-probability branch and leads to over-folding or over-calling. Decide on the weighted average vs the range.

steps.title: You play a range, not a hand
steps.feel: The same two cards can be a raise in one seat and a fold in another, not because the cards changed, but because of all the OTHER hands you'd be playing the same way. Your action tells a story about your whole range, so you play to that story, not to your single holding.
steps.formula: Decide by "what does my whole range do here," then play this hand consistently with it. Same 77, different seat, different action.
steps.proof: Take 77 on Q73. As the button caller in the big blind your range is condensed, mostly medium hands and draws, so you check the set to keep it consistent with everything else you'd check, and to keep the strong hands hidden. As the preflop raiser your range is polarized, you're firing many bluffs, so betting the set disguises it among those bluffs and checking would look suspicious. Identical hand, identical board, opposite action, because the surrounding range is different. A hand is one draw from a distribution; your strategy is defined over the whole distribution.
steps.memorize: Same hand, different range, different play. Play the distribution, not the two cards.

steps.prompt: You flop a set of 7s on Q♦7♣3♥. In one spot you check it, in another you bet it. What actually decided the difference?
options: Whether the set is likely to get outdrawn
The other hands in your range in each spot
The exact suits of your sevens
How many players saw the flop
steps.explain:
It's the rest of your range. As the big-blind caller your range is condensed (mostly medium hands and draws), so you check the set to play it like everything else and keep strong hands hidden. As the preflop raiser your range is polarized and firing bluffs, so betting the set hides it among those bluffs. Same hand, same board, opposite action, driven entirely by the surrounding range.

There's nothing deceptive about checking a strong hand by itself. What's deceptive is playing strong hands the same way you play your weak ones.

steps.title: Count combos, not hands
steps.feel: You stop asking "could he have it?" and start asking "how many ways?"
steps.formula: pairs: 6 combos · unpaired offsuit: 12 · suited: 4 · any unpaired: 16 (4×4) · full deck = 78+312+936 = 1,326 combos
steps.proof: 13 pair ranks × 6 = 78 pair combos. 78 suited hands × 4 suits = 312. 78 offsuit hands × 12 = 936. Card removal cuts these: if the flop and your hole cards use a rank, subtract those cards from the count. On A♣J♥9♥ holding A♦3♦, villain's AA drops to 1 combo (only A♠A♥), his top-pair AJ to 6 (2 aces × 3 jacks).
steps.memorize: The four magic numbers: pair 6, unpaired 16, offsuit 12, suited 4. Everything else is subtraction for blockers.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: every top pro thinks in combos. "Could he have the flush" is amateur. "He has 3 flush combos and 9 bluff combos, so I'm calling" is the game.

steps.prompt: Live 2/5. You hold A♦3♦ on A♣J♥9♥. Villain could have AA. How many AA combos does he actually have?
steps.explain: AA is 6 combos in a vacuum. But the A♣ is on the board and you hold the A♦ — two aces are dead. Only A♠A♥ remains, so 1 combo. That's card removal: your ace and the board ace gut his set-of-aces to a single combination. This is why blockers to the nuts are so powerful.

steps.title: Memorize the common all-in preflop matchups
steps.feel: Preflop equities barely matter unless the money's going in, but when it is, you shouldn't be counting anything — just recall it. A handful of matchups cover almost every shove-or-call spot. Suited holdings bump the offsuit numbers up by about 4%.
steps.formula:
Gaines' memory set:
Overpair vs underpair (AA vs 55) → 81% / 19%
Pair vs one overcard (88 vs A2o) → 70% / 30%
Pair vs two undercards (KK vs 87o) → 82% / 18%
Two overcards vs pair (AKo vs 55, "race") → 45% / 55%
Overcard vs two middle cards (A8o vs QJo) → 57% / 43%
Pair vs one undercard (AA vs AKo) → 93% / 7%
steps.proof: These are just software results committed to memory so you can look at a shove and instantly estimate. Vs a strong range you shift to Table 10: e.g. QQ vs a JJ+/AK shove ≈ 47%, JJ vs JJ+/AK ≈ 38%, QQ vs TT+/AQ ≈ 55%. Combine the matchup number with your pot odds (from the must-win chart) to decide fold or call in seconds.
steps.memorize: Coinflip = 55/45 pair over two overcards; overpair vs underpair = 80/20.

steps.prompt: A tight small blind shoves and you put him on JJ+/AK. You hold QQ. Roughly what's your equity, and is calling ~40% correct?
options: ~38%, fold
~47%, marginal call
~55%, easy call
~66%, snap
steps.explain: QQ vs a JJ+/AK range runs about 47% (Gaines' Table 10). If your pot odds only require ~40%, that's a fine call even though you're behind AA/KK — you're ahead of JJ and racing AK.

steps.prompt: MIT's Desmond teaches the Sklansky-Chubukov ranking: you open-push face-up (opponent sees your hand). For pocket aces, how large can your stack be and still be +EV?
options: About 70 big blinds
About 1,290 chips
Infinite — aces are +EV to open-push face-up at any stack
About 25 big blinds
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L4, Desmond: Chubukov found "Aces have infinity value here — you can have an unlimited amount of chips and then show Aces and push them, and it's plus EV." Kings only works to ~1,290 chips. Face-up means the opponent plays perfectly, so this ranks hands by raw pushing power — a cash-useful hand-strength backbone.

steps.title: MIT 15.S50, Kevin Desmond: folding is an action with a price tag
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 4 (Preflop Analysis), Desmond reframes a marginal 9-6 offsuit shove: pushing is worth about +253 chips, so "a more provocative way to describe it is if you don't do this, you are losing 250 chips." Folding isn't neutral — it forfeits the EV the shove would have captured. "By folding what seems like a very weak hand in this position, you are just giving him 250 chips of value."

His shock stat: open-folding that spot is "as bad as purposely calling all in with 3-4 versus Ace-King." Passivity has a measurable cost.
steps.formula: Cost of folding = EV of the +EV action you skipped. A +250 shove folded = −250.
steps.proof: Because the push is +EV against the villain's entire calling-range distribution (fold equity plus ~35% showdown equity when called), refusing it surrenders that value. In cash, chronically folding thin-but-profitable spots is a slow bleed that never shows up as a big loss.
steps.memorize: MIT/Desmond: folding a +EV spot isn't 0 — it costs you exactly the EV you passed up.

modules.title: Postflop
modules.sub: texture, c-bets, barreling, sizing, draws & multiway
modules.recap:
Where the money moves.
- Read the board, c-bet the right textures, barrel with equity, size by texture.
- Price your draws with implied odds; tighten up multiway.

steps.title: Dry boards freeze, wet boards move
steps.feel: Some flops are like dried concrete - once the cards land, whoever is ahead stays ahead. Others are like wet paint - the picture can change completely on the very next card. A-7-2 rainbow is concrete. 9-8-7 with two of a suit is wet paint. On concrete you can relax; on wet paint you have to worry about the turn.
steps.formula: Ask: how many turn cards change who's winning? Few turn cards matter → dry (static). Many turn cards matter → wet (dynamic). Rainbow + unconnected + one high card = dry. Two suited + connected + middling = wet.
steps.proof:
A board is "static" when the equity gap between hands barely moves across turn/river runouts. On A♠7♦2♣ the top pair holds roughly the same big edge on almost every turn - very few cards make a straight or flush, so the hand's equity is close to locked.

A board is "dynamic" when many runouts swap the lead. On 9♥8♥7♣ a huge fraction of the 47 unseen turn cards complete straights, flushes, or two pair, so a hand that leads now can be crushed next street.

Static = your equity is durable, so you can build the pot slowly. Dynamic = equity is fragile, so charge draws now or protect by betting.
steps.memorize: Concrete stays put; wet paint moves.

steps.title: Static vs dynamic boards
steps.feel:
Wet-vs-dry is the label everyone uses, but static-vs-dynamic is the axis that actually tells you what to do. Ask: will the ranking of hands change on later streets? On a static board (A-K-4 rainbow, K-7-3) rankings almost never change — a set is near-locked, top pair top kicker is a big favorite, and a bet carries a clear threat: "whatever you have, I have better and you can't catch up."

On a dynamic board (9-8-6 two-tone, K-T-9) equities run close and swing wildly. A♠Q♠, J♠J♣, and 8♦6♦ all have live equity; an overcard or flush card reorders everything. Here a bet only says "I have a good chance," to which villain says "so do I."
steps.formula:
Static: bet for value and thin value, pick which street to check, and if your bluff hasn't worked by the turn, usually give up. Dynamic: bet bigger to deny equity, bet earlier (draws call the flop, brick the river), and a river bluff can still land after failed barrels because opponents were drawing and missed.

An overcard reorders rankings more than a flush card: on 9♠7♣4♣ there are exactly 45 flush-draw combos but 180 hands contain a jack, so a jack turn leapfrogs your A9 far more than a third club does.
steps.proof: On a static board the equity gaps between tiers are large, so the turn and river rarely change who is ahead — which is why you can defer betting and why an unpaid bluff won't suddenly get through. On a dynamic board the tiers are packed together, so a single card can move a hand from behind to ahead or vice versa. Betting to deny that equity has real value, and because so many holdings improve or brick, later-street bets do heavy narrowing work. Dry is not static: 8-4-2 rainbow is dry but dynamic because an overcard is too likely.
steps.memorize: Static = rankings frozen, bet for value/thin, give up if bluff fails. Dynamic = equities swing, bet bigger to deny.

steps.prompt: Classify these two flops on the axis that actually matters. Flop 1: K♠ 7♦ 3♣. Flop 2: 8♣ 4♥ 2♠ (rainbow, no flush draw).
options: Both static — neither has a flush draw
Flop 1 static, Flop 2 dynamic — an overcard is too likely on 8-4-2
Both dynamic — any board can change
Flop 1 dynamic (three broadway gaps), Flop 2 static (low and dry)
steps.explain: Dry is not the same as static. K-7-3 is both dry and static: high cards, big equity gaps between tiers, rankings won't change. 8-4-2 rainbow is dry (no draws) but dynamic — an overcard on the turn or river is too likely, and any overcard reorders who's ahead. Miller prefers static/dynamic over wet/dry precisely because 8-4-2 fools people: it looks safe but a Q, K, or A turn overturns the ranking. On static boards you can defer betting and give up if a bluff fails; on dynamic boards bet earlier and a later bluff can still land.

steps.title: Range advantage: whose story fits the flop
steps.feel: Whoever raised before the flop is telling a story about strong cards - big pairs, big broadways, aces. When the flop comes A-K-4, that story fits perfectly, so that player 'owns' the board. When it comes 7-6-5, the raiser's story fits badly, and the caller who plays lots of connected middling cards is more comfortable.
steps.formula: Preflop raiser's range = high cards & big pairs. If the flop is A-high or K-high and dry → raiser has range advantage. If the flop is low and connected → caller's range catches up.
steps.proof:
Range advantage means one player's whole range has more equity than the other's on this specific board. The preflop aggressor's range is weighted toward AK, AQ, KQ, and big pairs. On A♦K♠4♥ those hands make top pair or better far more often than the flat-caller's range of suited connectors and small pairs.

Concretely, if the raiser's range averages ~58% equity across the board versus the caller's ~42%, the raiser can bet almost any hand profitably because the average hand is ahead.

Live players fire the flop on autopilot. On 7♣6♣5♦ the caller's range is actually ahead - blindly c-betting there donates chips.
steps.memorize: The flop that fits your preflop story is yours.

steps.prompt: You raised UTG preflop, one player called from the BB. Flop is A-K-4 rainbow. Who does this board favor?
options: You (the preflop raiser)
The BB caller
Neither - it's a coin flip
steps.explain: Your UTG raising range is packed with A-x and K-x and big pairs; the caller's flatting range rarely makes top pair here. Dry, high, disconnected - this is a textbook range-advantage board for the raiser. Bet small with your whole range.

steps.prompt: You open UTG and BB calls. Flop comes A♠ 9♥ 6♠. Who does this board favor, and what's the standard play?
options: Favors BB — she called wide, so she hits low boards; you should check
Favors you (~57% equity) — bet small with your whole range
Neutral — both should check and see a turn
Favors you, so overbet immediately to deny equity
steps.explain: A-high dry boards slam into the UTG opening range and miss the BB calling range. UTG has a little over 57% equity here, and Brokos notes there's probably no flop where BB is a favorite after an early-position open. BB is short on the nuts (she'd 3-bet AA/AK) and short on air (your unpaired hands are the best high cards). Bet small — 25%-33% pot — with your whole range and let her check her condensed range. Overbetting is a turn/river tool for a polarized range, not the small-and-wide flop play.

steps.title: Nut advantage: who holds the true monsters
steps.feel: Range advantage is 'who's ahead on average.' Nut advantage is 'who has the unbeatable hands.' These aren't always the same person. You can hold more good hands overall, yet your opponent holds the only sets or the completed flush. Whoever holds the top of the deck gets to make the biggest, scariest bets.
steps.formula:
Range advantage → who's ahead on average → bet often, small.
Nut advantage → who holds sets/straights/flushes → bet big / polarize.
You want both before you fire a large sizing.
steps.proof:
Nut advantage is about the top of each range, not the average. On A♦K♦4♦ (three diamonds), the preflop raiser may still have more top pairs (range advantage), but if the caller flatted a lot of suited diamonds, they may hold more flushes - the nuts.

The player with the nut advantage can apply maximum pressure because their big bets are credibly backed by hands nothing can beat. Betting big without nut advantage means your bluffs get called and your value gets raised.

Small bets lean on range advantage. Big bets require nut advantage - otherwise a strong opponent just raises you off it.
steps.memorize: Average edge lets you bet often; the nuts let you bet big.

steps.title: Range advantage vs nut advantage — not the same thing
steps.feel: Two flops, both "favor you," but one lets you overbet and the other only lets you min-bet.
steps.formula: Range advantage = more total equity / better bucket split · Nut advantage = you hold more of the effective-nut combos
steps.proof:
On A♥Q♦3♠ (BB vs UTG) UTG has BOTH: huge range equity AND all the AA/QQ/AK the BB 3-bet away pre — so UTG overbets across streets and banks 85% of the pot. On Q♥J♥T♥ UTG has the range advantage but NOT a nut edge: the BB's range is capped-but-polarized with flushes/straights it will happily stack off. So UTG min-bets to keep BB's trash in rather than blasting BB off air and isolating against the nuts. Range advantage says bet often; nut advantage says how BIG.
Same aggressor, three flop classes
A♥Q♦3♠: range+nut edge
→ overbet, 85% of pot
Q♥J♥T♥: range edge, no nut edge
→ high freq MIN-bet
654r: BB has equity edge
→ IP checks back more
steps.memorize: Frequency comes from range advantage. Size comes from nut advantage. Betting big without the nuts isolates you against the part of their range that crushes you.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: the classic leak is betting BIG on wet boards "for protection." You fold out the trash you beat and get called only by the nuts.

steps.title: Polarized vs condensed: the shape of your hand pool
steps.feel: Sometimes your hands split into two clumps - either you flopped something great or you have air, nothing in between. That's 'polarized,' and it wants big bets. Other times all your hands are mediocre and similar - a lot of second pairs and weak top pairs bunched together. That's 'condensed,' and it wants small bets or a check.
steps.formula:
Two clumps (monsters + air) → polarized → bet big, threaten to stack them.
One clump (medium made hands) → condensed → bet small or check, keep the pot small.
steps.proof:
Bet sizing follows the shape of your equity distribution. A polarized range wants a big bet because your value hands earn maximum, and your air borrows that same threatening size as a bluff - the opponent can't tell which is which.

A condensed range - lots of medium-strength hands - has little to bluff with and little that wants a huge pot. Big bets bloat the pot with hands that don't want a war, so you check or make small value/protection bets instead.

Ask 'do I have both nuts and air here, or just a pile of medium hands?' The answer picks your sizing before you ever look at the opponent.
steps.memorize: Two clumps bet big; one clump bets small or checks.

steps.title: Equity buckets: sort every range into 4 piles
steps.feel: You stop eyeballing "who's ahead" and start counting how the whole range splits.
steps.formula: Strong ≥75% · Good 50–74% · Weak 33–49% · Trash <33% (hand-vs-range equity, on THIS board)
steps.proof:
Buckets are dynamic, not static. Top pair is a Strong 82% hand on A♥Q♦T♠ but only a Good 60% on the single-suited T98. Averaged over all 1,755 flops in BB-vs-IP: the IP raiser holds ~22% Strong / 43% Good / 29% Weak / 6% Trash, while the BB holds ~7% Strong / 25% Good / 23% Weak and nearly HALF (45%) Trash. That lopsided split is why IP c-bets ~84% of flops.
The 4 equity buckets + avg BB-vs-IP split (all flops)
Strong≥75%
Good50-74%
Weak33-49%
Trash<33%
IP:22/43/29/6
BB:7/25/23/45
steps.memorize: 75 / 50 / 33 are the bucket walls. A range's shape = how its combos land in the four buckets on this specific board.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: a hand's bucket is relative to the ranges and the board — it moves street to street. Re-sort on every card.

steps.prompt: As the pre-flop raiser you have a clear range advantage on a MONOTONE flop like A♥K♥T♥. What's the GTO sizing instinct?
options: Overbet — punish their draws
Big bet 2/3+ for protection
Small bet (min / 1/3) at high frequency
Check the whole range
steps.explain: Monotone flattens your nut advantage — many of your Strong hands lose equity and the caller's trash becomes flush-draw Weak hands. Their range turns polarized while yours depolarizes toward Good-not-great. A big bet folds out the weak stuff you beat and isolates you vs made flushes and huge draws. Bet small, keep their junk in, deny cheaply. High range advantage → high frequency; low nut advantage → small size.

steps.title: Barrel the boards that hit you; brake on the ones that hit them
steps.feel: The simplest live edge: when the flop looks like the cards you raised with, keep swinging. When the flop looks like the trash your loose opponent limps and calls with, tap the brakes. Your loose-passive opponents show up with random low and connected cards - those flops belong to them, not you.
steps.formula:
Flop = A-high / K-high / broadway & dry → your board → bet.
Flop = low, connected, middling (T-9-8, 7-6-4, 8-7-6) → their board → check/give up your air.
steps.proof:
A c-bet's profit is driven by fold equity plus your equity when called. On A♠K♦4♣ your range crushes and your bluffs still have overcards - both parts are healthy, so you fire.

On 8♥7♥6♣ against a station's calling range, fold equity collapses (they never fold a pair or draw) AND your air has little equity when called. Both parts of the profit vanish, so betting just burns money.

The single biggest live c-bet leak: firing your whole range on low connected flops because 'I raised preflop.' Those boards favor the caller - check and fold your air.
steps.memorize: Bet the board that looks like your cards; check the one that looks like theirs.

steps.title: Ranges narrow street by street
steps.feel:
This is the single most important postflop idea, so let it sink in. A hand you face is one draw from a whole distribution. What matters is how much each bet shrinks that distribution. Picture villain's range as a bag of hands. The flop bet barely closes the bag. The turn bet dumps out the weak hands. The river bet leaves only two clumps: real value and a few bluffs.

The reason is equity. On the flop even trash has real equity and monsters are far from locked, so people c-bet almost everything and the bet tells you almost nothing. By the turn, hands have resolved into strong or weak. By the river there are no more draws, so a big bet is genuinely polarized. That is why the same $-per-pot bet means wildly different things depending on the street.
steps.formula:
Brokos: "On the flop, even very weak hands tend to have significantly more than 0% equity, and very strong hands significantly less than 100%." So a c-bet range is wide and only lightly polarized. "You'll do most of your biggest betting on turns and especially rivers."

Practical sizing corollary: bet 25%-33% pot with a wide range on the flop, then 75%-200% pot with a polarized range on the turn. Each bet-call re-condenses the caller: she folds her worst, may raise her best, so what stays is even more medium-heavy.
steps.proof: Trace a line: UTG opens, BB calls. After a flop c-bet-call, villain has shed only pure air, so the read "he called the flop" is nearly worthless. After a turn bet-call, the medium hands that floated the flop now fold; only value and strong draws call. By a river bet, the draws either got there or bricked, so a bet is real value plus a handful of chosen bluffs. The information content of a bet rises every street precisely because equities collapse toward 0% or 100%.
steps.memorize: Flop bet barely narrows. Turn bet is the big filter. River bet = value + a few bluffs.

steps.prompt: UTG opens, BB calls. Flop A♠9♥6♠, UTG bets, BB calls. Turn 4♦ checks through. River J♦. Now BB leads out for a big bet. What does she most likely have?
options: Nothing changed — she still has her whole flop-calling range
A polarized range: slowplayed nuts (A9/99/66), the odd improver, plus chosen bluffs
Only pure bluffs — she's stealing because UTG showed weakness
Exactly top pair — she'd only lead a made ace
steps.explain: The river bet is the big polarizing move, and here the roles flipped. When UTG checked the turn he removed his strong hands (they'd have bet), so BB inherits the polarized role. Her river betting range: slowplayed nuts she just-called the flop with (A9, 99, 66), the rare hand that improved, some still-strong value like AT, and bluffs drawn from her weakest flop-calls (missed T8/87 straight draws, weakest pairs). It's value plus a few bluffs — not her whole range, and not pure air. This is exactly why turn and river bets narrow so much more than flop bets.

steps.prompt: $2/$5, $500 stacks. You open A♦K♠ UTG-ish, get callers. Flop A♥ 7♥ 6♠, you bet, two call. Turn 8♥ (third heart, three to a straight). SB shoves all-in for $163. You have top pair top kicker. What now?
options: Call — top pair top kicker is too strong to fold
Fold — the turn shove is the big filter; it reps a flush/straight/set/two pair, none of which you beat
Raise — represent the flush yourself
Call — she's probably shoving a worse ace like AQ/AJ
steps.explain: A big turn shove is exactly the narrowing bet that carries real information — unlike a flop bet, it's not posturing. She'd never shove AQ/AJ/AT this way (she'd fear the card and bet small or check). The all-in reps a flush, a straight, a set, or two pair — nothing you beat. "You've got two pair. So what. If you can't beat the range, fold." This is Skill #2 (don't pay people off) meeting range-narrowing: the turn bet filtered her to hands that crush TPTK.

steps.prompt: Same setup - you raised, BB called. But now the flop is 9-8-7 with two hearts. Who does this dynamic board favor?
options: You (the preflop raiser)
The BB caller
Neither, but it's a great spot to fire big
steps.explain: Low, connected, and wet - this hits the caller's suited connectors and middling cards far more than your high-card raising range. You have neither range nor nut advantage. Check back your air; barreling here just funds their draws.

steps.title: The three reasons to fire a c-bet
steps.feel: Never bet just because you raised last street. Before you slide chips in, know which of three jobs the bet is doing: making a better hand fold, charging a draw so it can't outdraw you for free, or getting a worse hand to pay you. If your bet does none of those three, it's a leak.
steps.formula: Every c-bet must do at least one: (1) Fold equity - fold out a better hand or live overcards. (2) Protection - deny a draw its free card. (3) Value - get called by worse. No job → check.
steps.proof:
These map directly to how a bet makes money. A bet earns via fold equity (they fold hands with equity against you) and via value (they call with hands you beat). Protection is fold equity aimed specifically at hands that would draw out - denying equity is itself EV.

If a better hand never folds, a worse hand never calls, and nothing is drawing against you, the bet has zero paths to profit. That's the definition of a spot to check.

Say the reason out loud in your head: 'I'm betting for value' or 'I'm betting to deny the flush draw.' If you can't name it, don't bet.
steps.memorize: Fold 'em, protect, or get paid - one of the three, or check.

steps.title: The green-light c-bet: dry, heads-up, in position
steps.feel: The easiest, most profitable c-bet is the small one on a dry high board when you're heads-up and get to act last. You have the range advantage, few turn cards scare you, and acting last means you see them check before you decide. This is the bet you make almost every time.
steps.formula: Green light = range/nut advantage + dry board + heads-up + in position. Sizing: small, ~⅓ pot. Fire your whole range.
steps.proof:
On a dry range-advantage board a ⅓-pot bet only needs to work often to profit, and it does everything at once: worse hands call, air folds, and you rarely get raised because the caller has few strong hands. Position lets you check back turns safely, so a cheap flop bet doesn't commit you.

Because your range is so far ahead, you don't need to protect individual hands with big sizing - the small bet applies pressure across your entire range at minimal risk.

Betting big on a dry board wastes money: your value hands fold out the worse hands that would've called small, and your bluffs risk more than they need to.
steps.memorize: Dry board, heads-up, last to act - small bet, always.

steps.title: The check is a weapon, not a surrender
steps.feel: Checking isn't giving up - it's the right play when the board hurts your hand more than theirs. If you missed a wet flop, if there are three other players still in, or if you're first to act on a board that connects with callers, checking saves you from bleeding chips into a spot where you can't win enough.
steps.formula: Check when: you missed on a WET board, or the pot is MULTIWAY, or you're OUT OF POSITION on a dynamic board. When in doubt out of position on a scary board → check.
steps.proof:
Each condition kills the c-bet's profit. On a wet board your bluffs face draws and pairs that don't fold, so fold equity is low while risk-when-called is high. Multiway, fold equity compounds against you - needing two or three players to fold is exponentially unlikely.

Out of position you don't get the free information of seeing them act, and on a dynamic board you'll face tough turn decisions with the whole pot at risk. Checking controls the pot and lets you fold cheaply or realize your equity.

Checking a missed wet board is not weak - it's refusing a bet that loses money. You can still win the pot by checking down or improving.
steps.memorize: Missed and wet, or three-handed, or first and scared - check.

steps.title: Small on dry, big on wet - and why
steps.feel: Your bet size should match the board. On a dry board where you're just ahead across the board, bet small - you don't need much. On a wet board where you've got a real hand and want to charge draws or set up a big pot, bet bigger. The size tells a story; make sure it's the right one.
steps.formula:
Dry range-advantage board → small, ~⅓ pot, wide.
Wet board with a made hand/nut advantage → bigger, ~⅔ to ¾ pot, polar (value + bluffs with equity).
steps.proof:
Sizing follows equity shape and the need to deny equity. On a dry board your range is condensed and far ahead, so a small bet extracts thin value and denies little because few draws exist. On a wet board a big bet charges the maximum for the many draws present and builds a pot your nut hands want to play.

The big bet is only correct when you hold the nut advantage - otherwise strong opponents raise you off the second-best hand. Match the size to what you actually hold at the top of your range.

Small bet = 'I'm ahead of your average hand.' Big bet = 'I have the nuts or I'm bluffing - pick wrong and you lose your stack.'
steps.memorize: Dry small, wet big - and only bet big with the nuts on your side.

steps.prompt: Flop is K-7-2 rainbow, heads-up, you raised preflop. Your hand pool here is mostly K-x, over-pairs, and complete air. What's the correct read on shape and sizing?
options: Polarized - bet big to threaten stacks
Condensed - so check everything
Range advantage on a dry board - bet small with your whole range
steps.explain: Dry, high, disconnected: you own the range. Because there's little the caller can raise you with and few scary runouts, a small ~⅓-pot bet with your entire range prints - value gets called by worse, air folds out weak hands, all at a cheap price. Save the big polar sizing for wet boards where you hold the nut advantage.

steps.title: "You check, I bet" auto-profit
steps.feel:
Here's the engine that prints money at low stakes. When villain checks and you bet, you don't need a hand — you need him to fold often enough. A half-pot stab only needs him to fold about 30% of the time to show an immediate profit. Most players fold far more than that when they check-and-miss.

Miller's number: against a common weak style where villain checks and folds ~7/8 of hands to a half-pot bet on each street, just betting half-pot every time he checks earns roughly $6.25 per hand in a $20 pot — more than half the preflop raise, from cards you never even look at.
steps.formula:
Auto-profit fold threshold = bet / (bet + pot). Half-pot bet: 0.5P / (0.5P + P) = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3 ≈ 33%. A three-quarter-pot bet needs ~43%. If villain folds more often than the threshold, betting any two cards is +EV before you even see a card.

This is barreling, not "representing." The c-bet's success has almost nothing to do with what you hold — it's about whether opponents fold their junk. So c-bet 8-4-2 (obvious you missed, so they fold overcards), not K-4-2 (only a king calls, nothing worse folds anything).
steps.proof: Let pot = P and bet = b. Bet a hand with zero showdown value. EV = f·P − (1−f)·b, where f is villain's fold frequency. Set EV = 0: f·P = (1−f)·b → f = b/(P+b). At b = P/2, f = 1/3. Any fold rate above that is pure profit. Because low-stakes players check-fold their many missed hands well above 1/3 on the flop, and even more on the turn where the bet threatens a bigger river bet, the stab clears the bar with room to spare.
steps.memorize: Half-pot stab needs villain to fold ~30% (= bet/(bet+pot)). They fold way more than that when they miss.

steps.prompt: You raise J♣T♦ on the button, one caller. Flop K♦Q♠ 3♠ (open-ender), you bet, called. Turn 6♣ (a brick), villain checks. Pot is $120. You have jack-high — no made hand. What's the play?
options: Check back — you have no showdown value, so give up
Bet ~$100 — bet the turn: fold equity now plus nut-straight-draw EWC and a river bluff to fall back on
Bet tiny ~$20 — minimize risk since you're bluffing
Check back to realize your straight-draw equity for free
steps.explain: Bet the turn. The core barreling rule: when villain checks the turn and you can't win a showdown without improving, bet. A $100 bet into $120 with $500-ish stacks implies "it's $100 now and maybe all-in next card," pushing villain's turn fold rate well past the ~30% break-even into the auto-profit zone. And when called you're not dead — you have the nut-straight draw (equity-when-called) plus a river bluff option. Checking back forfeits all the fold equity that makes this spot print. Don't go tiny either; the threat of the big river is what does the work.

steps.prompt: $2/$5. You open in the cutoff and a weak-tight regular calls in the big blind. Flop comes 9♥4♣2♠. He checks. He's the kind of player who folds everything but top pair or better. You have A♠Q♠ (two overcards, no pair). What does the Brunson power-poker approach favor?
options: C-bet around half pot — his range folds too often, and you have two ways to win
Check back to see a free turn since you have no pair
Give up — you missed the flop and have nothing yet
Check-fold plan: pot control with air
steps.explain: Power poker: bet, don't call, and play the player. Against a weak-tight opponent who folds unless he has top pair or better, most of his range whiffs this dry board. Your c-bet wins now via fold equity, and if he calls you can still improve to the best hand — two ways to win. Checking back surrenders the free fold equity his over-folding hands you.

steps.prompt: Heads-up, in position, you raised preflop. Flop A-8-3 rainbow, you hold K-Q offsuit (missed). Villain is a standard-tight regular. Best play?
options: Small c-bet ~⅓ pot as a bluff
Bet ¾ pot to look strong
Check and give up
steps.explain: Dry, ace-high, heads-up, in position, vs a player who can fold: this is a green-light range bet. Your range owns the A-x, so a cheap ⅓-pot bet folds out his weak stuff and even your K-high has backdoor equity. Small sizing risks the least to do the job.

steps.title: Vs stations: fewer bluffs, more thin value
steps.feel: Your typical live opponent limps, calls, and almost never bluffs or folds a pair. That single fact flips your c-betting: bluffing them is pushing on a locked door, but value-betting them is a wide-open highway. So cut your c-bet bluffs way down and bet a much thinner range for value - second pair, weak top pair, even ace-high sometimes - because they call with worse constantly.
steps.formula: Vs calling stations & multiway: c-bet BLUFFS way down (fold equity ≈ 0). C-bet thin VALUE way up - bet any pair or better that beats their calling range. Give up your pure air.
steps.proof:
The EV of a c-bet is:

EV = foldEquity × pot − (1 − foldEquity) × risk-when-behind

Against a station, foldEquity ≈ 0. Plug it in: the first term collapses to zero and you're left with −(1) × risk whenever you're behind. So a pure bluff is pure loss - stop bluffing.

But flip it to value. When you're AHEAD of their calling range, the same near-zero fold rate is a gift: they call your thin value bets with worse, so your bet collects (call frequency × amount) with almost no fold-out of the worse hands you're targeting. Their inelastic calling turns thin value into big value.

The classic live leak is doing the opposite - firing air 'because I raised' and then checking back a weak top pair 'to control the pot.' Against stations that's backwards: bet the top pair thin, never bluff the air.
steps.memorize: Stations don't fold - so stop bluffing them and start milking them.

steps.prompt: Flop K-9-4 rainbow, heads-up vs a classic calling station who never folds a pair. You hold K-7 (top pair, weak kicker). What's the exploit?
options: Check to control the pot with a weak kicker
Bet for thin value - he calls with worse K-x, 9-x, and pairs
Bet big to bluff him off his hand
steps.explain: Against a station, top pair - even with a weak kicker - is a value bet, not a pot-control hand. He calls with K-x worse, 9-x, and small pairs all day. Bet a comfortable ½-pot for value. Checking 'to control' just leaves money on the table against someone who won't punish you.

steps.title: Barrel when the story still fits
steps.feel: A second or third bet only makes sense if the tale you're telling still holds together. If the turn is another card that helps the hands you'd have raised with, keep firing - your story is consistent and believable. If the turn helps their hands instead, the story breaks down and you should slow down.
steps.formula: Keep barreling when: your range/equity persists on the new card, the card is a scare card that favors YOU, and villain is capped (can't have the nuts). Slow down when the card helps their range.
steps.proof:
Barreling profits when your betting range on this street remains credibly stronger than their continuing range. A good turn shifts equity your way - it adds value hands and equity to your bluffs while adding little to the hands they called flop with.

"Capped" means their range can't contain the strongest hands (they'd have raised earlier). Against a capped range your big bets threaten a hand they simply can't have, so your fold equity is real and your value gets paid by their second-best hands.

Before firing again, ask: 'Did this card help me or help them?' Fire when it helped you; check when it helped them.
steps.memorize: Fire again only when the new card keeps your story true.

steps.title: The double-barrel: pick your card
steps.feel: The best turn card to fire a second bullet is one that could plausibly have hit you and scares them. An overcard to the board, a card that completes a draw you'd represent, or a card that pairs the top of the board are all good. A blank low card that changes nothing is a weaker spot to bluff - nothing new threatens them.
steps.formula: Good double-barrel turns: overcards to the flop (adds top pairs to your range), cards that complete draws you'd have, cards that extend your range's connection. Weak turns to bluff: bricks that help no one.
steps.proof:
A good barrel card increases the equity gap in your favor. If the flop was K-7-2 and the turn is an A, you now credibly hold A-x and A-K - the card added strong hands to your range and to your bluffs' equity (an ace gives you a pair to fall back on), while the caller's 7-x or 2-x got no help.

The bet leverages that shifted equity: value hands got better, bluffs got backup outs, and the scary card makes folds more likely. A brick turn does none of this - your range didn't improve, so a second barrel is just repeating a flop bluff with no new pressure.

Barrel the turn that lets you credibly say 'I just got there.' If the card doesn't change your story, it's a weak bluff card.
steps.memorize: Second bullet loves a card that just joined your team.

steps.prompt: You raised preflop and c-bet flop K-6-2 rainbow with A-Q (missed). One tight-ish villain called. Turn is the A♠. Best play?
options: Check - the ace didn't help me
Fire a second barrel
Give up and check
steps.explain: The turn ace is a perfect double-barrel card: it pairs YOU (now top pair, top kicker) and it's a scare card that hits your range hard while missing the caller's K-x, 6-x, and 2-x. Your story - that you have a strong ace or king - is now completely credible. Fire for value; you turned the second-best-case bluff into a value bet.

steps.prompt: You're the preflop raiser on two flops: (A) A-K-4 rainbow, and (B) 9-8-6 two-tone. How should your c-bet sizing differ?
options: Bet big on A-K-4 (you have the nuts advantage), small on 9-8-6
Same size on both — pick your standard and stick to it
Small on A-K-4 (static, wide condensed range), big on 9-8-6 (dynamic, polar, deny equity)
Size by your hand: big with overpairs, small with sets
steps.explain: Size by range width and texture, never by your hand. A-K-4 is static: rankings won't change, you're betting a wide condensed range, so bet small (25%-33% pot). 9-8-6 two-tone is dynamic: equities swing on turns/rivers, you're betting a more polarized range and want to deny equity, so bet bigger. "Same size on both" is right in spirit for one texture but wrong across textures — the correct constant is that you don't fork size by your two cards, while you absolutely do vary by board dynamism.

steps.prompt: You've barreled a bluff twice and been called both times. On which board is a third-barrel river bluff more likely to still work?
options: Static K♦Q♠3♥, turn 6♥, river 6♦ — he called twice, so blast again
Dynamic 9♠7♠4♠, turn 5♠, river K♦ — the K bricks the flushes and straights he was drawing to
Neither — two calls always means give up
Both equally — the river card doesn't matter after two calls
steps.explain: On the static K-Q-3 board, calling the flop and turn declared made hands (a queen+, made straights); a river bluff into that is a pure prayer, so give up. On the dynamic 9♠7♠4♠ board, villain could have been calling with one-pair, flush draws, or pair-plus-straight-draw — and the K♦ river bricks nearly all of it (flush missed, straights missed, and any TT now fears you had AK). Many of those weak drawing hands fold, so a ~$300 barrel into $522 works often enough. That's the static/dynamic payoff: on dynamic boards a river bluff can still land after failed barrels.

steps.title: The river bet is all-or-nothing
steps.feel: By the river there are no more cards - the hand is either the best or it's air. So your river bets, especially big ones, come in only two flavors: a genuine strong hand betting for value, or a real bluff chosen because you block the hands they'd call with. There's no room for weak, in-between bets on the end.
steps.formula: River bets are polarized: bet VALUE (a hand that beats their calls) or bet a chosen BLUFF (a busted hand that blocks their calls). Never bet a medium hand - check it and hope to win at showdown.
steps.proof:
On the river all equity is realized - a hand is 100% or 0% to win at showdown, so there's no draw to protect and nothing to deny. That's why river ranges are polarized: value bets get called by worse; bluffs get folds from better. A medium hand can do neither - worse hands fold to your bet and better hands call, so betting it only loses (this is why you check-call or check-fold your medium hands).

A good river bluff is chosen by blockers. If you hold a card that removes the opponent's most likely calling hands, the bluff works more often - you've reduced the number of combinations that can call you.

Big river bet? It's a monster or a picked bluff. If your hand is 'meh,' the bet is wrong - showdown it.
steps.memorize: River bets are nuts or nothing - never the middle.

steps.title: Know when to stop firing
steps.feel: The bravest and most profitable move against the wrong opponent is to shut it down. If your opponent is a station who literally will not fold, your bluffs have no target - stop. If the board ran out in a way that killed the draws you were representing, your story collapsed - stop. Firing anyway is lighting money on fire to look tough.
steps.formula: Give up (check/fold your bluffs) when: villain is a station who won't fold, OR the board bricked out so your bluff represents nothing, OR you ran out of credible scare cards. Take the free showdown when you have any.
steps.proof:
A barrel needs fold equity to profit. Against a player whose folding frequency is near zero, every bluff bullet is a pure loss: EV = foldEquity × pot − (1 − foldEquity) × bet ≈ 0 × pot − 1 × bet = −bet. You're guaranteed to lose the bet.

Likewise, if the runout bricked, your betting range no longer credibly contains the value hands you'd need to represent - the story is incoherent, so thinking opponents don't fold and stations never did. Multi-street bluffing only pays when both the opponent can fold and the board supports your story.

Sunk-cost barreling - 'I've already put two bets in, I have to fire the river' - is a top live leak. Prior bets are gone; only this bet's EV matters. Give up freely.
steps.memorize: No fold equity, no bluff - shut it down and keep your chips.

steps.prompt: River scene: you hold a busted flush draw (A♣ high, no pair). Board is Q-8-3-J-2 rainbow now, missed. Villain is a loose-passive station who called flop and turn. Best play?
options: Triple-barrel bluff - I've told a story
Check - no fold equity vs a station, take the free showdown
Bet small to 'block'
steps.explain: Two things kill the bluff: the villain is a station with near-zero fold frequency, and the river bricked so you can't credibly rep much. EV of the bluff ≈ 0×pot − 1×bet = a guaranteed loss. Don't throw good money after the prior barrels - that's sunk cost. Check; your ace-high even wins sometimes at showdown.

steps.prompt: River: you hold K-J on a Q-J-4-7-2 board - top pair (jacks) plus a king kicker, a strong made hand. Villain (calling station) called your flop and turn bets. River bricks the 2. Best play?
options: Check - top pair is medium, control the pot
Bet for value - a station pays off top pair with worse Q-x and J-x
Overbet as a bluff-catcher
steps.explain: Against a calling station, top pair with a strong kicker on a bricked river is a clear value bet, not a pot-control hand. He calls with worse J-x, Q-x, and small pairs all day. Under-bluff, over-value: bet ~⅔ pot for value. Checking a strong hand against someone who won't fold just refuses free money - the live cardinal sin.

steps.prompt: Middle position, you have A♠K♦. Button calls. Flop A♥9♥6♦, you bet, he calls. Turn 9♠, both check. River 6♥ (board A♥9♥6♦9♠6♥). Your read: loose and passive — calls too much, bets too rarely. You have top pair. Check or bet?
options: Check — top pair is only a medium hand, you don't want a big pot
Bet, even close to pot — exploit a station: induce calls with worse aces; plan to fold only if raised
Check to induce a bluff — he might bet worse
Overbet — polarize since it's the river
steps.explain: This is the thin-value-vs-a-calling-station spot. Out of position you can't guarantee a free showdown; if you check, he bets everything that beats you and you can't fold. But your read is he calls too much and bets too rarely — so bet to induce calls (not check to induce bluffs), plan to fold if raised (a passive player almost never raise-bluffs). Many players wrongly check this "medium" hand fearing a better hand or a raise; against a station that's leaving value on the table. Betting, even close to pot-sized, is the exploit.

steps.prompt: A tight player raises preflop from early position, you call on the button with 8♠8♣. Flop K♠K♣7♦, he bets small; turn 2♥, he checks; river J♠, he bets big. Running the Negreanu narration, which read is best supported by the action?
options: Pure air — he was bluffing the whole way
A trips-or-better hand: a strong Kx that value bets the small flop, checks the blank turn, then bets the river for value
A small pocket pair like 5s that never improved
A flush — he was drawing the whole time
steps.explain: Narrate street by street. Preflop EP raise from a tight player = strong, Kx-heavy range. Small flop bet on a paired K board is a classic thin-value / protection sizing that fits a good Kx. The turn check slows down but doesn't kill the hand. The big river bet after checking reads as value betting a strong made hand — trips or a full house — not air, since air rarely fires big into a player who just called a paired board. Your 88 is behind that story; fold.

steps.prompt: A weak player who's been on tilt and playing badly checks to you on the flop, and you 'feel' he has only bottom pair. Per Brunson's read, why does the check tell you he has something small rather than nothing?
options: Because a tilting player always slow-plays big hands
Because if he had nothing he'd have bet to try to steal the pot
Because bottom pair is the only hand he ever checks
Because he's out of position and scared
steps.explain: Brunson's 'feel' is disguised recall and logic. The check itself is the read: a losing, desperate player with nothing would bet to steal — so a check means he caught a small piece he wants to get to showdown. Now you bet a rag turn confident he'll call almost out of desperation, and you make money on the turn and river against a man who won't show you a hand unless he pairs his kicker.

steps.prompt: You've decided a strong opponent most likely holds three Fours (Second Set) after weighing his line all hand. On a later street doubt creeps in and you consider folding. What does Brunson advise?
options: Second-guess yourself and fold — doubt means you're beat
Stick to your first impression — you were probably right the first time
Split the difference and just call
Re-read the whole hand from scratch before acting
steps.explain: In a judgement situation you're always better off sticking to your first impression. Once constant observation lets you put a man on a probable hand, don't change your mind — you'll usually be right the first time. Have the courage of your convictions. Brunson would go with a good player having 3 Fours because his read, formed from watching the player, beats late-street hesitation.

steps.prompt: Brunson flops a set in a pot where a player raised pre-flop and is likely holding a big overpair. He's first to act. What does he do?
options: Check, planning to check-raise the raiser
Check to give the raiser a free card and trap on the turn
Lead right into the raiser
Slow-play by just calling any bet
steps.explain: Brunson's habit: always lead into the raiser when you turn a big hand. Betting looks like weakness — a draw, a steal, or a mediocre hand — so the raiser almost always raises you, and now his overpair is committed with too much already in. Check-raising gives him a chance to escape at minimum loss; leading gives him no savings. Brunson calls it one of the strongest plays in Hold'em.

steps.title: Bet-sizing families: small, big/polar, overbet
steps.feel: You quit picking a number by vibe and match the size to your range's shape.
steps.formula: Depolarized range (mostly Good) → small (min–1/3). Polarized range (Strong+Trash) → big/pot. Very deep + nutted → overbet. Geometric size makes the river all-in: R = (finalPot ÷ startPot)^(1÷streets).
steps.proof:
Solvers over 1,755 flops show one or two dominant sizes per flop; splitting into many sizes barely adds EV vs a GTO opponent (avg loss from collapsing to one size ≈ 0.21% of pot) and it leaks information a raiser can attack. Small bets suit paired/monotone boards (depolarized IP range, cheap to bet-fold trash). Big/overbets show up on dry high-card rainbow boards where IP is polarized and can barrel over 3 streets. Deeper stacks → bigger sizes (and overbets) matter more; shallow → small sizes and the occasional all-in.
Which sizing family fits which spot
Paired/monotone → MIN or 1/3
Dry Axx rainbow → big / pot
Deep + polar → overbet 120%+
Shallow SPR≤1 → all-in
One good size ≈ many sizes
steps.memorize: Pick the size from range SHAPE, never from your specific hand. Changing size by hand strength turns your hand face-up.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: you don't need infinite sizes. One well-chosen size holds ~all the EV vs a solver. Multiple sizes are for EXPLOITING readable humans.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: don't bifurcate your range with bet sizing
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8, Hawrilenko: "You don't want to needlessly bifurcate your distribution." Bet one size with strong hands and a different size with weak ones and "the game tree gets smaller really, really quickly" — you split 310 combos into two thin, exploitable buckets. His personal rule: "I basically don't bet different amounts with different hand types... the possible gain is so small and the possible loss is so big."

He does vary size by board texture (bigger, earlier, on draw-heavy boards), never by his own hand strength. A cash-table discipline that plugs the most common live tell.
steps.formula: One size per board texture, not per hand strength. Sizing tells split your range and let villains fold/call perfectly.
steps.proof: Every time you branch by hand type, each branch carries half the information and half the protection, so both your value and your bluffs become readable. Hawrilenko: if you must bifurcate, "have a really good reason" and "be really careful." Consistent sizing keeps your distribution opaque.
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: size by board texture, never by hand strength — sizing tells bifurcate your range.

steps.prompt: On a paired board (e.g. Q♦8♦8♣) as the aggressor, your range is depolarized — lots of Good-but-not-great, little Trash, few nutted. Best default size?
options: Overbet
Pot
Min-bet / very small
Check everything
steps.explain: Paired boards give the caller a polarized range (some trips/boats + lots of air) while yours stays depolarized. A tiny bet forces them to reveal info and fold their many trash/weak combos, and you lose the minimum when you have to bet-fold the bottom of your range vs a raise. Depolarized range = small size; you don't want to overcommit Good-not-great hands.

steps.prompt: It's the river. Facing a check, you want to value-bet, and you can pick your size. Which statement about size vs. your worst value hand is correct?
options: Bigger bets let you value-bet weaker hands, since more people call
Bigger bets require a stronger worst-value hand; small bets let you value-bet thinner and wider
Size doesn't affect which hands can value-bet, only how much you win
You should always overbet for value since the river is polar
steps.explain: The bigger your bet, the more polarized your range must be, and the stronger your worst value hand needs to be — because the average hand that calls a big bet is stronger than one that calls a small bet. Brokos' river scaling makes it concrete: 33% pot values down to AT; 75% pot's weakest value is AK; a 200% overbet needs AJ or better. Small bets force opponents to call with weaker hands, so you can value-bet thinner. This is why you size by range and situation, not by hoping "big" always wins more.

steps.prompt: Heads-up vs the blind, pot $1,325, board Q♣6♦4♠, villain (a 9-high whiff) checks. You hold K♥T♠. How much, and why that number?
options: $1,325 full pot — deny equity
$2,600 overbet — max fold equity
$750, about 55-60% pot — it folds out the same hands while saving chips when you run into a real hand
Check back, showdown king-high
steps.explain: Negreanu: if he folds for $1,325 he folds for $750. The smaller bet gets the identical result, and on the times villain has A-Q and check-raises you're out $575 less. Same size when bluffing or holding a set keeps you unreadable. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.title: The value-bet 50% rule
steps.feel: A bet is a value bet only if worse hands call it more than half the time. "I don't want to lose my customer" and "I want worse hands to call" both collapse into one test: are you getting called by more junk than monsters? If yes, fire. If the scary card just turned villain's callers into only hands that beat you, check.
steps.formula: Bet for value when: (hands worse than you that call) > (hands better than you that call). Break-even is exactly 50% — more worse-than-you callers = +EV bet.
steps.proof: Let x = % of calls that are worse hands. EV per $1 bet = x(+1) + (1−x)(−1) = 2x − 1, which beats 0 only when x > 0.5. Example: river, you have 64% (18 combos you beat, 10 beat you) but the A♥ scared villain into folding his 99/89 — now only better hands call, so betting is −EV and you check. Count his calling range, not his whole range.
steps.memorize: Value bet only if worse hands call more than half the time.

steps.title: Value on the End, Thin Value & Grading the Decision
steps.feel: You didn't lose because you got sucked out — you lost if the decision was wrong when you made it.
steps.formula: Sklansky / The Theory of Poker (Ch. 18, 23, 24). Bet for value on the end whenever a WORSE hand will call more often than a better hand raises — even thin. ‘Analyzing the Cost of a Mistake’: judge a play by its expectation at decision time (the ‘Sklansky bucks’ idea — you earn the EV of the correct decision regardless of the card that falls), and when two plays are close, weight the DOWNSIDE: pick the play whose error is cheap over the play that’s slightly favored but whose error is a disaster.
steps.proof: Thin value (Ch. 23, the classic hand): a player holds two small pair (6s up), an opponent has been representing a flush all the way. He BETS two pair on the end for value because he knows the opponent puts him on a busted four-flush and will ‘snap off’ with one pair — a worse hand calls, so betting beats checking. Cost-of-a-mistake (Ch. 24): calling a river bet when you’re ~50-50 is correct because folding when you’re actually best costs the whole POT, while calling when beaten costs one bet. His razz example: probability says raise is right only 45% and calling is right 55% — yet you RAISE, because raising is only ‘slightly wrong’ the 55% and calling is ‘very wrong’ the 45%. And the QQ-vs-AK/AA/KK no-limit reraise: even a slim favorite folds when the downside of being crushed dwarfs the upside.
steps.memorize: Value-bet the end when a worse hand calls more than a better hand raises. Grade decisions by EV at the moment, not the result. On close calls, fear the expensive error — losing the pot > losing a bet.

callouts.text: The Sklansky-bucks mindset: after a bad beat, ask ‘was my decision +EV when I made it?’ If yes, you WON the decision and pocketed the Sklansky bucks — the actual chips are just variance. Stop tilting on results.

steps.title: Made Hands Must Bet to Deny
steps.feel: You flopped a good hand on a board full of draws. If you check or dribble out a tiny bet, you let villain draw for free or cheap — and they'll snap you when a flush or straight lands. Charge them.
steps.formula: Bet ~⅔ pot with a vulnerable made hand. That gives draws a bad price and builds the pot while you're ahead.
steps.proof:
A flush draw is ~18% to hit on the next card, ~36% by the river. If you check, they realize that equity for free. If you bet ⅔ pot, they must call risking ⅔ to win 1 + ⅔ = required equity = 0.67 ÷ (1.67 + 0.67) ≈ 29% — more than a one-card draw is worth, so every call they make is a mistake and every fold hands you the pot.

MIT names it directly: 'under-betting, not protecting your hand' is a classic leak. A ⅓-pot dribble lets a flush draw call profitably; checking is worse. Size up to deny equity.
steps.memorize: Vulnerable made hand → bet ~⅔ pot to charge the draws.

steps.prompt: You have top pair top kicker on a wet, two-flush board against one opponent. What's the best bet size?
options: ≈ ⅔ pot — charge the draws a bad price
≈ ⅓ pot — keep it cheap
Check — pot control
steps.explain:
On a wet 2-flush board your top pair is vulnerable to flush and straight draws. A ⅓-pot bet lets a flush draw (~18-36% equity) call profitably; checking gives it away free.

A ~⅔-pot bet makes them pay a price higher than their draw is worth — every call is their mistake, every fold is your pot.

Under-betting to 'keep them in' with a vulnerable hand is the leak. Deny equity now; get the money in while you're ahead.

steps.title: Size UP for value against a station
steps.feel: A calling station is a person who hates folding. Against a normal opponent you keep value bets modest so they don't fold.
