But a station calls anyway — so shrinking your bet just leaves money on the table. When you have a real hand against someone who can't let go, make the bet fat. They'll call the big one about as often as the small one.
steps.formula:
Vs a station with a strong hand: bet ¾ to full pot, sometimes overbet.
Extra profit per street ≈ (big size − small size) × their call frequency.
If they call 80% either way, a $75 bet vs a $40 bet earns you ≈ ($35 × 0.80) = $28 more, every street.
steps.proof:
Value-bet EV = (call frequency) × (bet size) when you're ahead. Against a normal player, call frequency drops as size rises, so there's a peak. Against a station, call frequency is nearly flat — it barely falls as you bet more — so EV keeps climbing with size. You push the size up until they finally start folding, which for a true station is very high.

Their leak is not folding. Your counter-leak is not sizing small. Undersizing against a station is quietly refusing free money.
steps.memorize: Stations pay big bets. So make them big.

steps.title: Never bluff-size against a station
steps.feel: The whole point of a bluff is to make someone fold. A calling station won't fold — that's their defining trait. So a bluff against them isn't a bluff, it's a donation. The correct 'bluff size' against a station is zero: check it back or give up. Save your chips for when you actually have the goods, because that's when they'll hand you a pile.
steps.formula:
Bluff EV = (fold%) × (pot) − (call%) × (your bet).
If fold% ≈ 0, the first term dies and you're left with only losses.
Rule: villain rarely folds → bluff frequency = 0.
steps.proof:
A bluff needs fold equity. Its break-even fold frequency is bet ÷ (bet + pot). Bet ¾ pot and you need them to fold ~43% of the time just to break even. A station folds far less than that — call it 10-15%. The math is underwater before the cards are even relevant.

Firing a second and third barrel to 'represent' a hand against a station. They're not reading your story — they're staring at their own pair. Stop bluffing, start value-betting thin.
steps.memorize: You can't bluff someone who won't fold.

steps.prompt: You missed your draw on the river against a known calling station. The pot is 400. Do you fire a 300 bluff?
options: No — a station won't fold, so a bluff needing ~43% folds just burns money; give up
Yes — you must apply pressure
Yes — overbet to make it scary
steps.explain:
Break-even folds for a 300 bluff into 400 = 300 ÷ (400 + 300) = 300 ÷ 700 ≈ 43%.

A calling station folds well under 43% — often 15-20%. So the bluff loses money on average.

The single biggest live-cash leak: bluffing people who don't fold. Against stations, check-give-up your misses and bet your made hands thin. Exploit their inelastic calling, don't fight it.

steps.title: The Break-Even Bluff
steps.feel: When you bluff, you're paying to make villain fold. The bigger you bet, the more often you need it to work. Bet small and you don't need many folds; bet big and you're on the hook to get through a lot.
steps.formula:
A bluff of size b into a pot p needs folds ≥ b ÷ (p + b).

Bet 150 into 350 → 150 ÷ 500 = 30% folds to break even.
steps.proof:
EV of a pure bluff = (fold%)×(pot won) − (call%)×(amount risked). Set EV = 0:

f×p = (1 − f)×b → f×p + f×b = b → f = b ÷ (p + b).

Check the MIT example: bet 150 into 350. At f = 0.30: 0.30×350 − 0.70×150 = 105 − 105 = 0. ✓

At $1/$2-$2/$5 live, villains fold LESS than the math says — calling stations don't lay down. A pure bluff that needs 30% folds may only get 20%, so it bleeds money. Bluff into folders, not stations.
steps.memorize: Folds needed = bet ÷ (pot + bet).

steps.prompt: The pot is $350. You fire a pure bluff of $150. What fold percentage do you need just to break even?
steps.explain:
Folds needed = bet ÷ (pot + bet) = 150 ÷ (350 + 150) = 150 ÷ 500 = 30%.

Verify: 0.30×350 − 0.70×150 = 105 − 105 = 0. ✓

That's the floor with zero showdown value. Against a station who folds only 20%, this exact bluff is a loser — save it for hands with equity or opponents who actually fold.

steps.title: SPR tells you how strong a hand you need
steps.feel: SPR is the stack-to-pot ratio: how many pot-sized bets are left behind on the flop. It's the single number that tells you how good your hand needs to be to happily commit. Small SPR means there's little room to maneuver, so a decent made hand is fine to get in. Big SPR means there's a lot of money behind, so you should hold out for a monster before you commit your stack.
steps.formula:
SPR = effective stack ÷ pot (measured on the flop).
Low SPR ≤ 3-4 → top pair good kicker is happy to stack off.
High SPR > 8 → you want two pair+ (a set or better) to stack off.
steps.proof:
SPR compresses the whole hand into one decision. At SPR 3, one pot-sized bet and a raise gets it all in — there's no room for skill or draws to develop, so the hand that's ahead now (top pair) is usually the hand that wins. At SPR 10, stacking off means winning many bets across streets, which only the top of your range (sets, big two pair) can profitably do, because weaker hands get outdrawn or outplayed over that much money.

Effective stack is the SHORTER of the two stacks — you can only win or lose what the smaller stack allows.
steps.memorize: Low SPR, one pair is plenty. High SPR, bring the nuts.

steps.prompt: $1/$2. Preflop got big: the flop pot is $120 and effective stacks are only $200 behind. You have A-Q and flop top pair, top kicker. What does this SPR tell you?
options: SPR ≈ 1.7 — low. Top pair top kicker is happy to get it all in here.
SPR is high, so fold top pair to any aggression
SPR doesn't apply once the flop is out
steps.explain: SPR = $200 ÷ $120 ≈ 1.7. At that low an SPR there's barely room for one bet and a raise before stacks are in, and top pair top kicker is well ahead of the range that stacks off this shallow. You commit. High-SPR caution (needing two pair+) simply doesn't apply when there's less than two pot-sized bets left.

steps.title: Once you're committed, the decision was earlier
steps.feel: Being 'committed' means the pot has grown so large relative to your remaining stack that folding is mathematically wrong — you're getting such a good price that you call almost anything. The mistake players make is realizing this on the river. The truth is your commitment decision happened back on the flop when you chose to build the pot. Decide whether you're stacking off before you inflate the pot, not after.
steps.formula:
You're committed when the bet you face is ≤ ⅓ of your remaining stack AND you have a reasonable hand.
Roughly: once more than half your chips are in the middle, you're calling the rest with any real equity.
steps.proof:
Say $180 is in the pot and you have $60 behind facing a shove. You're getting $240-to-$60 = 4-to-1, needing only 20% equity to call. Almost any pair or draw clears that. The lesson isn't 'call the river' — it's that by making the pot this big with this hand, you already committed. So the real skill is choosing low-SPR lines only when your hand can handle getting it all in.

Building a big pot with a marginal hand at high SPR, then agonizing on the river. If your hand can't stack off, don't bloat the pot with it in the first place.
steps.memorize: Plan your commitment on the flop, not the river.

steps.title: SPR and chunking your stack to get all-in
steps.feel: No-limit pots grow exponentially — a tiny preflop pot can't reach a stack-off by the river without an ugly overbet, while the right size lets three clean bets do it. SPR (stack ÷ pot on the flop) tells you which betting line naturally gets it all in, so you plan streets instead of dumping chips awkwardly on the river.
steps.formula:
SPR = effective stack on the flop ÷ flop pot. Chunking lines to stack off by the river:
SPR ~13 → pot, pot, pot
SPR ~7 → ¾-pot × 3
SPR ~5.5 → pot, ½, ½
SPR ~3.5 → ½, ½, ½
steps.proof: Four pot-size bets exhaust a 100bb stack. Open pot to 7.5bb, one caller, you have ~96.5bb left → SPR = 96.5 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 13, and pot-pot-pot gets it in. A bigger preflop raise lowers SPR so fewer/smaller streets are needed. Watch how 50¢ preflop swings the river: a $6.50 vs $7.50 preflop pot becomes a $58.50 pot where you either bet $71 (awkward) or sit $12.50 above pot — plan it early.
steps.memorize: SPR = flop stack ÷ flop pot; ~13 means three pot bets stack off.

steps.prompt: You have 96.5bb behind and the flop pot is 7.5bb. What is your SPR, and which line stacks off by the river?
options: SPR ~13, pot-pot-pot
SPR ~7, ¾-pot ×3
SPR ~5.5, pot-half-half
SPR ~3.5, half-half-half
steps.explain: SPR = 96.5 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 13. At SPR ~13, three consecutive pot-size bets get the whole stack in by the river — exactly the top row of Gaines' chunking table.

steps.prompt: $2/$5. You flop top set on a wet board and the pot is $80. The player across from you is a classic station who calls down with any pair. Effective stacks are $600. What's the best sizing plan?
options: Bet big each street (~$70, then ~$200, then jam) to get max value and charge draws
Bet small (~$25) each street so you don't scare them
Check to trap since he'll bet for you
steps.explain: Against a station with the near-nuts on a wet board you want big bets: they pay you off AND they make draws pay to chase. Small sizing against someone who calls anyway just leaves money on the table. Trapping is worst — you have a strong hand on a draw-heavy board and want to build the pot now while you're ahead, not give free cards.

steps.prompt: You have second pair with a decent kicker on a dry river vs a calling station who never folds pairs. River goes check to you. What's the exploitative play?
options: Bet thin for value (~⅓ to ½ pot) — a station pays off worse hands
Check back — second pair can't bet
Overbet as a bluff
steps.explain:
Against a station the winning adjustment is value, value, value. They call with worse pairs and ace-highs, so a thin ~⅓-½ pot bet gets paid by hands that would never bet or raise you.

Never bluff a station — they don't fold. But DO bet thinner for value than you would vs a thinking player. Milk the calls; skip the bluffs.

steps.prompt: $2/$5. Three-way pot, $90 in the middle. You completely missed with A♥Q♥ on 9-6-2 rainbow. Two loose-passive stations are still in. It checks to you. Best play?
options: Check — bluffing 3-way vs two stations almost never works; take a free card
Bet $60 to represent an overpair
Bet $90 pot to fold both out
steps.explain: To win by bluffing you need both stations to fold. If each folds even 50% (generous for a station), that's 0.50² = 25% — and real stations fold far less, so it's closer to a few percent. You'd need ~40%+ fold equity to break even; you don't have a fraction of it. Check, keep the pot small, and maybe your ace-high is even good, or you improve.

steps.title: Turn outs into a percentage instantly
steps.feel: You need a fast way to know your chance of hitting. Count your outs — the cards that complete your hand. On the flop with two cards still to come, multiply outs by 4. On the turn with one card left, multiply by 2. That gives you a percentage close enough to make the decision. No long division at the table.
steps.formula:
Flop (2 cards to come): equity % ≈ outs × 4.
Turn (1 card to come): equity % ≈ outs × 2.
Flush draw = 9 outs. Open-ended straight = 8 outs. Gutshot = 4 outs.
steps.proof:
Each unseen card is ~1 in 47 on the flop. One out is about 1÷47 ≈ 2.1% per card, so ×2 per card, ×4 for two cards — the rule is just that arithmetic rounded. Flush draw: 9 outs × 4 ≈ 36% to hit by the river (true value ~35%). Open-ended: 8 × 4 ≈ 32% (~31.5%). The ×4 slightly overcounts for big draws because it double-counts, so shave a couple points on 12+ out monsters.

Flush draw ≈ 36% on the flop, ≈ 18% on the turn. Memorize those two and you'll rarely need the multiplication.
steps.memorize: Outs × 4 on the flop, × 2 on the turn.

steps.title: Direct odds vs implied odds
steps.feel: Direct pot odds ask: is the price I'm paying right now good enough given how often I hit? But that ignores the future. Implied odds are the extra chips you expect to win on later streets when your draw completes and your opponent pays you off. A draw that looks slightly too expensive at the direct price is often a clear call once you count the money you'll win when it gets there — especially against someone who can't fold.
steps.formula:
Direct: call if pot odds ≥ your chance of hitting.
Pot odds % = call ÷ (pot + call).
Implied: you can call below the direct price if the extra future winnings cover the gap.
steps.proof:
Direct pot odds compare the immediate risk to the immediate reward. Implied odds fold in future streets: the true reward isn't just the current pot, it's the current pot plus what you extract after you hit. So the break-even shifts. A gutshot getting only 5-to-1 direct (needs ~11-to-1) can still be a call if hitting it wins you 3-4 more big bets from a station who'll pay off your straight.

The pot on the table is a floor on your reward, not the ceiling. Implied odds count the money that isn't in there yet.
steps.memorize: Price the draw by what you'll win, not just what's in the pot now.

steps.prompt: You hold 6♦7♦ on 8♥ 9♣ 2♠ (open-ended, 8 outs). The pot is 320 and villain bets 150. Call or fold on pot odds?
options: Call — you have ~32% vs ~24% needed
Fold — a draw is never a call for this price
Raise all-in
steps.explain:
Pot odds: you call 150 to win 320 + 150 = 470. Required equity = 150 ÷ (470 + 150) = 150 ÷ 620 ≈ 24%.

An open-ended straight draw has 8 outs ≈ 32% by the turn's worth of equity (~4% per out × 8).

32% > 24% → profitable call before you even count implied odds. Straights are well-hidden, so the delta is easy to extract too.

steps.title: Semi-Bluff & the 1.5× Shortcut
steps.feel: A semi-bluff is a bluff with a backup plan: if villain calls, you can still hit your draw and win. That equity means you need FEWER folds than a stone-cold bluff — so betting a good draw is often clearly profitable even against loose callers.
steps.formula:
Start from the break-even fold%. Then for a ~pot-sized bet, subtract about 1.5 for each 1% of showdown (draw) equity.

Break-even 37% − 1.5×16 ≈ 24 → you only need ~13% folds.
steps.proof:
MIT straight-draw spot: bet 450 into 775. Break-even folds = 450 ÷ (775 + 450) = 450 ÷ 1225 ≈ 37%.

Your draw gives ~16% equity when called. Each 1% of equity buys back a chunk of the fold% you'd otherwise need — for a roughly pot-sized bet the multiplier lands near 1.5 (bounded between 1 and 2).

37 − (1.5 × 16) = 37 − 24 = 13. You now need only ~13% folds.

Almost anyone folds 13% of the time. That's why betting your draws beats meekly calling — you win now sometimes AND you win later sometimes.
Sklansky coined the term "semi-bluff" in The Theory of Poker.
Correction. The 1.5 multiplier is an approximation valid near pot-sized bets; it runs from about 1 (small bets) to 2 (big overbets) and assumes your equity is realised when called. Gaines' exact form: needed folds = (B − e·(P + 2B)) / (P + B − e·(P + 2B)).
steps.memorize: Semi-bluff fold% ≈ break-even − 1.5×(draw equity%).

steps.prompt: You bet 450 into a 775 pot with a straight draw worth ~16% equity when called. Roughly what fold% do you actually need for this semi-bluff to break even?
steps.explain:
Raw break-even folds = 450 ÷ (775 + 450) = 450 ÷ 1225 ≈ 37%.

Credit the draw: subtract ~1.5 per 1% equity → 1.5 × 16 ≈ 24.

37 − 24 ≈ 13%. You only need ~13% folds.

Even a station-ish caller folds this often, and when they don't you still have a live straight draw. Clear bet.

steps.prompt: You c-bet ~1800 into a similar-sized pot with a gutshot (break-even folds ≈ 33%). Adding fold-equity credit for the gutshot, is this stab profitable?
options: Yes — the gutshot equity drops your required folds well below 33%, and you'll get folds often enough
No — a gutshot has too little equity to ever bet
Only if you have the nuts already
steps.explain:
Break-even folds ≈ 33% for this sizing. A gutshot is ~4 outs ≈ 8-9% equity by the river's worth of cards, so credit ≈ 1.5×8 ≈ 12 points off.

33 − 12 ≈ 21% folds needed. On a K-J-3 board where you rep the top of your range, villain folds far more than 21% of the time.

A♦Q♦ also has overcard + backdoor equity on top of the gutshot, so the real break-even is even more forgiving. Fire it.

steps.title: Call 20 to win 200 with a small pair
steps.feel: Small pairs like 5-5 rarely improve, but when they hit a set on the flop they're a hidden monster that wins big pots. The trick is to only pay to see the flop when the potential payoff is huge relative to your call. If there's a lot of money behind to win, a cheap call is great. If stacks are short, you can't win enough to justify chasing a card that misses most of the time — so fold.
steps.formula:
Set-mine when effective stacks ≥ ~15-20× the amount you must call.
You flop a set ~1 in 8.5 (≈ 12%).
Call $20 to a raise only if there's ≈ $300-400 behind to win.
steps.proof:
You flop a set about 11.8% of the time — call it 1 in 8.5. To break even on a $20 call that only cashes when you hit, you'd need to win roughly 7.5× your call back on those hits (the other 7.5 misses each cost you the $20). Winning 15-20× the call means the winning hands more than cover all the misses, with profit to spare. Against a station who stacks off with top pair, the multiplier you actually realize is even higher.

Set-mining short-stacked. If there's only 8× behind, you can't win enough on your rare sets to pay for all the times you whiff. Fold the small pair and wait for a deeper spot.
steps.memorize: Set-mine only when the payoff is 15-20× the call.

steps.prompt: $2/$5. A tight player opens to $25. You have 4♦4♣ on the button. Two players have already called. Effective stacks are $600. Call to set-mine?
options: Call — $600 behind is 24× the $25 call, well past the 15-20× threshold, and multiway sweetens the payoff
Fold — small pairs should never call a raise
3-bet to $90 to build a pot with your pair
steps.explain: $600 ÷ $25 = 24×, comfortably above the 15-20× set-mining threshold. You flop a set ~12% and the deep stacks let you win a full stack when you do. Multiway callers add dead money and more people to stack. 3-betting a small pair just bloats the pot with a hand that misses the flop 88% of the time — set-mine, don't inflate.

steps.title: Implied Odds, Done Right
steps.feel: Sometimes the current price is too high to call a draw — but if you'll get paid off BIG when you hit, the call is fine. The trick: figure out how much extra money you need to win later, then ask honestly whether it's actually there.
steps.formula:
Required final pot = bet ÷ your equity.

Delta = (required pot) − (current pot). That delta is the dead money you must extract later.
steps.proof:
MIT flush-draw spot: you have ~18% equity facing 180 into 300.

Required final pot = 180 ÷ 0.18 = 1000.

Current pot after the call ≈ 300 + 180 = 480... but MIT frames it against the 300 pot: you need the final pot to reach 1000, so you need roughly 340 MORE dead money to come in on later streets. Call only if that 340+ is realistically extractable.

Hidden-ness ranking (how much you'll get paid when you hit):

Sets = invisible → huge implied odds. Straights = medium. Flushes = obvious (three to a suit on board) → small implied odds.

Paired board? You may be drawing DEAD to a full house. And don't assume you'll see BOTH remaining cards — if villain barrels, your "two cards" of equity shrinks to one. Discount accordingly.
Gaines’ shortcut: required final pot = bet ÷ your equity%; the extra beyond the current pot is what you must win later.
steps.memorize: Required pot = bet ÷ equity; the delta must be truly extractable.

steps.prompt: You have an ~18% flush draw facing a bet of 180 into a 300 pot. What final pot do you need to justify the call, and how much extra dead money must come later?
options: Need a ~$1000 final pot → about $340 more must be extractable
Need a ~$480 final pot → nothing more required
Need a ~$1800 final pot → about $1500 more
steps.explain:
Required final pot = bet ÷ equity = 180 ÷ 0.18 = $1000.

Against the current $300 pot, that's roughly $340 of additional dead money you need to win on later streets (beyond the immediate bet you're calling).

A flush draw is the most OBVIOUS draw — three suited cards will hit the board and villain slows down. So this $340 is often hard to get. Sets get paid; flushes get respected.

steps.prompt: You have a draw worth ~15% (use the 6× row). Villain bets $6 on the turn. How much total must you win to justify the call?
steps.explain: 15% equity → multiply his bet by 6: 6 × $6 = $36 total needed. You then subtract the pot already in front of you to see how much MORE you must extract on the river.

steps.prompt: $1/$2. You have the nut flush draw on the flop. Villain (a station) bets $30 into a $60 pot. Effective stacks are $400. Do the direct odds alone make it a call, and does it matter?
options: Direct odds are borderline (~33% needed vs ~35% equity) but implied odds vs a deep station make it a clear call
Fold — a flush draw is never worth chasing against a bet
Raise all-in; a flush draw has more equity than a made hand
steps.explain: You need $30 ÷ ($60+$30+$30) = $30÷$120 = 25% to call directly, and your 9-out nut flush draw is ~35% by the river (~18% next card) — already fine. Add the $370 behind and a station who pays off your nut flush and it's a slam-dunk call. Shoving a draw with no fold equity vs a station just turns your equity into a coinflip you didn't need to gamble.

steps.title: Reverse implied odds — the hands that cost you when you 'hit'
steps.feel: Some draws are dangerous precisely because they complete into second-best hands. Chasing a weak flush with a low card, or a bottom-end straight, you can hit your card and still be beat by a bigger version of the same hand — and now you lose a big pot instead of a small one. These hands have reverse implied odds: hitting can cost you more than missing. Discount them, especially out of position.
steps.formula:
Reverse implied hands: low flush draws (e.g. 6♠4♠ chasing spades), bottom-end straights (dummy end), weak two-way draws.
Rule: lower the payoff when hitting can make you the second-best hand.
steps.proof:
Standard implied odds assume that hitting = winning. Reverse implied odds are the correction: sometimes hitting = paying off a bigger hand. A 6-high flush draw might complete, get you excited, then run into the ace-high flush — you don't just miss the profit, you lose stacks. The true value of such a draw is its winning outs minus the expensive losing outs, which can drag a 'made' hand into negative EV.

Treating every flush draw as equal. A nut flush draw is a green light; a baby flush draw out of position against a raiser is a trap. Same 9 outs, opposite money.
steps.memorize: If hitting can still lose, the draw is worth less than it looks.

steps.prompt: $1/$2. You hold 7♠5♠ and flop a baby flush draw. A tight, aggressive nit fires $40 into $50 on a board with two spades. Stacks are $250. He shuts down whenever draws complete. Call to chase your flush?
options: Fold — baby flush draw with reverse implied odds vs a nit who won't pay when the third spade lands
Call — any flush draw is a mandatory call getting near the right price
Raise to represent the flush draw as a made hand
steps.explain: Two problems stack up: reverse implied odds (a 7-high flush can complete and still lose to a bigger spade), and a nit who folds exactly when the flush arrives, killing your implied odds. So you have little future money to win and real risk of paying off a bigger flush. The direct price isn't good enough on its own, and the implied case is gutted. Fold.

steps.prompt: You hold a bare flush draw, but the board is PAIRED and villain fires a big bet on the turn. What's the disciplined play?
options: Fold — reverse implied odds; even if you hit, a full house may already have you dead
Call — a flush is a flush
Raise — represent the boat
steps.explain:
On a paired board, villain's value range includes trips and full houses. If you complete your flush, you can be drawing DEAD to a made boat — you pay to hit and still lose.

Reverse implied odds mean your effective equity is lower than the raw 18%, and you may lose a big pot even when the card 'comes in.'

Never auto-play a flush draw. Pair the board + big bet = the classic 'don't draw here' spot. Fold.

steps.prompt: Jacobson at the WSOP: you hold A♣J♣ on 7♦ 8♠ T♥ 2♣ — a nut-flush draw plus an open-ender, ~42% equity (10.5 outs). Villain jams 4525 into a 14450 pot (you're contributing ~31% of the call). Call or fold?
options: Call — ~42% equity beats the ~31% you need to put in
Fold — you have no made hand
Call only if you have the nuts
steps.explain:
Nut-flush draw (9 clubs) + open-ender adds ~1.5 clean straight outs beyond the flush = ~10.5 outs ≈ 42% equity.

You must contribute ~31% of the final pot to call the 4525 jam into 14450. Since 42% > 31%, calling is +EV.

A monster combo draw with the NUT flush means no reverse-implied worries — when you hit clubs you have the best hand. Snap call.

steps.prompt: You hold 5♠5♦ (set of 5s) on 3♣ 5♥ A♦ 6♣ — two clubs out there. Villain bets a small 200 into a large pot. What do you do?
options: Call — you have 7 outs to a boat/quads and villain is under-betting
Fold — a flush is coming
Fold — the ace beats you
steps.explain:
You have bottom set. Even against a made flush you have redraw outs: the case 5 (quads) plus pairing the board (three 3s, three As, three 6s) → the board pairs give you a full house. That's roughly 7+ outs to improve.

Villain's tiny 200 bet into a big pot is a classic under-bet — a great price to continue, and often it's a weaker hand or a semi-bluff. You're getting huge odds to draw and you may already be ahead.

Sets are invisible — villain has no idea you're this strong, so your implied odds are enormous when you fill up.

steps.prompt: Button: you raise 6♥4♥, BB calls in a way that screams strength. Flop K♥7♦3♠ — you have a gutshot + backdoor flush, out of the betting lead's crosshairs. Villain is a trapper. Best line per Negreanu?
options: Bet 60% to represent the king
Check behind / take the free card so a check-raise can't blow you off your belly-buster
Check-raise all in as a semibluff
Fold face-up
steps.explain: Negreanu: the worst play is betting yourself off a draw. If you bet and the trapper check-raises, you must fold and lose the chance to fill the gutshot or pick up the backdoor. Take the free card. (He also warns: don't ALWAYS check your draws or you become readable.) Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.title: When below-price calls are right — and when they're a leak
steps.feel: Put it together. A slightly-too-expensive draw is a call when the future money is real: you're deep, you have position, and your opponent is a station who'll pay you off when you get there. It's a fold when the future money isn't real: stacks are shallow so there's little to win, or your opponent is a nit who shuts down the moment the obvious draw completes, or your draw is a reverse-implied trap.
steps.formula:
Call below direct price when: deep stacks + position + station who pays.
Fold below direct price when: shallow, out of position, vs a nit, or holding a reverse-implied draw.
steps.proof:
Implied odds are the entire justification for a below-price call, and implied odds only exist if you can actually collect future bets. Depth provides the chips to win; position lets you control the pot and extract on your terms; a station provides the payoff. Remove any one and the math that made the call profitable disappears — you're now just calling a losing price and hoping.

Draw math has three inputs: your equity, the price, and the collectible future money. Change the opponent and the third input changes — so the same draw is a call vs one player and a fold vs another.
steps.memorize: Chase light only when deep, in position, and paid off.

steps.title: Every extra player shrinks your edge
steps.feel: Heads-up, you only have to get through one hand. In a family pot with four callers, someone almost always connected with the flop. Range and nut advantage barely exist multiway - the board belongs to whoever hit it, and with more players, someone always did.
steps.formula:
Heads-up: range advantage is real → bet often.
3+ players: assume someone hit → bet only real value, check your bluffs.
steps.proof:
Fold equity multiplies against you. If each opponent folds 60% of the time, one opponent folds 60%, but getting all of two to fold is 0.60 × 0.60 = 36%, and three is 0.60³ ≈ 22%. Your bluff needed folds - now you rarely get them.

Simultaneously, the chance that at least one player flopped a strong hand climbs fast with more players, so your average hand is ahead far less often. Range advantage - an average-equity concept - evaporates.

Multiway, stop bluffing and start value-betting only hands that beat a pair. The pot is big and someone will pay you - you don't need to fold anyone out.
steps.memorize: More players in, fewer bluffs out.

steps.title: In a crowd, somebody connected
steps.feel: Heads-up, most flops miss your opponent and a single bet often takes it. But when three, four, or five players see the flop, the board almost always smacks somebody. That changes everything: a hand that would happily bet for value heads-up is now often beat by one of the several people who called. Respect the crowd. Assume someone has a real piece and only push hard with hands that beat 'a real piece.'
steps.formula:
Chance nobody hit ≈ (miss rate) ^ (number of opponents).
If each opponent misses top pair+ ~65% of the time: 2 players → 0.65² ≈ 42% nobody hit; 4 players → 0.65⁴ ≈ 18%.
So with 4 opponents, someone has a piece ~82% of the time.
steps.proof:
Independent opponents multiply. If one random opponent connects with the board 35% of the time, the chance ALL of them miss is 0.65^N. With N=1 that's 65% miss (35% someone hit). With N=4 it collapses to 0.65⁴ ≈ 18% — meaning 82% of the time at least one of them has something worth continuing with. The field, not any single player, is what you're up against.

Each extra caller multiplies the chance the board hit someone. Four callers ≈ 'assume the flop hit the table.'
steps.memorize: More players in, higher the odds someone flopped it.

steps.title: Raise your value threshold
steps.feel: Because someone probably connected, the hands you're willing to bet big and stack off with need to be stronger multiway. Heads-up, top pair is a monster. Four-way, top pair with a weak kicker is a hand that's often already beat and can only get called by better. Marginal made hands slide from 'value bet' to 'pot control' — check, keep the pot small, and don't get married.
steps.formula:
Heads-up value bar: top pair, any decent kicker.
Multiway (3+) value bar: top pair top kicker, an overpair, or better — otherwise check.
Top pair weak kicker multiway → pot control, not value bet.
steps.proof:
A value bet needs worse hands to call you more than half the time. Heads-up, one opponent's calling range contains plenty of worse pairs and draws. Multiway, you must beat the calling ranges of everyone still in — and the more players, the more likely at least one of those ranges has you crushed. Your hand's equity against 'the best of four random continuing ranges' is far lower than against one, so the bar for a profitable value bet rises.

Value-betting top-pair-weak-kicker into three callers and getting raised. You weren't ahead of the field — you were ahead of one player and behind the group.
steps.memorize: Multiway, only strong hands bet for value.

steps.prompt: $1/$2. Four players see the flop. You have A♣8♣ and flop top pair, weak-ish kicker on K-8-3. It checks to you last. Pot is $40. Best play multiway?
options: Check — top pair weak kicker is marginal 4-way; keep the pot small and pot-control
Bet $35 for value; top pair is always a value bet
Bet $60 to blast everyone off their hands
steps.explain: Four-way, someone connects with K-8-3 far more often (0.65⁴ ≈ 18% nobody hit, so ~82% someone has a piece). Middle pair with a weak kicker is well behind the field's continuing range and gets called mostly by better. Betting bloats a pot you're often losing; a big 'blast' bluff into three players almost never clears the field. Check, keep it small, reassess.

steps.title: Bluffs die in multiway pots
steps.feel: To win a pot by bluffing you have to get everyone to fold. Getting one person to fold is hard enough; getting three or four to fold all at once is nearly impossible — someone almost always has enough to call. So in multiway pots, drastically cut your bluffing. If you don't have a real hand or a strong draw, check and give up. Bluffing into a crowd is lighting money on fire.
steps.formula:
Everyone-folds chance ≈ (one fold%) ^ (number of opponents).
If each folds 60% to your bet: heads-up 60%, but 3-way 0.60³ ≈ 22%, 4-way 0.60⁴ ≈ 13%.
Rule: 3+ players → bluff frequency ≈ 0.
steps.proof:
Fold equity multiplies against you. A bet that folds out any single opponent 60% of the time clears the whole field only 0.6^N of the time. Three-way that's ~22%; four-way ~13%. Meanwhile your bluff needs roughly bet ÷ (bet + pot) fold equity just to break even — say 40%+. You're not close. Add live stations who don't fold at all and multiway bluff EV is deeply negative.

One caller kills a bluff. In multiway you need EVERY player to fold, and that product shrinks fast.
steps.memorize: You can't bluff a crowd — check and give up.

steps.prompt: You raised, THREE players called. Flop Q-J-9 two clubs, you hold A-K offsuit (gutshot + overs, no pair). Four players total. Best play?
options: C-bet ½ pot - I have the range advantage
Check - multiway, wet board, no made hand
Bet big to protect against the flush draw
steps.explain: Range advantage barely exists four-handed, and this wet, connected board smashes calling ranges. Fold equity against three players is tiny (you'd need all three to fold), and you have no made hand to protect. Check, see a cheap turn, and try to hit your straight. Bluffing here burns chips.

steps.title: Nut hands and nut draws gain value; one-pair loses it
steps.feel: Multiway isn't all bad news — it's actually great for your very best hands and your best draws. With more players in, there are more people to pay off when you have the nuts, and more callers to build a big pot behind your nut flush draw. The flip side: marginal one-pair hands lose value because they're more likely beaten and get less credit. Play a polarized game multiway: hammer the top of your range, fold the mush.
steps.formula:
Multiway value shift:
Nut hands / nut draws → UP (more payers, bigger pots).
One-pair / marginal made → DOWN (more likely beaten).
Bet big with the nuts; check-fold the marginal.
steps.proof:
A nut draw's implied odds scale with the number of opponents who can pay it off — three callers means roughly triple the potential payoff of a heads-up pot. And a made nut hand collects from every second-best hand in the field. But a one-pair hand's chance of being best decreases with each added opponent (that 0.65^N effect), so its raw equity and its value-betting profitability both fall. The result: multiway pushes correct play toward the extremes.

Multiway rewards the nuts and punishes the marginal. It's a polarizing dynamic — be strong or be gone.
steps.memorize: Multiway: nuts go up, one-pair goes down.

steps.prompt: $2/$5. Five-way limped pot, $50 in the middle. You have the nut flush draw plus an overcard on the flop. It checks to you in the cutoff with $500 behind everyone. What's the multiway read?
options: This is a great spot — nut draws GAIN value multiway; bet big to build a huge pot for when you hit and get many payers
Check because multiway means you should always play passively
Fold the flush draw since multiway someone likely has a set
steps.explain: Nut draws are exactly the hands that go UP in value multiway: five opponents means five potential payers, so your implied odds balloon. You have ~35% equity to river the nut flush plus overcard outs, and no reverse-implied worry since it's the nut flush. Betting builds the pot you'll win big when you hit; passivity and folding both throw away the multiway upside.

steps.title: Position is worth even more with a crowd
steps.feel: Acting last is always an advantage, but multiway it's huge. When you're last to act you get to watch several players reveal their intentions before you commit a chip. If two of them show strength, you fold your marginal hand for free. Out of position against a crowd, you're guessing against many unknowns at once. Play tighter out of position multiway, and lean on position to control the pot and realize your equity.
steps.formula:
Multiway, in position: see the whole field act, then decide → widen slightly, control pot.
Multiway, out of position: acting into many unknowns → tighten, check more, avoid bloating.
steps.proof:
Position converts information into money. Heads-up you gain the read of one player by acting last; multiway you gain the reads of everyone who acts before you — and each read lets you fold losers and value-bet winners more accurately. Out of position you invert this: you commit chips before seeing a single response, and against N opponents the odds one of them wakes up with a hand behind you are high (0.65^N again). So the equity you actually realize out of position multiway is much lower than your raw equity.

Position = free information. Multiway there's more information to be had, so position is worth more.
steps.memorize: The more players, the more position pays.

steps.title: Keep marginal pots small; check and give up more
steps.feel: The default multiway mistake is trying to make things happen with mediocre hands — betting middle pair, barreling weak draws, ballooning a pot you're likely to lose. Do the opposite. With marginal hands multiway, keep the pot small: check, take free cards, and be willing to give up when you face resistance. Save the big pots for your big hands. Pot discipline multiway is most of the edge.
steps.formula:
Marginal hand multiway → check, keep pot small, give up to aggression.
Only bloat the pot with nut hands and nut draws.
When in doubt with one pair vs a crowd, check-fold beats bet-call.
steps.proof:
Every chip you put in a pot you'll usually lose is negative EV, and multiway you'll usually lose the marginal pots (0.65^N says someone has you beat). Keeping the pot small caps your losses on the hands where you're behind — which is most of the marginal ones — while you still occasionally win a small pot when everyone misses. Reserving big pots for nut hands maximizes the money in when you're a favorite. The asymmetry (small when weak, big when strong) is exactly what raises your win rate multiway.

'I have to bet, someone might fold.' Multiway they usually won't, and you've turned a cheap loss into an expensive one. Check the marginal hands.
steps.memorize: Small pots with mush, big pots with the nuts.

steps.title: Blockers pick your bluffs and raises
steps.feel:
A blocker is a card in your hand that tells you what villain can't have — and he doesn't know you hold it. When you can only bluff or raise with a few combos, let blockers break the tie. Pick the hand that blocks villain's continues and unblocks his folds.

Classic: you hold A♠K♥ on Q♠ J♦ 7♠ 6♦ 4♠. Your A♠ is the nut-flush blocker — no one can have the nut flush, and no one else knows. The risk of running into a flush collapses, so bluffing becomes profitable.
steps.formula:
Brokos: "Blockers are the be-all and end-all of no-limit strategy. Usually they function as tiebreakers." To value-raise, hold the card that blocks the hand that beats you — raise AJ over 99 because AJ blocks JJ. A J in your hand means villain has fewer JJ and AJ, so you're far less likely to run into the nuts.

To bluff-catch, prefer hands that block villain's value bets (hold a J when he reps AJ/JJ). At equilibrium river bluffs are usually indifferent — EV 0 — except with your weakest hands and when you hold important blockers, where bluffing turns strictly +EV.
steps.proof: Combinatorics. There are 6 combos of any unpaired hand and 3 combos of a pair given one blocker. If villain's value range on a J-high runout is AJ and JJ, holding a J removes half his AJ combos and a third of his JJ combos, materially cutting the hands that beat you. So AJ (two pair) makes a safer value-raise than 99 (a set) against a possible JJ, because AJ itself blocks JJ. The same math is why "BB never folds when she has a J": the J blocks the exact hands UTG value-bets, so she calls or raises, never folds.
steps.memorize: Bluff/raise with cards that block villain's continues. Raise AJ over 99 — AJ blocks JJ.

steps.prompt: River, board Q♠ J♦ 7♠ 6♦ 4♠. You check-raise for value. You can rep it with either 9♦9♣ (a set) or A♦J♠ (top two). Villain's most likely better hand is a set of jacks (JJ). Which is the safer value-raise?
options: 99 — a set beats more of villain's calling range
AJ — it blocks JJ, so villain is far less likely to hold the hand that beats you
Neither — the A♠ means you should just bluff, not value-raise
99 — AJ can't beat a flush and 99 can
steps.explain: Prefer the value-raise that blocks the hand that beats you. AJ contains a J, which removes JJ combos from villain's range — so holding AJ makes a better-hand JJ much less likely than holding 99 does. Brokos: BB raises top-two (AJ) over middle-set (99) versus an overbet precisely because AJ blocks JJ, cutting the risk of running into a better hand. Neither hand's raw rank is the point; the blocker is. (The A♠ also blocks the nut flush, which is why bluff-raises here want a J and/or the A♠ too.)

steps.prompt: River, pot is $100, you bet $100 (pot). To be balanced (unexploitable), villain must be indifferent, so you want roughly a 2:1 value-to-bluff ratio. You have 6 value combos. How many bluff combos should you bet?
steps.explain: A pot-sized bet lays villain 2:1, so at equilibrium your betting range should be ~2 parts value to 1 part bluff. With 6 value combos you want ~3 bluff combos (6:3 = 2:1). Bigger bets allow MORE bluffs (an overbet shifts toward 1:1); smaller bets allow fewer. You build the range by counting combos to hit the target ratio — then pick the bluffs by blocker quality.

steps.title: Bigger bets need more bluffs; pick the size for the range you want
steps.feel: The size you choose is really a choice about villain's range. Bet small and he calls wide and weak; bet big and only his strong hands stay. So decide which of his hands you want to be up against, then price it.
steps.formula: River value fraction = (X+1)/(2X+1) where X is the bet in pot-sized bets. Half-pot (X=0.5): 3/4 value, 1 bluff per 3 value. Pot (X=1): 2/3 value, 1 per 2. 1.5x overbet: 5/8 value, 3 bluffs per 5 value. Bigger bet -> worse odds for villain -> you get to add more bluffs.
steps.memorize: Small bet = wide/weak caller + fewer bluffs allowed. Big bet = narrow/strong caller + more bluffs allowed. Choose size by which of villain's hands you want to face, not by habit.
steps.proof: River value fraction = (X+1)/(X+2) where X is bet in pot-sized bets. Half-pot (X=0.5): 3/4 value, 1 bluff per 3 value. Pot (X=1): 2/3 value, 1 per 2. 1.5x overbet: 5/8 value, 3 bluffs per 5 value. Bigger bet → worse odds for villain → you get to add more bluffs. Working the whole street chain: 75% pot each street ⇒ ~34% of flop bets are value; allow a river overbet ⇒ only ~31%.

steps.title: How many bluffs a value bet supports, by street
steps.feel: On the river you bet good hands and bluff a little. But when you fire the flop planning three barrels, most of your betting range should be bluffs — because bluffs get to peel off street by street while the value bets keep going.
steps.formula: Work backwards from the river. A bet of X pot-sized bets makes villain indifferent when your betting range is V value / (V+B) bluffs with V/(V+B) = (X+1)/(2X+1). That same fraction is the frequency the earlier street must keep betting. Chain them: each street's value fraction is the product of the later streets' bet frequencies, so value's share compounds toward the nuts as streets run out.
steps.memorize: Same value hands fire every street; you shed a layer of bluffs each street. Value-bet share compounds toward the nuts as streets run out. Flop ≈ mostly bluffs, turn ≈ half bluffs, river ≈ a quarter to a third bluffs.
steps.proof: Work backwards from the river. A bet of X pot-sized bets makes villain indifferent when your betting range is V value / (V+B) bluffs with V/(V+B) = (X+1)/(X+2). That same fraction is the frequency the earlier street must keep betting. Chain them: flop value fraction = (turn bet freq)(river bet freq)(river value fraction). Pot-sized bets, perfectly polarized: river = 2/3 value, turn = (2/3)² = 4/9 value, flop = (2/3)³ ≈ 30% value — so ~70% of your pot-sized flop bets are bluffs.

steps.title: Building the turn & river betting range
steps.feel: Value hands to bet each street are the ones that can barrel again for value — not marginal made hands that turn into bluff-catchers the moment you check. For bluffs, earlier streets want equity, the river wants blockers.
steps.formula: Earlier streets: bluff with hands that retain equity and whose future card 'signals' improvement (a gutshot+overcards that picks up a draw), so you can keep firing when you improve and give up when you don't. River: all bluffs have 0 equity when called, so bluff with the best card removal — block villain's calling combos, avoid blocking his folding combos. Your value share rises each street because the worst bluffs check-fold behind.
steps.memorize: Bet value hands that can fire again. Flop/turn bluffs = equity + a signal to continue. River bluffs = blockers. Bluff share falls, value share climbs, on every later street.
steps.proof: Earlier streets: bluff with hands that retain equity and whose future card 'signals' improvement (a gutshot+overcards that picks up a draw), so you can keep firing when you improve and give up when you don't. River: all bluffs have 0 equity when called, so bluff with the best card removal — block villain's calling combos, avoid blocking his folding combos. Your value share rises each street because the worst bluffs check-fold behind.

steps.title: When the polarized overbet is correct
steps.feel: Overbet the river when villain simply can't have many strong hands — usually a wet turn that just bricked. He couldn't slowplay a monster on a draw-heavy board without risking getting outdrawn, so a blank river caps him and you bomb it.
steps.formula: Overbet ≈ maximally polarized: 1.5x pot needs only 5/8 (62.5%) value, and the optimal-river-size formula gives the exact amount given how often you're effectively beaten (Y). Correct when villain's calling range is capped — draw-heavy turn (J♥T♥6♣5♣) makes slowplaying too costly, so a brick river leaves him almost no nutted hands. On dry turns (Q♥Q♠7♣2♦) he can slowplay cheaply, so his range isn't capped — bet smaller.
steps.memorize: Overbet when villain is capped: wet turn + blank river. Dry turn = he can slowplay = don't overbet. More streets left = don't overbet yet (that's why overbets cluster on the river).
steps.proof: Overbet ≈ maximally polarized: 1.5x pot needs only 5/8 (62.5%) value, and the optimal-river-size formula gives the exact amount given how often you're effectively beaten (Y). Correct when villain's calling range is capped — draw-heavy turn (J♥T♥6♣5♣) makes slowplaying too costly, so a brick river leaves him almost no nutted hands. On dry turns (Q♥Q♠7♣2♦) he can slowplay cheaply, so his range isn't capped — bet smaller.

steps.title: Don't leave your checking range too weak
steps.feel: If you bet every hand that can 'get called by worse,' your checks become a pile of trash and villain hammers you — check-raising when you bet, stabbing when you check. Some strong-ish hands have to check on purpose to protect the check.
steps.formula: Betting all hands but medium pairs pushes your flop bet frequency toward 80% and makes villain's check-raise crush you. Keep some strong hands back (top pair good kicker as a check-call/turn value bet) and even slowplay a few nuts on dry boards so villain can't overbet your capped range. On the river, out of position, a small bet ≈ checking; and a small in-position bet is often worse than checking when villain can check-raise, since a bluff-raise makes you effectively lose the whole pot.
steps.memorize: Betting too much → weak checks → exploited by check-raises and river stabs. Protect checks by trapping some value and slowplaying a few nuts. Betting reopens the action, so a thin in-position bet loses to a check-raising villain.
steps.proof: Betting all hands but medium pairs pushes your flop bet frequency toward 80% and makes villain's check-raise crush you. Keep some strong hands back (top pair good kicker as a check-call/turn value bet) and even slowplay a few nuts on dry boards so villain can't overbet your capped range. On the river, out of position, a small bet ≈ checking; and a small in-position bet is often worse than checking when villain can check-raise, since a bluff-raise makes you effectively lose the whole pot.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: read your OWN distribution first
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8 (Decision Making), WSOP bracelet winner Matt Hawrilenko: "I think you should not think about anything else in poker until you have bought and paid for a house by knowing where you are in your own distribution... Everything else is just window dressing compared to this concept."

The move most players make — put the villain on a hand, do pot-odds magic — he calls a trap: "Any time you try to divine your opponent's strategy, she can do the same thing back to you." So forget their hand. Rank YOUR whole range on this exact runout, find where your actual hand sits, and act from there.
steps.formula: Rank your range on the runout. Continue with the top 1/(1+s) of it; fold the rest. Your hand's percentile decides — not a guess at his.
steps.proof:
Hawrilenko's own hand: deep, he holds aces on K-J-8-5-K facing a 1.5× pot bet. 1/(1+s) with s=1.5 → call 40% of hands that beat a bluff. He ranks his range, finds aces sit at the 62nd percentile — below the 40% threshold — so aces are a clear fold. "Of the hands that beat a bluff, like half of them have trips." His distribution is so strong that even a 90%-bluffing villain can't exploit the fold.

Correction. "Not exploited even by a 90% bluffer" is true only in the unexploitable sense. Against a villain you know bluffs 90% of the time, folding aces is a large EV loss: exploit him and call.
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: know thyself — locate your hand in YOUR ranked range, then apply 1/(1+s).

steps.prompt: MIT's Hawrilenko: villain bets 40% of the pot on the river. What fraction of your range that beats a bluff should you continue with?
options: About 71% — call 1/(1+s) with s=0.4
50% always
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L8: continue 1/(1+s). With s=0.4, that's 1/1.4 ≈ 71%. He bluffs s/(1+s) = 0.4/1.4 ≈ 29% of the time. Bigger bet → call less; smaller bet → call more. This makes his bluffs exactly zero-EV regardless of what he actually holds.

steps.prompt: In MIT's example Hawrilenko finds he must fold aces (which beat many hands) to a big river bet. What does he say that discomfort really signals?
options: The math is wrong; never fold a strong hand
Maybe he built the wrong distribution getting there — he should have arrived with a wider range so aces would be a call
He should stare the villain down for a tell
River folds are always correct with one pair
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L8: "one thing we could do is I probably want a distribution where I don't have to fold it." The fix is upstream — play/value-bet more hands earlier so your river range is wide enough that aces become a call. Same spot, same hand, different action, because the path to get there was different.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: one hand's plan sets every other hand's plan
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8, Hawrilenko on the Ace-King-Queen toy game: "Your strategy for what you do with one hand determines your strategy for other hands." If you bet all your aces (value), you must bluff the very bottom of your range; if you call all your aces, you must call some kings too. Get one leg out of proportion and "now I'm out of whack, now I'm out of balance, and I'm going to lose more."

Quoting Jerrod Ankenman at MIT: "If I truly played optimally, I could write down my entire strategy on a piece of paper... give it to you and you couldn't beat me." Balance, not deception, is the shield.
steps.formula: Widen value → widen bluffs to match (keep the value:bluff the bet size demands — 2:1 at a pot bet, 3:1 at half-pot). Widen calls → the whole calling region shifts. They move together.
steps.proof: The Apollo inscriptions Hawrilenko cites: know thyself (know your distribution), nothing in excess (play balanced). When his aces don't want to be a fold, the fix isn't to hero-call — it's to have arrived with a wider value-betting range earlier so the distribution stretches and aces become a call. "You see these really good players making crazily thin value bets — this is why: they're bluffing a lot so they value bet a lot."
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: value width and bluff width are locked together — imbalance in one leaks in the other.

steps.title: G-bucks: judge the decision, not the flip
steps.feel: Villain flipping over aces doesn't mean you misplayed — you were never playing against his exact cards, you were playing against his range. Real-bucks (what you won) and Sklansky-bucks (EV vs his revealed hand) both mislead. G-bucks scores your decision against the range you correctly put him on, which is all the information you actually had.
steps.formula: G-bucks EV = (your equity vs his assumed RANGE) × (pot) − (what you risk). Compare to Sklansky-bucks, which uses equity vs his one revealed hand.
steps.proof: You get it in with KK vs a JJ+/AK shoving range. He tables AA. Sklansky-bucks: 0.18($1,280) + 0.82(−$720) = −$360 (looks awful). But vs his whole JJ+/AK range KK has 66%: 0.66($1,280) + 0.34(−$720) = +$600. Same decision, and G-bucks correctly calls it great — you just ran into the top of his range this time. Don't let the flip talk you out of a +EV call.
steps.memorize: Grade against the range you read, not the card he happened to flip.

steps.prompt: You get it in with KK ($1,280 pot, you risk $720) vs a JJ+/AK range where KK has 66% equity. Villain tables AA. What are your G-bucks?
steps.explain: G-bucks uses equity vs the RANGE, not the revealed hand: 0.66($1,280) + 0.34(−$720) = $844.80 − $244.80 = +$600. Running into his AA (Sklansky-bucks −$360) doesn't make the decision wrong.

steps.title: Bluff the small pots, own the big ones
steps.feel: Where your money should be when the chips go in.
steps.formula: small pots → do your bluffing here | big pots → have the best of it
steps.proof: Negreanu's governing rule of postflop small ball: 'do the majority of your bluffing in the small pots while having the best of it in any of the big pots you play.' Your $750 stabs are cheap and frequent; you only build a monster pot when you've actually flopped a big hand. That's why he calls tight raises with 5♠7♠: on Q♠4♠8♦ he's got a flush draw + gutshot for cheap, and if a 6 hits he stacks the K-K that can't fold. You risk the worm, they risk the stack.
steps.memorize: You're not making monster bluffs that risk your tournament life. Losses stay small; wins come when you're ahead. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.title: Free Cards, Position & Deception
steps.feel: A mistake that costs one bet is cheap; a mistake that costs you the pot is a catastrophe.
steps.formula: Sklansky / The Theory of Poker (Ch. 8, 10, 15). Giving a free card = checking a hand you could bet with cards to come, handing opponents ‘infinite odds’ (zero investment) to outdraw you. Deception (slowplaying, check-raising) is worth its cost only under his five criteria: (1) good/super-reader opponents, (2) pot small vs future bets, (3) present betting round small vs future rounds, (4) only one or two opponents, (5) you hold a monster. The first two matter most; three of five usually suffice.
steps.proof: Sklansky’s hierarchy of harm: “a mistake that costs you the pot is a catastrophe... a mistake that costs you one bet is not.” So with the probable best hand you almost always bet — checking risks the whole pot to a draw, while betting into a better hand costs at most one bet. Free cards are only correct when (i) the pot is tiny and future deception gains more, (ii) you’re setting up a check-raise, or (iii) your hand is so strong it’s barely outdrawable. Position amplifies everything: last position lets you take a free card when weak and value-bet when strong; first position can’t give itself a free card, so semi-bluff there. Deception’s cost is the information you leak — his Brunson/Berland hand shows a player getting X-rayed BECAUSE he always played AA/KK the same way. Against bad players and big pots, drop the tricks and bet: they call anyway, so disguise gains nothing and free cards cost you.
steps.memorize: Bet the probable best hand — one lost bet beats one lost pot. Slowplay/check-raise only with a monster, small pot, few opponents, and thinking opponents. Bad game or big pot = play it straight.

callouts.text: Slowplaying the same monster the same way every time is how good readers X-ray you (Brunson’s Bones Berland read). The deception only pays if your straightforward line and your trap line look identical.

steps.prompt: $1/$2, loose-passive table. Two limpers, and you're on the button with 7♦6♦. It folds to you. Which line best fits Negreanu's small-ball style?
options: Make a big raise to 8x to blow them off the pot
Limp/call cheaply behind, see a flop in position, and play for implied odds
Fold — suited connectors are trash
Raise huge and stack off on any flush draw
steps.explain: Small ball loves cheap flops in position with speculative hands. 7♦6♦ wants to see a flop for as little as possible: when it connects big (straight, flush, two pair) it can stack a made hand — that's the implied-odds payoff — and when it misses you fold for almost nothing. Blowing up the pot preflop with a hand that plays great postflop wastes its cheap-flop, high-upside nature. Keep it small and in position.

steps.prompt: You've been card-dead. The player to your right is a calling station who never folds postflop and pays off big. The table nit folds to almost every raise. You want one plan for the session. Which blend is most profitable?
options: Blast aggression at everyone, including the station
Play pure small ball against the whole table
Aggression/steals against the nit for fold equity; against the station, value bet thin and stop bluffing
Only play premium hands and wait for the nuts
steps.explain: Pick the style per opponent. The nit folds too much, so aggression prints on fold equity — steal and c-bet him relentlessly. The station never folds, so bluffs are worthless there; instead lean small-ball value: bet your made hands thin and let him pay you off, but don't try to blow him off pots. Same table, two different exploits. Blasting the station burns money, and pure small ball leaves the nit's free folds on the table.

modules.title: Reading & Exploiting Players
modules.sub: player types, limpers & the adjustments that print
modules.recap:
The low-stakes money-maker.
- Tag each player fast, punish limpers, and expand to the margins by read strength.
- Never bluff a station; steal from nits; read your OWN range first.

steps.title: You do not beat poker, you beat people
steps.feel: Imagine you are playing chess but your opponent has a habit — say, they always push their queen out early and never protect their king. You do not need a genius plan. You need to notice the habit and lean on it. Live low-stakes is exactly this: every player leaks money in a predictable direction. Your job is to spot which direction, then push.
steps.formula:
Strategy = find the mistake → attack that mistake.

No mistake to attack yet? Play solid and keep watching.
steps.proof:
Against a perfectly balanced opponent, no strategy earns more than break-even before rake — that is what game-theory-optimal (GTO) play guarantees. But nobody at $1/$2 is balanced. Their range and their bet-sizing are systematically off in one direction, and every deviation from balance is money you can extract by deviating right back.

GTO is the defense that cannot be exploited. Exploitative play is the offense that punishes players who are not using GTO — which is everyone at these stakes.

So typing is not a nicety. It is the entire engine. The label you assign tells you which lever to pull: value bet more, bluff less, steal more, fold more. Get the type wrong and you pull the wrong lever.
steps.memorize: Find the leak, then pour money through it.

steps.title: The Calling Station: loose and sticky
steps.feel: This is the friendliest face at the table and your favorite person in the room. They play half their hands, they call almost any bet with any piece, and they almost never raise. They are not trying to outplay you — they just want to see cards and hope. When you bet, they look you up. When they have it, they still just call.
steps.formula:
Enters lots of pots (high VPIP) + rarely raises (low PFR) = loose-passive Station.

Your counter: bet your good hands over and over, and never try to bluff them.
steps.proof:
Think of VPIP as how often they put money in preflop and PFR as how often that money is a raise. A Station might voluntarily play 45%+ of hands but raise only 3-5% — a huge gap between the two numbers. That gap is the tell: they enter with junk and call rather than raise even good hands.

The wide gap between how often they play and how often they raise is the fingerprint of a Station. Big gap, low aggression = call everything.

Because they call too much, bluffing loses (they will not fold) and value betting wins big (they pay off with worse). This one type is where most of your profit at $1/$2 comes from.
steps.memorize: Plays everything, raises nothing — bet for value, never bluff.

steps.title: The Nit: tight and timid
steps.feel: The Nit folds and folds and folds, then suddenly there is money in the pot and their eyes are locked on the table. They wait for premium hands like a fisherman waiting for the one big bite. They rarely bluff and they hate risking chips without the goods. When a Nit finally bets big, the polite thing to do is get out of the way.
steps.formula:
Enters few pots (low VPIP) + rarely raises = tight-passive Nit.

Your counter: steal their blinds and limps relentlessly; when they wake up with aggression, believe them.
steps.proof:
A Nit might play only 12-15% of hands. That means most flops, they have missed or hold a marginal hand they are scared to defend. So you can attack their blinds and open-limps constantly — they fold too often, and folds are free money.

A Nit's raise is a narrow, honest range. When they escalate, they are almost never bluffing, so their strength is fully readable — and fully avoidable.

The math: if a Nit folds 65%+ of the time to a steal, a raise that risks $10 to win the $5 pot only needs to work about ⅔ of the time to profit — and it works more than that. Free profit, over and over.
steps.memorize: Steal until they bite; when they bite, let go.

steps.title: The TAG: tight, aggressive, competent
steps.feel: This player has read a book. They fold junk, they raise their good hands, and they bet when they smell weakness. They are the one at the table who could beat you if you go to sleep. You will not print money off a TAG — you avoid fighting them without a real hand and pick up the pots they let go.
steps.formula:
Few pots (low VPIP) + often raises when in (higher PFR) = TAG.

Your counter: respect their raises, do not bluff-raise them, and target the softer seats instead.
steps.proof:
A TAG's VPIP and PFR are close together — maybe 20% / 16% — because when they play, they usually raise. That tight gap signals a thinking, aggressive player whose bets mean something.

Close VPIP-to-PFR gap = aggression on their good hands = a real range behind their bets. This is the one seat where a fold is often your best exploit.

You do not need to beat the TAG to win the session. Money flows from the Stations and Nits; the TAG is just the shark you swim around. Do not spew chips into the one competent player when three fish are waiting.
steps.memorize: Do not fight the shark — feed on the fish.

steps.title: The Maniac / LAG: pressure everywhere
steps.feel: Chips fly when this player is in a hand. They raise light, they bet every street, they put you to constant tough decisions. A true Maniac does it with air far too often; a controlled LAG picks better spots. Either way, the instinct to fight fire with fire is a trap. You want to sit back, let them hang themselves, and pay them off only when you have it.
steps.formula:
Lots of pots (high VPIP) + lots of raising (high PFR) = LAG/Maniac.

Your counter: stop bluffing them, widen the hands you call with, and trap your monsters.
steps.proof:
A Maniac shows a high VPIP and a high PFR — both numbers big, because they play a lot and raise most of it. That means their betting range is stuffed with weak hands and bluffs.

When someone bets too wide, the correction is not to bet back — it is to CALL wider. You are not adding aggression to a raiser; you are catching their bluffs.

Against a bettor whose range is mostly air, a medium hand that would fold to a solid player becomes a profitable call. Let them bet your hand for you. Check-call, trap, and cash their bluffs.
steps.memorize: Do not out-crazy the Maniac — out-wait him.

steps.title: Label in one orbit, update forever
steps.feel: You do not need a HUD or a spreadsheet. Sit down and just count roughly: over one lap of the table, how many pots did each player enter, and how many did they raise? Two numbers per player, kept in your head. That is enough for a starting label. Then you keep watching and nudge the label whenever they surprise you.
steps.formula:
Per player, track two things: How often IN? How often RAISING?

Many in / rarely raising = Station. Rarely in = Nit. Often in / often raising = Maniac. Rarely in / raises when in = TAG.
steps.proof:
This is intuitive VPIP and PFR with no software. VPIP is the how often IN count; PFR is the how often RAISING count. You do not need decimals — you need direction. One orbit of nine hands gives you a rough read that is right far more often than not at these stakes, because low-stakes players are extremely consistent.

Labels are hypotheses, not verdicts. A Nit who suddenly 3-bets light just told you he is not a Nit — rewrite the tag on the spot.

The cost of a wrong-but-corrected label is tiny; the cost of NO label is that you play everyone the same and leave the whole edge on the table.
steps.memorize: Two counts per player: how often in, how often raising.

steps.title: Read the buy-in and the body before the cards
steps.feel: You get free information before a single hand is dealt. The short buy-in playing scared, the guy who straddles every button, the player who slams chips in the second you bet versus the one who agonizes — these are all labels you can pre-fill. A player who reloads to exactly the minimum plays tight and scared. A player who straddles and splashes is telling you he came to gamble.
steps.formula:
Quick calls = weak/drawing (wants to see the next card).

Deliberate raise, chips stacked neatly = strength.

Min buy-in + tight = Nit. Straddles + big buy-in + loose = Maniac/gambler.
steps.proof:
Behavioral tells are just a second data stream that agrees with the betting patterns. Buy-in size correlates with risk appetite; straddling is a voluntary blind that only loose-aggressive players do habitually; call speed reveals intent — a snap-call is usually a draw or a marginal hand that did not want to think, while a long pause before a raise is often genuine strength being disguised as a decision.

Do not over-trust a single physical tell in a vacuum. Use it to CONFIRM the betting-pattern read, not to override it. Chips talk louder than faces.

Stack the two streams together and you can type a player before you have even seen them play a hand — then confirm it once they do.
steps.memorize: Watch the buy-in, the straddle, and the speed of the call.

steps.title: Reads by Player Type
steps.feel: Before you read a hand, read the human. Classify the player, then apply the one adjustment that beats that type. Do not stereotype by looks; classify by the context of their actions (positions, sizings, how often they take a line).
steps.formula:
Old-school passive: never 3-bets, never bluff-raises, only raises premiums (position-blind). Their raises are HUGE reads. Adjustment: fold your marginal hands to their raises/3-bets; never bluff-raise or 4-bet-bluff them, they have it.

Modern 3-bettor: 3-bets premiums plus light bluffs, position-sensitive (attacks steals). Adjustment: build a 4-bet range including 4-bet bluffs; don't auto-fold to their 3-bet.

Rational caller: folds worse to pressure. Adjustment: with a mediocre made hand, check at least once, then bet river / let them bet, since they won't pay off with worse and rarely bluff.

Irrational caller (station): calls down with any piece. Adjustment: value-bet thin and relentlessly, never bluff them, and bet your mediocre hands small for extra streets.

LAG: tons of hands, fires two barrels for a cheap fold, then gives up. Adjustment: your range is stronger, so call/raise flop and turn and simply wait him out; check the river and let him surrender, but respect a genuine large third barrel.

The Bully: zero respect for money, fires to the end with air OR nuts, hides info. Adjustment: don't try to read him, play the course, build accurate range-vs-texture counter-strategies, since he is still a slave to the same math.
steps.proof: Each adjustment falls straight out of attack-weakness. The old-school player's raise is a narrow range (fold). The station never narrows on the call, so worse hands stay in (value-bet, never bluff). The LAG's two-barrel-then-quit pattern means his river checks/small bets are depleted ranges (attack) while his rare big third barrel is a concentrated one (respect). The Bully's range never narrows in a readable way, so reads fail and you must fall back on structural (GTO-flavored) play.
steps.memorize: Classify first, then apply one counter: old-school = fold to their raises; modern = 4-bet range; rational = check/bet-river; station = value thin, never bluff; LAG = wait him out; Bully = play the course, not the man.

steps.scene: An older player at your $1/$2 table has folded for two hours, has never once 3-bet or check-raised anyone, and only ever raises when he clearly has a big hand. You open A-J offsuit from the cutoff and he 3-bets you from the big blind.
steps.prompt: Classify this player and pick the correct adjustment.
options: Old-school passive 3-bettor: his 3-bet is a tiny, premium-only range, so fold AJo without hesitation
Modern position-aware 3-bettor: he's attacking your steal, so 4-bet-bluff him
Irrational calling station: just call and stack him postflop
The Bully: his 3-bet is unreadable, so flip a coin
steps.explain: Never-limps context aside, the giveaway is that he never 3-bets and never bluff-raises: this is the old-school passive type whose raises concentrate to premiums (AA/KK/QQ/AK/JJ). His 3-bet is one of the strongest, tightest ranges at the table. AJo is a clean fold, and you would never 4-bet-bluff him. Classify by the context of his actions, not by his age or appearance; appearance is at most a tie-breaker for experience level.

steps.prompt: A player at your table has seen 6 of the last 9 flops, and in every one of those pots he just limped or called — you have not seen him raise once. What is he, and what is your plan?
options: Calling Station — value bet him thin and relentlessly, never bluff
TAG — play carefully and respect his bets
Nit — steal his blinds every chance you get
steps.explain: Playing 6 of 9 pots is very high VPIP; never raising is near-zero PFR. That wide gap between playing a lot and raising never is the exact fingerprint of a loose-passive Calling Station. Against him you value bet good hands over and over and cut bluffs to zero — he calls with worse and never folds.

steps.prompt: A player has folded nearly every hand for two orbits. He now open-raises to $15 from early position, sets his chips down deliberately, and stares at the felt. You have K-Q offsuit in the cutoff. Best read and action?
options: He is a Nit with a premium — fold K-Q offsuit
He is bluffing as usual — 3-bet to punish him
He is a Maniac opening light — call wide and float
steps.explain: Two orbits of folding is a rock-tight Nit. Nits almost never bluff, and their raises are a narrow, honest range of premiums. K-Q offsuit is dominated by most of what he shows up with (A-K, A-Q, big pairs). Believe the aggression and fold. Steal his blinds all day — but when he finally bites, let go.

steps.prompt: A new player sits with a max buy-in, straddles his first button, and raises three of his first four hands. What label do you pre-fill, and how do you counter it?
options: Maniac/LAG — stop bluffing him, widen your calls, and trap big hands
Nit — steal relentlessly and fold to his raises
TAG — avoid him and target softer seats
steps.explain: Max buy-in plus a voluntary straddle plus raising 3 of 4 hands screams loose-aggressive gambler. His raising range is packed with weak hands, so you do not bluff into him — you let him bluff into you. Widen the hands you call with and check-call or trap your monsters so he barrels his stack off.

steps.title: Attack Weakness, Avoid Strength
steps.feel:
Every opponent's range is strong in some spots and weak in others. Your whole edge in a live game comes from pushing chips in exactly where their range is thin or capped, and pulling back exactly where it's dense with strong hands. You are not playing the person's soul, you're playing the shape of their range.

Concretely: a bet from a player who sometimes limps his weak hands is a narrow, strong range, so you back off. A raise from a never-limps, plays-everything player is a wide, weak range, so you attack with more 3-bets, more calls, more barrels. Same action, opposite meaning, decided by what the range must contain.

Ask on every street: is their range here capped/weak (attack) or dense/strong (fold)? That single question is the engine of exploitative play.
steps.formula:
Money available = opponents' willingness to put chips in with hands a perfect player would fold. You capture it two ways:

(1) bet/raise into ranges that are too wide, and (2) get out of the way once their line has narrowed them to only strong hands.

So the read reduces to: wide range → apply pressure; narrow range → concede.
steps.proof: A hold'em game is negative-sum after rake (~$10-15/hr). Ten perfect players each lose. Your profit must come from a specific source: opponents entering pots with bad hands. Those extra hands beyond a perfect player's range are, by definition, hands you can attack. When a line forces their range down to only good hands, there is no longer any bad-hand money to win there, so betting into it just donates. Hence: attack where the range stayed wide, fold where the line squeezed it strong.
steps.memorize: Bet where their range is weak/capped; back off where it's dense with strong hands.

steps.prompt: A tight regular who normally opens with position discipline instead limp-calls preflop from early position with what you've seen are hands like small pairs and weak suited junk. The flop comes A-K-x rainbow and he checks to you. On the attack-weakness framework, what does this spot represent?
options: His checking range is weak here because his limping range whiffs ace-high/broadway flops, so you should attack (bet/barrel) with impunity
His check means a trap on the top pair, so you should check back and give up
You should only attack if you personally hold an ace or a king
Limpers are unpredictable, so the correct default is to fold and wait for a clearer spot
steps.explain: An aggressive limper's range (8-5s, 2-2 type junk) performs terribly on any ace-high or broadway flop, so his check is a depleted, weak range, exactly the spot to attack. Whether you hold a piece is beside the point: barreling punishes the junk he'll fold, it isn't about representing the ace. This is the core of attack-weakness: bet where the range is thin, regardless of your own cards.

steps.title: How Actions Narrow a Range
steps.feel:
An action is a filter. When a player takes an aggressive line, the weak hands drop out and only the strong ones remain, so the range gets stronger and tighter. When they take a passive line, the strong hands leave (they'd have bet) and the weak ones stay, so the range gets weaker.

Miller's phrasing: a shove concentrates strength, a check depletes it. A big turn shove is an action taken with a tiny sliver of a range, and that sliver is the nutted part. A check leaks the strong hands out and leaves the medium/weak stuff behind, which is exactly why a check is an invitation to attack.

Betting reveals little on the flop (everyone has equity), but a lot on the turn and river, where hands are cleanly strong or weak and the draws have all resolved.
steps.formula:
Aggressive line (raise, shove, big bet late) ⇒ range narrows UP toward the nuts ⇒ concede.

Passive line (check, flat-call, small bet) ⇒ strong hands removed, range weakens ⇒ attack.

Each street re-filters: a caller who calls flop and turn keeps folding her worst and (sometimes) raising her best, leaving an ever more medium-heavy range.
steps.proof: Consider the flagship pair from The Course: identical flop and turn play, top-pair-good-kicker in a loose pot. Case A, the field checks to you on the turn: a strong hand would have bet to protect and get value, so the check depletes strength, and you shove for value. Case B, a player instead shoves the turn: that shove uses only the top of the range (sets, two pair, made straights/flushes) because nobody open-shoves a bluff there, so it concentrates strength, and you fold. Same texture, opposite conclusion, driven entirely by which hands the action leaves behind.
steps.memorize: A shove concentrates strength; a check depletes it. Aggression = tighter/stronger range; passivity leaves the weak hands in.

steps.scene: $2/$5, deep. You raise the button, the big blind calls. Flop 9-7-4 two-tone; BB checks, you bet, BB calls. Turn is an offsuit brick; you bet again, and this time the big blind check-RAISES you.
steps.prompt: The big blind check-raised the turn. Compared to a hand where she had just called, is her range now stronger or weaker, and why?
options: Stronger and tighter: a turn check-raise is an aggressive line that filters out her weak hands, concentrating her range toward two-pair-plus, sets, and completed/strong draws
Weaker: check-raising is a passive line that leaves the weak hands in
Unchanged: a check-raise gives no more information than a call
Stronger only if she is a known bluffer, otherwise weaker
steps.explain: Aggression narrows a range upward. A shove concentrates strength; here a turn check-raise plays the same role: it removes the marginal made hands and pure air (those check-call or fold) and leaves the strong, committed hands.
