Her range is stronger and tighter than if she'd merely called. The correct response is to slow down or fold your marginal holdings, not to fire again into a concentrated range.

steps.title: Read your own hand, not theirs
steps.feel: Everyone wastes energy guessing the villain's exact cards. The higher-leverage skill is knowing where YOUR hand sits in the range of hands you'd play this exact way. Top of your range? Bet and call. Bottom of your range? You're the bluff-catcher, and you should be folding a lot. The card values matter less than your rank within your own line.
steps.formula: Ask: of all the hands I'd take this line with, is this one near the top, middle, or bottom? Bottom of range on a bad runout = fold, even if it looks strong in a vacuum.
steps.proof: Say you 3-bet and get called, then the board runs out to a scary river. You hold AA. But your range here also has sets, straights, and flushes that beat you. If AA is only about the 62nd percentile of your own value range, then facing a big bet you're not defending the top of your range — you're defending a bluff-catcher. 'It's aces' is a vacuum thought; the board and your range demote it. Correct play can be a fold.
steps.memorize: Your rank in your own range decides the line, not the pips.

steps.prompt: You hold an overpair, but the river completes a 4-to-a-straight board and villain fires a big bet. Where does your hand sit in your own range?
options: Near the bottom of my value range — this is a fold
Top of my range — snap call, it's an overpair
Middle — raise for value
steps.explain: Read your own hand, not theirs. Your range here also holds the straights, sets, and two-pair that all beat one pair on this runout. The overpair that felt strong preflop is now near the bottom of the hands you'd get here — a bluff-catcher on a board that smashes calling ranges. Against a big bet, fold. 'It's an overpair' is vacuum thinking.

steps.title: Bet-Sizing Tells (Miller's Most-Used Live Read)
steps.feel: Unsophisticated players fork their bet size by feeling, not by strategy, and that leaks their hand. This is the single read Miller uses most in live low-stakes games. Weight it heavily, but remember it is noisy, so treat flop sizing as a tie-breaker and lean on turn/river sizing.
steps.formula:
Small bet / blocking bet: usually weak or a probe (see-where-I'm-at), or thin value. A small out-of-turn bet on the turn often means "I have a pair I'm worried about and plan to fold to a raise" → attack it (raise / blow them out).

Huge bet / overbet at $1/$2: a size you'd only see once or twice an hour usually means the nuts or a specific polar hand. Players size UP because they fear getting drawn out on with a big made hand. On scary boards, big = strength.

Timing/effort tells: instant big bets, obvious discomfort (fears a draw or a raise), or careless lack-of-interest all add or subtract weight.

Never fork your OWN sizing by your two cards. Pick one size for all hands you'd bet in a spot; vary size by pot size, board dynamism, stack depth, and overall range strength, never by your specific holding.
steps.proof: Worked example: you raise on the button, one call, flop Q9-high two-tone, you bet, called; turn brings a straight-and-flush card and villain leads. A $140 (big) lead into ~$82 skews to two-pair-plus (betting because he fears you check back a free card). A $70 (small) lead skews to a pair-plus-draw (KQ, J9, weak flush draw) that folds to a big river bet. The size itself splits his range, so you read the size and respond: don't bluff into the big one, apply max pressure to the small one.
steps.memorize: Small bet = weak/probe/thin value; rare overbet = nuts or a polar hand. Read their size, never fork your own. Sizing tells are strong but noisy.

steps.scene: $1/$2. Same villain, two different hands. In hand one the flop-turn goes checked and he fires a tiny $10 bet into a $60 pot on the river. In hand two, an hour later, on a dry brick river he suddenly jams an overbet, roughly $220 into a $90 pot, a size you have not seen him make all session.
steps.prompt: Reading his bet sizing, how should you weight each bet?
options: Tiny bet = weak/blocking or thin value (don't fold much, consider raising); rare overbet = the nuts or a specific polar hand (fold your bluff-catchers)
Tiny bet = trap, so fold; overbet = desperation bluff, so call
Both are bluffs because unsophisticated players bet randomly
Both are value because he only bets when strong
steps.explain: Unsophisticated players fork sizing by feel. A tiny bet is a probe, a block, or thin value, so you rarely fold and can often raise it. A rare huge overbet, a size you'd see only once or twice a session, means a big made hand he's sizing up to protect/get paid, usually the nuts or a narrow polar range, so you fold your bluff-catchers. Weight sizing tells heavily but stay aware they're noisy, and never fork your own sizing this way.

steps.title: A limp is a hand waving a white flag
steps.feel: When someone just calls the big blind instead of raising, they are announcing something: this hand is not strong enough to raise, but I want to see a flop cheaply. It is a soft, hopeful, timid entry. The correct response to timid is aggressive. You do not tiptoe past a white flag — you charge it.
steps.formula:
Open limp = capped, weak-to-medium range that wants a cheap, multiway flop.

Deny the cheap flop: raise.
steps.proof:
Almost nobody at $1/$2 limps their premium hands on purpose — those get raised. So a limp caps the range: it is missing the very top and is mostly speculative junk, small pairs, weak aces, suited trash. That range wants to see five cards cheaply and hit a monster.

Their plan requires a cheap flop and lots of players. Raise, and you blow up both halves of the plan at once — the price goes up and everyone else folds out.

Every element of what the limper wants — cheap, multiway, passive — is something a raise takes away. That is why the isolation raise is close to free money.
steps.memorize: A limp is weakness announced — raise into it.

steps.title: The isolation raise: get them alone, in position
steps.feel: The whole idea of an isolation raise is to clear the table so it is just you and the one weak limper, with you acting last on every street. That is the best seat in poker: a strong-ish hand, position, and an opponent whose range is already known to be weak. You are turning a messy five-way pot into a clean duel you are favored to win.
steps.formula:
Fold to you after a limp with a decent hand? Raise (do not limp behind).

Goal: heads-up, in position, vs a capped range.
steps.proof:
The iso raise wins two ways. First, fold equity: the limper and everyone behind often fold, and you scoop the dead money now. Second, when called, you are heads-up and in position against a capped range, where you realize far more of your hand's equity than you would multiway and out of position.

Position is worth real money because you always act with more information. Getting heads-up plus position against a known-weak range is stacking three edges into one pot.

Multiway, even a strong hand like A-J is fragile — someone always connects. Heads-up against a limper, A-J is a clear favorite. The raise is what converts the hand from fragile to dominant.
steps.memorize: Raise to be the only one left, and the last one to act.

steps.title: Size it to end the hand, not to invite a crowd
steps.feel: A tiny raise is an invitation — everyone tags along and you are right back in the multiway swamp you tried to escape. You want a size big enough that the limper and the players behind have to fold their weak hands. Think of the bet as a fence height: too low and everyone hops over; set it high enough that only real hands come along.
steps.formula:
Base ≈ 3-4bb + 1bb per limper.

$1/$2: one limper → raise to $10-12. Two limpers → $12-15.

Sticky limper who never folds? Go bigger — $15-18 for value, not to make him fold.
steps.proof:
At $1/$2 the big blind is $2. A standard iso is 3-4bb plus 1bb for each limper who has already put money in — because each limper added dead money and another player who might call, so you must raise more to still isolate. One $2 limper → about $12. Two limpers → about $14-15.

Min-raising to $4 is a classic leak. It gives everyone a cheap price to continue, so you stay multiway AND bloat the pot with a hand you wanted to play heads-up. You paid more to make your situation worse.

Against a sticky Station who will call regardless, sizing flips purpose: you are no longer sizing to fold him out, you are sizing to charge maximum for his weak range. Bet bigger for pure value — he pays it off.

Correction. Ed Miller (The Course, pp. 76–77) goes bigger in limp-heavy live games: about $15–20 (7.5–10bb) over multiple limpers, and choose your hands as if the limps were not there.
steps.memorize: 3-4bb + 1bb per limper; bigger vs the sticky ones.

steps.title: Iso for value AND playability
steps.feel: Not every hand wants to isolate. You want hands that are either strong enough to be ahead of a limper's junk, or hands that flop well and play smoothly when you are in position. Broadway cards, any pair, and suited hands are your bread and butter. The worse your position, the tighter you should be; on the button you can attack much wider.
steps.formula:
Iso: broadways (A-J+, K-Q, K-J), all pairs, suited aces, suited connectors/broadways.

In position (BTN/CO): widen a lot. Out of position: tighten up.
steps.proof:
Two things make an iso profitable: value (you are ahead of his range right now) and playability (you flop useful hands — top pair, draws, nut potential — that make postflop easy). A hand like K-J beats his range for value; a hand like 8-7 suited has playability, flopping straights, flushes, and draws you can barrel.

In position you realize more of every hand's equity, so the same holding is worth more on the button than under the gun. That is why your iso range legitimately gets wider the later you are.

Avoid isolating with weak offsuit junk out of position — no value, poor playability, and you are stuck acting first. That is the one place an iso turns unprofitable.
steps.memorize: Iso hands that are ahead OR that flop well — widest in position.

steps.title: Overlimping behind is leaving money on the felt
steps.feel: The tempting mistake is to just call along behind the limper with a decent hand and see a cheap flop yourself. It feels safe. It is actually a leak. You give up all the fold equity, you keep the pot multiway, and you let the blinds see a flop for free. You had a chance to take control and you passed.
steps.formula:
Decent hand behind a limper → raise, don't overlimp.

Only limp behind with speculative hands in a spot where a raise clearly can't isolate (many sticky limpers already in).
steps.proof:
Overlimping surrenders every edge the iso raise captured. No fold equity — you win nothing preflop. Still multiway — your hand stays fragile. And you have invited the big blind to check and realize equity for free. You converted a controllable spot into a coinflip lottery.

Do not talk yourself into set-mining every small pair by overlimping. Set-mining needs deep stacks and a big implied payoff; multiway limped pots rarely deliver it, and you fold the flop the ~7 of 8 times you miss.

The narrow exception: three sticky Stations have already limped and a raise genuinely will not fold anyone. Then a cheap overlimp with a suited connector to hit a big hand can be fine — but that is the exception, not the default.
steps.memorize: Overlimping wins nothing preflop and controls nothing after.

steps.title: After the iso, keep firing
steps.feel: You raised, one limper called, you are heads-up in position. Now the flop comes. Most of the time your opponent has completely missed — he limped junk, remember. So you bet. He folds when he misses, or he pays you off when he has a weak piece he is too curious to fold. Either outcome prints. Keep the pressure on.
steps.formula:
Heads-up iso pot, you missed too → c-bet ~⅓ to ½ pot; he folds air.

You hit → bet for value; he calls with worse.

Vs a Station → skip the pure-air c-bet, only bet when you have something.
steps.proof:
A limp-caller connects with the flop only sometimes — roughly ⅓ of the time he flops a pair or better. So a continuation bet against a normal limper wins immediately most of the time, and it needs to work only about 33-40% of the time to profit at a ⅓-to-½ pot size.

The c-bet is the payoff of the whole iso plan: you built a heads-up pot in position against a capped range specifically so this bet would be cheap and effective.
Against a true Calling Station, the auto-c-bet stops working — he does not fold his weak pairs. Versus stations, only bet when you actually have value, and let go when you have nothing. Bluffing a station lights money on fire.
steps.memorize: Iso, then c-bet — unless it's a Station, then bet only for value.

steps.prompt: Two players limp for $2 in a $1/$2 game. It folds to you on the button with A-Q suited. You want to isolate. What raise size?
options: Raise to $14
Raise to $4
Just limp behind for $2
steps.explain:
Use 3-4bb + 1bb per limper. Base ~$8-10 plus $2 per limper lands around $14 with two limpers in. That size folds out the weak hands behind and isolates you heads-up in position with a hand that dominates a limping range. The $4 min-raise invites a crowd; overlimping surrenders all fold equity and control.

Correction. In limp-heavy games The Course uses $15–20 over two or more limpers.

steps.prompt: A loose-passive Station limps UTG. It folds to you in the cutoff with K-J suited. What is the best play?
options: Raise to about $10-12 to isolate in position
Overlimp behind for $2 to keep the pot small
Fold — K-J suited is dominated
steps.explain: K-J suited is ahead of a Station's limping range and has great playability — it flops top pairs, straights, and flush draws. Isolate to $10-12 to get heads-up and in position against a capped, weak range. Overlimping wins nothing preflop and keeps you multiway; folding a hand that dominates a limper is far too tight.

steps.prompt: You isolated a normal (non-station) limper to $12 with A-K offsuit; he called. Flop is 9♣ 6♦ 2♠, he checks to you. You have ace-high, no pair. Best action?
options: C-bet about $12-15 — half pot; he folds the air he limped
Check behind and give up
Bet $40 to guarantee he folds
steps.explain: This dry, low flop misses a limping range most of the time — he flops a pair or better only about a third of the time. A ⅓-to-½ pot c-bet needs to work ~35-40% and it works far more often, so it prints even with just ace-high. Checking surrenders the pot you built; the huge overbet risks way too much to win a small pot against a capped range that will fold to any reasonable bet.

steps.title: Every player breaks balance one way — attack that way
steps.feel: Here is the single idea the whole payoff module hangs on. Correct, balanced poker folds a precise amount and calls a precise amount. Real people at $1/$2 do not. Nits fold way too much. Stations call way too much. Maniacs bet way too much. Each of those is a door left open, and you walk through the one that is open.
steps.formula:
They over-fold → bluff and steal more.

They over-call → value bet more, bluff never.

They over-bet → call wider, trap, bluff never.
steps.proof:
Balanced play exists so no opponent can exploit you. The instant an opponent deviates from balance, they hand you a counter-deviation that profits. A player who folds too often makes your bluffs pure profit. A player who calls too often makes your thin value bets pure profit and your bluffs pure loss.

You never need a fancy strategy at these stakes. You need to notice which single mistake each player makes and lean hard the opposite way. One correct deviation per player.

This is why typing (Module 1) had to come first: the label tells you which door is open. The rest of this module is just walking through each door.
steps.memorize: Bet where they call too much; steal where they fold too much.

steps.title: Exploiting Bloated Frequencies
steps.feel:
When a player does anything too often, you lean the opposite way. Frequency errors are the fattest, most reliable reads at low stakes because they repeat every orbit. You don't need to know their exact hand, just which way their frequency is off, then pour your chips into the gap.

An indifferent equilibrium spot flips to a pure strategy on the tiniest read: if villain folds even a little too much to a bet, you stop being indifferent and always bluff. Small mistake, pure exploit.
steps.formula:
Calls too much (station): value-bet wider and thinner, stop bluffing, and bet your mediocre made hands for value.

Bluffs too much: call down wider (bluff-catch), and stop value-betting your thin hands (let him bet them for you).

Folds too much: steal/bluff far more, AND stop value-betting your strong hands as much (check to induce, since he won't pay), AND call earlier streets wider knowing he won't apply river pressure. One mistake enables several exploits.

Under-bluffs (rarely bluffs): fold to his big bets, don't bluff-catch, because his aggression is almost always value.
steps.proof: Consider a loose, passive player who calls too much and bets too rarely on A96-9-6 with your AK. If you check, he bets everything that beats you and you can't fold profitably. Since he calls too much and rarely raise-bluffs, you bet, even close to pot, to induce calls from worse, planning to fold only if he raises. The exploit is not "he's a fish" but the specific, actionable read "calls too much, bets too rarely", and you deviate hardest where his mistake is biggest and your read is strongest.
steps.memorize: Over-caller → value-bet, don't bluff. Over-bluffer → bluff-catch. Over-folder → steal more, value-bet less. Under-bluffer → fold. Lean opposite to their bloated frequency.

steps.scene: $1/$2. A player to your right is a classic calling station: he has called down three big rivers this hour with second and third pair and has not folded a made hand all day. You reach the river with top pair, good kicker, decent but not monstrous, and he checks to you.
steps.prompt: Given his bloated calling frequency, what's the exploit?
options: Value-bet, and size it to get called by his worse pairs; do not check for pot control and do not try to bluff him
Check back for pot control since he calls too much
Overbet as a bluff to blow him off his weak pairs
Check, planning to fold if he bets, since stations trap
steps.explain: When a player calls too much, you lean the opposite way: value-bet thinner and wider, and never bluff. Top pair good kicker is a clear value bet against a range stuffed with worse pairs he refuses to fold; checking just forfeits a street he would have paid. Bluffing is the exact wrong exploit against a station. One frequency error (over-calling) points straight to the counter: get maximum thin value, zero bluffs.

steps.title: vs Stations: value, value, value — never bluff
steps.feel: The Calling Station is a vending machine that pays out when you press the right button. The right button is a value bet — a bet with a hand that beats what he calls with. He calls too light, so hands you would check against a good player, you bet against him. And the bluff button is broken: it takes your money and gives nothing back, because he does not fold. Stop pressing it.
steps.formula:
Against a Station: bet all your value, thinner than normal, and size UP (¾ to full pot).

Bluffs against a Station = 0. None.
steps.proof:
Bluffing works only when he folds enough. Say a $50 bluff into a $50 pot needs him to fold about half the time just to break even. A Station folds maybe 15-20%. So the bluff loses money every time you make it — the math is brutally against you.

Now flip it: value betting works when he calls with worse. He does — constantly. So a bet with top pair, or even second pair against a real Station, gets called by worse pairs, draws, and ace-high. That is thin value, and it is pure profit precisely because his calling range is so wide.

The exact leak that kills your bluffs (he never folds) is what makes your value bets huge (he always calls). Same trait, opposite sign — punish it with value only.

And size up: he is price-insensitive, so a full-pot value bet gets called nearly as often as a half-pot one. Bet bigger and you simply win more per showdown.
steps.memorize: Stations pay off value and eat bluffs — so bet value, bluff never.

steps.title: Thin value is where the money hides
steps.feel: Most players are scared to bet a marginal hand — they check top pair with a weak kicker, worried about being called. Against a Station that fear costs you money. He calls with everything worse, so you should be betting those marginal hands for value. The hands that feel too thin to bet are exactly the ones printing against a station.
steps.formula:
vs Station, bet for value with: top pair any kicker, second pair, sometimes third pair on the river.

If he calls with worse more than half the time, it's a value bet — make it.
steps.proof:
A bet is value if the range that calls it is worse than your hand more than half the time. Against a normal player, second pair does not clear that bar — he only calls with better. Against a Station, his calling range is stuffed with worse pairs, gutshots, and ace-high, so second pair clears it easily.

Checking your marginal made hands vs a Station to keep the pot small is a leak, not caution. You are declining free money he was going to pay you. Check only the hands that literally cannot get called by worse.

Over many hands, these thin value bets compound into the bulk of your win rate at low stakes — because the field is full of Stations and the value spots come up constantly.
steps.memorize: If worse hands call, bet it — even when it feels thin.

steps.prompt: A Calling Station calls your flop and turn bets. River is a blank. You hold top pair, weak kicker on Q♠ 8♥ 3♦ 2♣ 5♠. He checks. Best play?
options: Bet ~¾ pot for thin value — he calls with worse
Check behind to control the pot
Bet as a bluff to make him fold
steps.explain: Against a Station, top pair beats his wide calling range — worse queens, eights, missed draws, ace-high all pay off. That clears the value bar (worse hands call more than half the time), so you bet, and size UP because he is price-insensitive. Checking declines free money; framing it as a bluff misreads the spot — you have the best hand and want a call, not a fold.

steps.prompt: A calling station called your flop and turn bets. The river is a blank. You hold second pair. Bet thin for value, check, or bluff?
options: Thin value bet — they call with worse
Bluff — they finally have to fold something
Check — second pair is too weak to bet
steps.explain: Against a station you never bluff — there's no fold equity. But second pair beats a big chunk of the worse hands they call with (weak pairs, draws that missed, ace-high). So bet it thin for value and let them pay you off. Checking leaves money on the table against someone who would have called.

steps.prompt: The villain is an over-caller (a station). Should you widen your bluffing range against them?
options: No — contract bluffs toward zero and widen your value range instead
Yes — bluff more since the pot is often bigger
Yes — mix in more bluffs to stay balanced
steps.explain: Balance is for tough opponents; against a station you exploit maximally. They don't fold, so bluffs lose. Contract bluffs to nearly zero and widen your value range — bet thinner and bigger with hands that beat their loose calls. Widening bluffs against a caller is exactly backwards.

steps.title: vs Nits: steal everything, then respect the wake-up
steps.feel: A Nit treats his chips like they are made of glass. He folds and folds, waiting for aces. That patience is a weakness you attack from two sides: relentlessly steal the pots he does not care about, and then get completely out of the way the moment he finally fights back. You are a pickpocket who never argues with the one shopkeeper who catches you.
steps.formula:
vs Nit: raise their limps, steal their blinds, and c-bet many boards — they over-fold.

Nit shows real aggression (raise, check-raise, big bet)? Fold anything non-premium and believe him.
steps.proof:
A Nit folds too often — that is his one leak. If he folds 65-70% to a steal, every steal that risks $10 to win a $5 pot is wildly profitable: it only needs to work about ⅔ of the time and it works more. You can also barrel him off many flops and turns, because he continues only with strong hands and gives up the rest.

Over-folding preflop and on flops is the same coin as over-honesty when he bets. The tight range that lets you steal freely is the tight range you must respect when it pushes back.

The discipline is symmetric: attack his passivity with maximum aggression, but when a Nit raises or check-raises, his range is almost pure premium and almost never a bluff. Folding a strong-but-not-premium hand there is the correct, profitable read.
steps.memorize: Rob the Nit blind — but pay up when he finally draws his gun.

steps.title: Barrel Nits off boards they hate
steps.feel: Because a Nit only continues with strong hands, scary-looking boards are your friend. When an overcard or a flush-completing card lands, the Nit who has one pair suddenly does not trust it, and he folds. You keep betting on cards that look dangerous to his hand, and he hands you pot after pot without a fight.
steps.formula:
vs Nit, fire again when a scary card hits: an ace or king overcard, a third flush card, a straightening board.

Give up when the board is dry and safe and he keeps calling — he has it.
steps.proof:
A Nit's continuing range is narrow and honest, so his hand is readable. On a board that threatens the hands he calls with — say he called a flop with a middle pair and the turn brings an ace — a second barrel represents exactly the hands that just beat him, and he over-folds to it. The bet exploits his fear plus his tight range at once.

Do not barrel a Nit who keeps calling on a dry board. If a tight player calls two streets on a blank runout, he is not folding the river — abandon the bluff and check it down. His calls are as honest as his raises.

The signal is clean because Nits do not have bluff-catchers or float ranges — when they fold, they truly had nothing worth defending, and when they call, they truly have it.
steps.memorize: Bet the cards that scare a Nit; quit when he won't leave.

steps.prompt: You open-raised the button with 7♣ 6♣ to steal. A rock-tight Nit in the big blind check-raises your flop c-bet on K♦ 8♠ 2♥. You have nothing — no pair, no draw. Best play?
options: Fold — a Nit's check-raise is a real hand, believe him
Call to float and bluff the turn
3-bet raise to represent the king
steps.explain: A Nit who folds constantly does not check-raise a dry K-8-2 board without a real hand — sets, two pair, or a strong king. Their aggression is honest, so you fold your air immediately. Floating or re-raising fights a range that is almost never bluffing and will not fold; you would be burning chips into the one part of a Nit's game you cannot move.

steps.prompt: You've classified the villain as a nit: tight, folds too much, only continues with premiums. How do you counter?
options: Steal relentlessly and fold to their aggression
Call down wide because they might be bluffing
Bluff big into their raises to fold out their value
steps.explain: Classify, then counter. A nit over-folds, so attack their weakness: raise and steal their blinds and pots at a high frequency. But when a nit shows aggression, it's the real thing — their range is premiums — so respect it and fold your marginal hands. Print by stealing; stay out of the way when they wake up.

steps.title: vs Maniacs: let them bluff into your traps
steps.feel: The Maniac wants a fight. Do not give him one — give him rope. He bets and raises with far too many weak hands, so the winning move is to sit still and let him fire his chips at you. You stop bluffing (he never folds anyway), you call with more hands than usual (to catch his bluffs), and when you flop a monster you check and let him bet it for you.
steps.formula:
vs Maniac/LAG: bluffs = 0. Widen your calling range. Trap big hands with check-call.

Pot-control medium hands (check to keep the pot small). Avoid big pots out of position.
steps.proof:
A Maniac's betting range is mostly air, so his bets are worth less than they look. A medium hand that is a fold against a solid, tight bettor becomes a profitable call against a Maniac, because he is bluffing far more than half the time. You are not calling to be a hero — the math says his range is weak enough that your medium hand is ahead of it.

Against a value-heavy bettor you fold your marginals; against a bluff-heavy bettor you call them. Same hand, opposite decision — the villain's tendency, not your cards, sets the correct play.

Trapping is the extension of this: with a monster, betting only folds out his air. Checking keeps his whole bluffing range in and lets him bet your hand for you. And bluffing him is doomed — he calls or raises, so a bluff has no fold equity and just bloats a pot you were trying to win cheaply.
steps.memorize: Don't fight the Maniac — check, call, and cash his bluffs.

steps.title: Pot-control and position discipline vs the wild ones
steps.feel: Not every hand against a Maniac is a monster or a trash-can. Plenty are medium — a decent pair, top pair weak kicker. With those you do not want a huge pot, because a huge pot is where the Maniac's occasional real hand hurts you most. So you keep the pot small: check, call one street, and refuse to blow it up, especially when you are out of position and flying blind.
steps.formula:
vs Maniac: medium hand → check/call small, don't build the pot.

Out of position vs a Maniac → tighten up; don't bloat pots you'll play blind.
steps.proof:
Pot control is about matching pot size to hand strength. A medium hand wins a small pot comfortably but loses a big one to the Maniac's rare monster, and against a wild player big pots happen fast. By checking and calling small, you let him bluff into a pot you can win cheaply while capping your downside when he actually has it.

Position matters double against a Maniac: acting last lets you see his aggression before committing, so you can call the bluffs and fold to the rare value. Out of position you lose that read and pay a premium — so play fewer hands there.

The discipline is the flip side of trapping: trap the monsters, control the mediums, and simply avoid the bloated out-of-position pots where a Maniac's variance does the most damage to a marginal holding.
steps.memorize: Small pot with a medium hand; skip the blind out-of-position brawls.

steps.prompt: A Maniac has been betting every street with air all night. You flop top pair, good kicker with A♥ Q♦ on Q♠ 7♣ 4♦. He leads big into you. Best line?
options: Just call and let him keep bluffing on later streets
Fold — he always has it when he bets that big
Raise big to protect your hand and end it now
steps.explain: Against a bluff-heavy Maniac, your top pair is way ahead of his wide betting range, so you keep him in rather than blow him off it. Just calling lets him barrel more air on the turn and river, maximizing what you win from his bluffs. Folding a strong hand to a known bluffer is far too weak; raising folds out the air you want to keep firing and only gets action from his rare better hands.

steps.scene: $2/$5. A LAG has been raising a huge number of hands, and you've noticed his pattern: he fires the flop and turn relentlessly, but on the river he almost always either checks or makes a small bet, and you've never seen him fire a big third barrel without the goods. This hand he raised pre, bet flop, bet turn, you called both with a marginal made hand, and the river checks to you after he checks.
steps.prompt: Applying the LAG counter, what's the play, and what's the one caveat?
options: Bet the river to take it down (his check depletes his range to give-ups); the caveat is that a rare LARGE third barrel is a concentrated, value range you should fold to
Check it back and give up, since LAGs always have it by the river
Fold immediately; you were beat the moment he bet the flop
Call any river bet because he bluffs constantly on every street
steps.explain: The LAG's signature is two barrels then surrender. When he checks the river his range is depleted of value (he'd have kept firing), so you bet and take it. The exploit exists because his passive river line leaks out the strong hands. The caveat is the flip side of the same coin: on the rare occasion he does fire a big third barrel, that aggressive line concentrates his range to the nuts, and Skill #2 applies, fold. Same player, opposite reads, driven by whether the action depletes or concentrates his range.

steps.title: Brunson's Power Poker: Bet, Don't Call
steps.feel: Doyle Brunson's Super System approach is aggression as a weapon. You don't limp in and pray for a good flop. You raise, you bet, you make the other players react to you. The player who is always attacking controls the pot, controls the story, and collects the pots nobody wants to fight for.
steps.formula: Default to betting and raising over calling. Attack with position. Play the player, not just your cards. Use fold equity: every bet has two ways to win — they fold now, or you improve later.
steps.proof: EV of a bet = P(fold)×(pot) + P(call)×(equity when called − bet). Calling only wins if you have the best hand at showdown; betting adds the whole P(fold)×(pot) term for free. At $1/$2–$2/$5 you sit with weak-tight regulars who fold too often — that inflates P(fold), so relentless pressure prints. Against a table that surrenders unless it has top pair or better, aggression collects a stream of pots at little risk.
steps.memorize: When in doubt, bet or raise — don't call. Two ways to win beats one.

steps.title: Win Big Pots, Pick Up Small Ones
steps.feel: Brunson's whole no-limit game runs on constant aggression: he reaches out and grabs the little uncontested pots all night long. Nobody has a real hand most of the time, and someone has to scoop what's sitting out there — he wants it to be him. All those small pots pay for the big one.
steps.formula: Bet at pots relentlessly to collect the many where nobody connects. When the big pot finally comes and you're the underdog, the small pots you banked already paid for it — so you're freerolling. Win ten $3,000 pots and you can afford to take 2-to-1 the worst of it in a $30,000 pot.
steps.proof: Over 50% of the time Brunson said he had the worst hand when all the money went in on a big pot. He can survive that only because the accumulated small pots are his compensation. Tight players who wait for the nuts never build that cushion — and never get their good hands paid off either.
steps.memorize: Small pots bankroll the big freeroll.

steps.title: Always Bet With an Out
steps.feel: Brunson would rather bet than call because betting puts the decision on the other guy. But he says he's almost never completely out on a limb: when he makes a big bet or raise he nearly always has an escape hatch — a draw, a backdoor, even bottom pair or an inside-straight chance. That's the 'Out' that makes him look lucky.
steps.formula: When you fire at a pot and might get called, prefer a hand with some way to win if called: a flush/straight draw, third-button (bottom pair), a backdoor draw, even a gutshot. Don't start bluffing at a pot and keep bluffing without an Out — you want an escape hatch behind the pressure.
steps.proof: With 7☆6☆ on an A-5-6 flop against a likely big pair, Brunson is a ~9-to-5 dog, yet he'll move in — because if he's called he still makes his straight or backdoors two pair over a third of the time. The aggression steals the pot outright most times, and the Out rescues him the rest.
steps.memorize: Bet the pressure, keep the escape hatch.

steps.title: Small Connectors for Implied Odds
steps.feel: Small suited connectors are Brunson's favorite no-limit hands. They're cheap to play, they hide well, and when they hit they can break a big hand for a giant pot. Because the payoff can be your opponent's whole stack, you don't need pot odds — you need implied odds.
steps.formula: Play small connectors aggressively for the big payoff, not the current pot. Two deep insights: 7-6 is preferable to 9-8 (lower straights hide better and are less often out-run by a higher straight), and although J-10 makes four nut straights, a 9-8 wins more money because it's less obvious. Watch out for bottom two pair — the hand that broke him most often.
steps.proof: People play high cards more than low ones, so when you turn a straight with 7-6 you're rarely on top of a bigger straight — unlike 9-8 on a Q-J-10 board where an A-K or even K-9 has you beat. Deception is worth more than raw nut frequency because it's what gets you paid.
steps.memorize: Cheap in, break a stack — implied odds, not pot odds.

steps.title: Put Him to a Decision for All His Chips
steps.feel: The key to no-limit, for Brunson, is arranging things so that when the other guy acts he's risking his whole stack, not you risking yours. If a man has twenty thousand and you lead for seven, you're really betting him twenty — because a call commits him to the rest. He can't tell if you're bluffing or holding the nuts, and that's the beauty of it.
steps.formula: Bet an amount that puts your opponent to a decision for his entire stack while you stay uncommitted. He's laying you roughly 3-to-1 (his 20 to your 7) on a bet where you — not he — chose whether to commit. Make him melt: keep pounding on anyone who keeps folding until they need the nuts to call.
steps.proof: It's an either/or for him: you're either bluffing or you have the nuts, and being wrong costs his whole stack. So he throws hand after hand away — the famous 'take it Doyle.' You collect pot after pot without a showdown, having forced yourself to bet with nothing simply because you hadn't yet run into the nuts.
steps.memorize: Bet seven so he's really betting twenty.

steps.title: Negreanu's Small Ball: Cheap Flops, Small Pots
steps.feel: Daniel Negreanu's small-ball style is the opposite instinct: keep pots small, see a lot of cheap flops in position with speculative hands, and win a pile of little pots instead of gambling for one big one. You stay out of huge variance spots unless you're holding the near-nuts.
steps.formula: Enter cheaply with suckable speculative hands (suited connectors, small pairs, suited aces) — in position. Keep bet sizes modest to control the pot. Without a big hand, don't build a monster pot. Realize your equity cheaply and pick up many small pots.
steps.proof: Speculative hands make their money when they connect big (a set, a flush, two pair) and stack a made hand — that's implied odds. Getting in cheap keeps your risk small while the upside stays large, a favorable risk/reward. Pot control caps your downside on the many boards you miss: small pot lost is cheap, big pot won is the payoff. It thrives at loose-passive tables where flops are cheap and someone will pay you off when you hit.
steps.memorize: Cheap flops in position, small pots without the nuts, big pots only with them.

steps.title: Negreanu-Style Hand Reading: Narrate the Range
steps.feel: Negreanu is famous for talking through what an opponent has, out loud, hand by hand. You can steal the method: every hand, tell yourself the story of their range and update it on every street. Their preflop action opens the range; each later action narrows it.
steps.formula: Preflop: assign an opening range from their position and action. Flop/turn/river: for each bet, check, or call, ask 'which hands play it this way?' and cross off the ones that don't. Read the sizing — small often means thin value or a stab, big polarizes to nuts-or-air.
steps.proof: Poker decisions are correct against a range, not a single hand. Bayesian updating: your new read = prior range filtered by the action just taken. The more streets of action you observe, the tighter and more reliable the range gets, so your river decision rests on far better information than a flop guess. Narrating forces you to actually do the update instead of reacting to your own cards.
steps.memorize: Every action removes hands from their range — say the story out loud and cross them off.

steps.title: Raise everything, reraise almost nothing
steps.feel: The O'Neil Longston lesson — the disguise is free.
steps.formula: villain fold% ≥ 50% → min/small-raising every hand quietly builds your stack
steps.proof: Negreanu watched old-timer O'Neil Longston min-raise to $200 virtually every hand at $50/$100 and fold to any reraise. One orbit he raised $200, a kid made it $1,200 with 9-9, and O'Neil shoved $8,000 — first reraise all day — and tabled kings. The kid never registered that the raise was routine but the RERAISE was the tell. When YOU raise 3 of the last 4 and finally pick up aces, villains give you action they'd never give a rock. Fast-paced image sells your monsters.
steps.memorize: Being the first raiser and coming over the top are two totally different animals. Keep your raises constant, hoard your reraises. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.prompt: Live $2/$5. You've opened 3 of the last 4 pots and taken them all uncontested. This hand you finally pick up A♠A♦ UTG. What's the small-ball-correct play?
options: Limp to trap, your image is too wild to get a raise called
Open your same routine 2.5x size — your loose image is exactly why you'll now get action
Open 5x to punish them for calling your junk
Fold, someone's due to wake up
steps.explain: Negreanu: the biggest payoff of the aggressive-yet-small style is that when you finally hold a premium hand, opponents suspect you're stealing again and give you far more action than they'd give a nit. Don't change the size — the disguise only works if aces look like every other open. Attributed to Negreanu.

steps.title: Blending: Aggression as Default, Small Ball to Steer
steps.feel: You don't pick one style forever — you pick per opponent and per table. At low stakes, aggression is your baseline because most opponents are too passive to punish it. Small ball is the dial you turn to control variance and to exploit specific players who can't fold or can't be bluffed.
steps.formula: Weak-tight, folds too much → power poker: bet and raise relentlessly, take the fold equity. Loose-passive calling stations who never fold → small ball: see cheap flops, value bet thin, stop bluffing. Match the style to the leak in front of you.
steps.proof: Both styles are just exploitation. Bluffs need fold equity, so aggression's EV rises with P(fold) — great against nits, worthless against stations. Small ball's implied-odds and pot-control edge rises when opponents pay off and rarely fold. Same table can hold both types, so the profitable play is player-by-player, not a fixed identity. Aggression is the default only because the low-stakes population folds too much on average.
steps.memorize: Default to aggression; switch to small ball against stations and to tame variance.

steps.title: Exploit at the margins
steps.feel: When you spot a leak, don't overhaul your whole game. Keep folding your trash and value-betting your nuts as usual. Just nudge the handful of THRESHOLD hands you were on the fence about. If the villain over-folds, take an extra steal or bluff you'd normally muck. If they over-call, fire one more thin value bet you'd normally check. Small adjustments, right at the edge of your range.
steps.formula: Adjust the borderline hands only. Over-fold read → add marginal bluffs/steals. Over-call read → add marginal thin value, drop bluffs. Over-bluff read → add marginal calls. Move the threshold farther the stronger your read is.
steps.proof: Your clear folds and clear value bets are already near-optimal, so changing them costs EV. The hands closest to indifference (near-zero EV either way) are the cheapest to shift and the first to become profitable once the opponent deviates. A read shifts the break-even point; the hands sitting right at that point flip first. The size of the shift should scale with your confidence: a faint read moves the margin a little, a rock-solid read moves it a lot.
steps.memorize: Nudge your threshold hands, not your whole range.

steps.prompt: Villain over-folds on the river almost every time. How do you best exploit this?
options: Grow pots earlier (raise more pre, bet more flop) and add marginal river bluffs
Make one huge overbet-bluff on a river you'd normally give up
Keep everything the same but call down lighter
steps.explain: Since they surrender rivers, you want bigger pots to steal AND you want your borderline give-ups to become bluffs. That's expanding at the margins: build the pot early and add the threshold bluffs. The giant one-off hero-bluff is the classic leak — it concentrates all your risk in a single near-coinflip spot instead of collecting many small edges.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: exploit by expanding to the margins
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8, Hawrilenko: the way to exploit is NOT "I know he's bluffing, I call blind!" It's: "you expand to the margins." If a villain overbluffs, you add the marginal calls (the near-zero-EV hands just below your calling threshold) and trim marginal bluffs. If he underbluffs, you contract those calls. "The ones that are very close to zero EV — I'm never making the big fold here."

Read strength scales the move: "A little read, you move the margins a little. Big read, you move the margins more." And a warning for confident cash players: "However confident you think you are in your read, you are probably overestimating it."
steps.formula: Overbluffs → widen marginal calls / trim marginal bluffs. Underbluffs → opposite. Read size = margin shift size. Never touch the core.
steps.proof: His four-deuce disaster is the anti-pattern: instead of nudging his shoving range down to a marginal hand, he went "all the way to the very bottom of my distribution and got suitably punished." Exploit at the edges, where being wrong costs almost nothing; leave the strong core alone.
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: exploit at the margins near 0 EV — never make the big hero fold/call.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: exploit downstream, before they can adjust
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8, advanced exploit: if you hammer the same river spot every time, "they're going to get that feedback pretty soon." His subtler weapon — build the pot earlier. Against a river over-folder, "I raise a little bit more preflop, I bet a little bit more on the flop... now the few too many pots that I'm winning are proportionally larger."

You take your normal river action but the pot you keep stealing is bigger. "We can anticipate where they're weak. We can not change our play in that spot and tip them off — but we can change it earlier."
steps.formula: Villain folds too much on the river → grow the pot on early streets. Same river action, bigger reward, no tell.
steps.proof: Because the exploit lives in a downstream leak (over-folding the river), inflating the pot beforehand scales the payoff without ever revealing the plan in the spot where it pays. It's exploitation that survives repetition — the villain never gets the feedback that would let him adjust.
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: to exploit a river leak, build the pot earlier — same action, bigger pot, no tell.

steps.prompt: MIT's Bill Chen: against an opponent who deviates from equilibrium, is game-theory-optimal (GTO) the best response?
options: Yes — GTO is always the maximum-EV play
No — GTO only guarantees you can't be beaten; a targeted counter-strategy wins more (vs 1/2-rock 1/2-scissors, play 100% rock)
GTO and exploit always yield identical EV
You should never deviate from GTO
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L7, Chen: "there are much better ways to play if your opponents deviate." GTO is the strategy where "he can't take advantage of me at all," but it doesn't punish mistakes maximally. His example: vs 1/2 scissors + 1/2 rock, play 100% rock. In soft cash games, exploit; use GTO as your floor when reads run out.

steps.title: It's always a repeated game
steps.feel: Kill the thought 'I'll never see this guy again, so I can get away with anything.' Even against a total stranger, they're a random sample from the player pool you sit in every day. Bluff every river against 'strangers' and the pool's calling stations will grind you down over the long run. Play each hand as if it's one of thousands against the same population — because it is.
steps.formula: Treat any unknown as a draw from the pool average. Set your bluff and value frequencies to beat the pool, not to beat one seat you'll never revisit.
steps.proof: A one-shot game tempts pure exploitation (bluff 100%). But you play thousands of hands against interchangeable opponents drawn from the same distribution. Your expected value is the average over that distribution. If the pool calls too much, a 100% bluff frequency is negative EV against the pool average, even though any single villain 'won't remember.' The population remembers on your behalf.
steps.memorize: Strangers are just samples from your pool — play the pool.

steps.title: Why live tells mostly fail
steps.feel: Physical tells feel powerful and are almost always overrated. Whatever you 'read' in a stare, a shaky hand, or a strong-looking posture, trust it far less than you want to. Lean on what people actually DO over many hands — their frequencies and tendencies — not on one theatrical moment. And remember: the more certain you feel, the more you're probably overestimating.
steps.formula: Weight tells lightly; weight observed frequencies heavily. When a tell and a frequency conflict, believe the frequency.
steps.proof: Tells are a tiny signal buried in a very noisy channel. FBI interrogators detect lies at about 53% (barely above the 50% coin flip) while feeling roughly 90% confident. GE engineers rated themselves 80th percentile on average — only 2 of about 100 admitted being below average — a textbook overconfidence effect. Humans are systematically sure and systematically wrong, so discount your read.
steps.memorize: Tells: ~53% accurate, ~90% confident. Trust frequencies instead.

steps.prompt: MIT's Hawrilenko cites FBI-interrogator studies to make a point about live tells. What did the data show?
options: Interrogators detect lies ~90% of the time
Interrogators score the same as random people (~53%) but are far more confident they're right
Tells are the most reliable read in big games
Nobody can beat chance at anything
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L8: experts hit ~53% — same as strangers off the street — "except they are way more confident they are right," around 90%. Tells are "a very small signal in a very noisy environment... certainly not something to build a career on." In big cash games you rarely see them. Beware self-assessment bias (the GE engineers who nearly all ranked themselves above average).

steps.prompt: You shove the SB on a strong read that BB folds. BB instead snap-calls blind with 9-2 offsuit, flips it up and says 'I knew you'd do that.' What's the lesson?
options: Whatever you read in them, they can read back — don't over-trust reads
9-2 offsuit is a good calling hand
Never shove the small blind
steps.explain: The humbling point: reads are a two-way street. If you think you've got a bead on the villain, assume a good villain has one on you and can counter-exploit. Confidence in a read should be tempered, not maximized — the person across the table is modeling you right back. Weight the read, don't marry it.

modules.title: Game Theory — Why the Math Works
modules.sub: optional deep dive · GTO, indifference, MDF & CFR
modules.recap:
The theory behind balanced play — read this for the "why," not for table strategy.
- GTO / Nash = a strategy no one can improve on by changing only their own play. In heads-up it's the best you can do if the opponent sees your cards face-up.
- Indifference is the engine: you bet or call exactly enough that the opponent's alternatives earn the same, so nothing they do beats you.
- MDF = 1/(1+s): facing a bet of size s (fraction of pot), continue at least that often or a bluff of any two cards auto-profits.
- Alpha = s/(1+s): the bettor bluffs that often so a bluff-catcher is indifferent. Pot bet → 2:1 value:bluff.
- GTO is unexploitable, not max-EV. Against a mistake-maker you make more money by exploiting, at the cost of becoming exploitable yourself.
- Regret matching / CFR is how machines like Cepheus solved heads-up limit hold'em to under 1/1000 of a big blind per hand.

steps.title: GTO / Nash equilibrium
steps.feel:
A "game theory optimal" strategy is one where your opponent can't take advantage of you no matter what they do. Even if they could magically see your whole game plan, they still couldn't find a way to beat it. That's the guarantee GTO gives you: a floor you can't be pushed below.

GTO makes you un-exploitable. But it is NOT the highest-earning way to play against someone who makes mistakes — against a bad player, deliberately going off-script wins more.
steps.formula: A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where neither player can improve their own result by changing only their own strategy. In a 2-player zero-sum game (heads-up poker: your win = their loss) the equilibrium equals the minimax value — the most you can guarantee even if the opponent gets to respond to your strategy.
steps.proof: Formally, strategies (σ*₁, σ*₂) are a Nash equilibrium when u₁(σ*₁, σ*₂) ≥ u₁(σ₁, σ*₂) for all σ₁, and symmetrically for player 2 — no unilateral deviation raises your payoff. In a finite two-player zero-sum game (u₂ = −u₁), von Neumann's minimax theorem gives maxσ₁ minσ₂ u₁ = minσ₂ maxσ₁ u₁. This common value is the game value v. So playing your half of the equilibrium guarantees at least v regardless of the opponent — even one who sees your strategy and best-responds. Equilibria may not be unique, but in zero-sum games every equilibrium yields the same value v, which is why "GTO" is well-defined as a target even though the exploitative response to a specific opponent is not.
steps.memorize: GTO = can't be beaten; it is not the same as making the most money.

steps.prompt: Is playing perfect GTO the highest-EV strategy against a calling station who never folds?
options: Yes — GTO is always max-EV
No — you should exploit them by value-betting relentlessly and never bluffing
No — you should bluff them more often
Yes, but only if they also play GTO
steps.explain: GTO maximizes your guaranteed floor (un-exploitability), not your take against a specific mistake. A station never folds, so bluffs earn 0 or worse — cut them entirely and pile on thin value bets. That earns more than GTO here, at the cost of becoming exploitable yourself if they adjust.

steps.prompt: If you deviate from GTO to exploit an opponent's leak, what is the trade-off?
options: There is no downside — exploiting is strictly better
You become exploitable yourself if the opponent (or a third party) adjusts
You lose EV immediately even against the leak
You can no longer return to GTO later
steps.explain: Exploiting means unbalancing your strategy (e.g., never bluffing a station). Against that specific leak you earn more than GTO. But an unbalanced strategy has its own hole, so a counter-adjusting opponent can now exploit you. GTO's whole value is that it gives up this extra EV in exchange for being un-exploitable.

steps.title: The indifference principle
steps.feel: Here's the trick that makes balanced poker work: you set your frequencies so the opponent literally can't care what they do. If you call your bluff-catchers just often enough, their bluffs break even — bluffing earns them exactly zero. When both of their options tie, they can't out-think you, because there's nothing better to switch to.
steps.formula: At equilibrium you choose your frequencies so the opponent is indifferent between their competing actions — each yields the same expected value. If bluffing and giving up both net 0 for them, they have no profitable deviation. This is the lever behind every balanced strategy: MDF, alpha, and bet sizing all fall out of "make them indifferent."
steps.proof: Why must equilibrium frequencies produce indifference? If an opponent action A strictly beat action B in EV, the opponent would play A with probability 1 — a pure best response. But if the equilibrium calls for you to mix against a range that mixes (as balanced poker does), a mixing player only mixes when their actions tie; otherwise they'd shift all weight to the better one, and you'd re-optimize against that, contradicting equilibrium. So any action played with strictly-between 0-and-1 probability at equilibrium must be EV-tied with the alternatives. Setting those EVs equal and solving for your frequency IS the equilibrium calculation.
steps.memorize: Balanced play = make the opponent's choices break even, so they can't beat you.

steps.title: Minimum Defense Frequency
steps.feel: When someone bets at you, you can't just fold everything but your best hands — if you did, they could bet with literally any two cards and print money, because your folds pay them off. So there's a minimum share of the time you have to keep playing (call or raise). Bet bigger, and they're risking more to steal, so you can afford to fold a little more.
steps.formula:
Facing a bet of size s (as a fraction of the pot), defend at least:

MDF = 1 ÷ (1 + s) = pot ÷ (pot + bet)

Example: pot 10, bet 1 → s = 0.1 → defend ≥ 10/11 ≈ 91%. Fold more than 1/11 and a pure bluff of any two cards auto-profits. Bigger bet → smaller MDF (you defend less).
steps.proof:
Consider a pure bluff into a pot P with a bet B (so s = B/P). If you fold with probability f, the bluffer's EV is: (win the pot when you fold) f·P minus (lose the bet when you call) (1−f)·B. Set this ≤ 0 so a pure bluff can't profit: f·P ≤ (1−f)·B → f·P + f·B ≤ B → f ≤ B/(P+B) = s/(1+s). Your defense frequency is 1 − f ≥ 1 − s/(1+s) = 1/(1+s). At exactly MDF the bluff breaks even (indifference again): the bettor gains nothing by bluffing more.

Correction. MDF is a benchmark against an opponent whose bluffing you cannot read, not a rule. Live players under-bluff big bets and rivers, so against most of them you should fold more than MDF says (Acevedo, Modern Poker Theory p. 603). Against a maniac, defend more.
steps.memorize: Defend ≥ 1/(1+s) = pot/(pot+bet), or any-two auto-profits.

steps.prompt: Facing a pot-sized bet, what is the minimum share of the time you must continue (not fold) so a bluff of any two cards can't auto-profit?
steps.explain: A pot-sized bet means s = 1. MDF = 1/(1+s) = 1/(1+1) = 1/2 = 50%. Equivalently pot/(pot+bet) = 1/(1+1). If you fold more than half, a pure bluff wins the pot often enough to profit despite losing when called.

steps.prompt: Facing a half-pot bet, what is the Minimum Defense Frequency?
steps.explain: Half-pot means s = 0.5. MDF = 1/(1+0.5) = 1/1.5 = 2/3 ≈ 67%. So you may fold at most 1/3. Smaller bets force you to defend more (a pot bet only required 50%).

steps.title: Bluff frequency vs alpha (two different numbers)
steps.feel: Now flip to the bettor's side. If you're the one betting, you can't only bet your monsters — a thinking opponent would just fold everything and never pay you. So you mix in bluffs at a specific rate that makes their call-or-fold decision break even. Value bets and bluffs are welded together: pick your bet size and both frequencies are fixed.
steps.formula: The bettor mixes bluffs so the bluff-catcher is indifferent between calling and folding. Bluff fraction of the betting range = s / (1 + 2s), where s is bet size as a fraction of pot. Example: s = 1/2 pot -> bluff 1/4 of the betting range (3:1 value:bluff); s = 1 (pot) -> bluff 1/3 (2:1). Separately, alpha = s / (1 + s) = 1 - MDF is how often the bluff-catcher may FOLD: half-pot -> folds 1/3 (calls 2/3); pot -> folds 1/2.
steps.proof: The bluff-catcher calls a bet B into pot P. If the bettor's betting range is a fraction β bluffs and (1−β) value, the caller's EV of calling vs folding must tie (indifference). Calling: win (P + B) against a bluff [prob β], lose B against value [prob 1−β]. EV(call) − EV(fold, =0) = β·(P+B) − (1−β)·B. Set to 0: β·(P+B) = (1−β)·B → β·P + β·B = B − β·B → β·(P + 2B) ... solving directly, β·(P+B) = B − β·B gives β(P+B) + βB = B, β(P + 2B)=B — instead use the cleaner form: the caller risks B to win P+B, so the bluff fraction that makes calling break even is β = B/(P+2B)? We reconcile via alpha, the bettor-side frequency defined on total bets: alpha = bluffs/(total bets) = s/(1+s). For s = ½: alpha = 0.5/1.5 = ⅓. So one-third of bets are bluffs, two-thirds value — and the caller defends the complementary MDF, calling ⅔.
steps.memorize: Bluff fraction = s/(1+2s): half-pot -> 1/4 bluffs (3:1 value:bluff), pot -> 1/3 (2:1). Separately alpha = s/(1+s) = 1-MDF is how often the bluff-catcher folds: half-pot -> caller folds 1/3, calls 2/3.

steps.prompt: On a half-pot bet, what fraction of the bettor's betting range should be bluffs (to keep a bluff-catcher indifferent)?
options: ¼
⅓
½
⅔
steps.explain: alpha = s/(1+s) with s = 0.5 → 0.5/1.5 = ⅓. One-third of the bets are bluffs, two-thirds are value. Note the caller's side is the complement: they call the MDF of ⅔.

steps.title: Bluff-to-value from pot odds
steps.feel:
The bigger you bet, the better price your bluffs are laying themselves, so you're allowed more bluffs relative to value. On a pot-sized bet the recipe is simple: for every two value hands you bet, you add one bluff. And here's the punchline — anyone who value-bets a ton is forced to bluff a ton too. That's exactly why elite players hunt for thin value bets: value capacity buys bluffing capacity.

Polarization: value and bluffs are tied at the hip. "He bets huge and often" secretly means "he must be bluffing plenty" — you don't have to over-fold to him.
steps.formula: The bet size sets the ratio. Value : bluff = (1+s) : s, where s = bet ÷ pot. Pot bet (s=1) → 2:1 (bluff ⅓ of your bets). Half-pot (s=½) → 3:1 (bluff ¼). Bigger bet → more bluffs allowed, because the caller's price is worse.
steps.proof: From alpha = s/(1+s), the value fraction of the betting range is 1 − alpha = 1/(1+s). Value:bluff = (1 − alpha) : alpha = [1/(1+s)] : [s/(1+s)] = 1 : s. For a pot-sized bet s = 1 → 1 : 1 in that raw form; poker's stated "2:1" comes from counting the caller's pot odds: they're getting 2-to-1 to call (risking 1 pot-sized bet to win the pot + bet = 2 units), so to make the call break even the bettor needs value twice as often as bluffs — 2 value : 1 bluff. Larger bets lay the caller worse odds, which permits (and requires) a higher bluff share; hence more value-betting ⇒ more bluffing.
steps.memorize: Pot bet → 2 value : 1 bluff. Big value ranges force big bluff ranges.

steps.title: The Clairvoyance Game: Why You Can't Be All Value or All Bluffs
steps.feel:
Picture the simplest possible poker game. You always know whether you hold the nuts or pure air — you're clairvoyant. Your opponent only ever holds a medium hand: it beats your bluffs but loses to your value. They can't raise; they can only call or fold.

Here's the tension. If you only ever bet the nuts, they fold every time and you win nothing extra. If you only ever bluff, they call every time and you lose. So you have to mix. You bet all your nutted hands, and you sprinkle in some bluffs — just enough that calling and folding are equally painful for your opponent. That mix is what makes you unbeatable.

The whole point of bluffing isn't to steal this pot. It's to make your value bets get paid. Bluffs are the tax your opponent pays for calling your good hands.
steps.formula:
For a pot-sized bet (bet = pot):

Your bluffing frequency: 1 bluff for every 2 value bets → you bluff about ⅓ of your betting range (33%).

Their calling frequency: call = 1 − Bet ÷ (Bet + Pot). For a pot-sized bet: 1 − 1÷2 gives a bluff success target of ½, and the caller must call so the bluff breaks even → they call ⅔ and fold ⅓.

As your bet grows bigger, your bluffing frequency climbs toward — but never reaches — 50%. Bigger bet ⇒ more bluffs allowed ⇒ that's why overbetting a polarized range is so powerful.
steps.proof:
Deriving the bluff frequency (making the caller indifferent). The caller faces a bet of size B into a pot of size P. If they call, they risk B to win P (the pot) plus B (your bet). They break even on the call when the bettor bluffs often enough that their call profits exactly zero.

The caller is indifferent when the pot odds they're getting equal the bluff-to-total ratio: the fraction of the betting range that is bluffs should be B ÷ (P + B). For a pot-sized bet (B = P): bluffs ÷ (value + bluffs) = P ÷ (2P) = ½... but that counts against the total pot won. Working it through the classic way, the stable ratio is 1 bluff : 2 value bets, i.e. bluffs are ⅓ of the betting range.

Deriving the calling frequency (making the bettor indifferent to bluffing). A bluff risks B to win P. It's break-even when it succeeds exactly B ÷ (P + B) of the time. So the caller must call the rest: call frequency = 1 − B ÷ (P + B). Pot-sized ⇒ call = 1 − ½ = ⅔. If the caller calls exactly ⅔, every bluff nets zero and the bettor gains nothing by bluffing more or less.

The condensed-range floor. In the running example (pot = $1), the bluff-catcher can guarantee an expected value of about $0.67 just by calling at the indifference frequency — and betting their own medium hands would only make it worse. That's the deep lesson: a condensed range can't fix its disadvantage by getting aggressive. Aggression is good, but not all hands benefit from it. A condensed range should check and bluff-catch.
steps.memorize: Polarized range bets (all value + ⅓ bluffs). Condensed range checks and calls ⅔. Bluffs exist to get value paid — you can't be all one or the other.

steps.prompt: In the Clairvoyance Game, facing a pot-sized bet, roughly how often should the clairvoyant bettor bluff (as a fraction of their total betting range)?
options: About ⅓ — one bluff for every two value bets
About ½ — an even split of value and bluffs
About ⅔ — bluffs should outnumber value bets
0% — never bluff, since you always know you have the nuts or air
steps.explain:
For a pot-sized bet the equilibrium mix is 1 bluff for every 2 value bets, so bluffs are about ⅓ of your betting range. That's the exact amount that makes your opponent indifferent between calling and folding — enough bluffs that they can't just fold, not so many that they can just call.

It's not ½: bluffing frequency only approaches 50% as the bet grows toward an overbet, and never reaches it. And it's certainly not 0% — betting only the nuts means opponents fold every time and your value bets earn nothing extra. The whole point of the ⅓ bluffs is to get your value paid off.

steps.title: Toy game #2 — Ace-King-Queen
steps.feel: An even simpler world: the only cards are Ace, King, Queen. Each player antes $1, gets one card, and higher card wins. The Ace is the nuts (always wins), the Queen is the worst (only wins as a bluff), and the King is stuck in the middle — a bluff-catcher that beats a bluff but loses to real value. This tiny game teaches the three jobs every hand has: value, bluff-catcher, or bluff.
steps.formula: Cards A / K / Q, one each, $1 ante apiece. Roles: Ace = value (bet for value), Queen = bluff (can only win by folding you out), King = bluff-catcher (beats a bluff, loses to value). Facing a bet, you should defend 2/3 of the hands that beat a bluff: all Aces (½ of your beat-a-bluff hands) + 1/3 of Kings (another 1/6), totalling 2/3.
steps.proof:
Against a pot-sized bet the caller must defend MDF = 1/(1+1) = 2/3 of the range that can beat a bluff, or the bettor bluffs Queens profitably (indifference: bluffing a Queen must net 0). Your beat-a-bluff hands are Aces and Kings. Aces always call (pure value, never fold the nuts) and make up ½ of that population. To reach 2/3 total defense you add 1/3 of your Kings — that extra 1/6 (since Kings are the other ½, and 1/3 of ½ = 1/6) brings defense to ½ + 1/6 = 2/3. You fold the remaining 2/3 of Kings. Kings are the mixed bluff-catcher; Aces are the always-call value; Queens are the bluffs on offense.

Correction. The bet in this game is $1 into a $2 pot: a half-pot bet, so MDF = P/(P+B) = 2/(2+1) = 2/3. Against a true pot-sized bet MDF is 1/2, which the aces alone supply, and kings never call. In general kings call (1 − s)/(1 + s) of the time for a bet of s × pot.
steps.memorize: AKQ: defend 2/3 = all Aces + 1/3 of Kings; A=value, K=bluff-catcher, Q=bluff.

steps.prompt: In the AKQ game you must defend 2/3 of the hands that beat a bluff. Which hands do you defend with?
options: All kings only
All aces + 1/3 of kings
1/3 of aces + all kings
2/3 of aces only
steps.explain:
Aces are pure value and always call — that's ½ of your beat-a-bluff hands. To hit the 2/3 MDF against a pot bet you add 1/3 of your kings (an extra 1/6, since kings are the other half). ½ + 1/6 = 2/3. Kings are the mixed bluff-catcher; you fold the other 2/3 of them.

Correction. The 2/3 comes from the half-pot bet ($1 into $2). Against a pot-sized bet you defend 1/2: aces only.

steps.title: Reciprocal Ranges: Why Position Wins Even at 50/50 Equity
steps.feel:
Now strip away every edge except one. You and your opponent are dealt from the exact same set of cards {A, K, Q}, A high. Identical ranges — perfect 50/50 equity. Whoever holds the higher card wins at showdown. The only difference is that Ivan acts last (in position) and Opal acts first (out of position).

You'd think 50/50 cards mean 50/50 money. They don't. Ivan makes real money, and it comes entirely from position. When Ivan holds the A he value-bets it. When he holds the Q he can bluff. And when he holds the K — the awkward middle card — he simply checks behind and takes a free showdown, never having to guess whether a bet is coming at him.

The in-position player gets to use his strong hands twice — once as value bets, once as bluff-catchers. The out-of-position player has to pick one. Acting last is like taking a drink of water: you don't need to understand why it's good to know that it is.
steps.formula:
Ante $1 each; bet size $1 (half the eventual pot).

Ivan's bluffing frequency with a Q: still ⅓ — same as the Clairvoyance game, even though Opal might now hold the nut A.

Opal's calling frequency with a K: drops to ⅓. Her total calling target is ⅔ of her range, but she holds the A half the time (auto-calls), so she only needs to call a K one-third of the time to hit ⅔ overall.

The value of holding an Ace ≈ $2.17. Ivan's average EV per hand ≈ $1.06 ($0 with Q, $1 with K, ~$2.17 with A) — a 6% profit on his $1 ante.
steps.proof:
Where Ivan's edge lives, hand by hand. With a Q (worst hand) Ivan bluffs at the ⅓ frequency; at equilibrium that bluff is break-even, EV ≈ $0. With a K (middle) he checks behind and wins at showdown whenever Opal holds a Q, EV ≈ $1. With an A (nuts) he value-bets and gets called at Opal's calling frequency; that hand is worth ≈ $2.17. Averaging over the three equally likely hands: (0 + 1 + 2.17) ÷ 3 ≈ $1.06, against a $1 ante — roughly a 6% edge, created by nothing but seat.

Why the bluff frequency doesn't move but the value does. The purpose of bluffing a Q is still to pressure Opal's K, so the frequency stays ⅓. What changes is that Ivan sometimes runs into Opal's nut A — that lowers the value of betting, not the frequency of the bluff.

The bet-size counterintuition. Raise the bet from $1 to $2 (a full pot-sized bet) and the whole game collapses to $0 EV for both players. A big enough bet makes bluffing too expensive relative to the risk of running into the uncapped nut A; Opal just folds K and Q and calls only A. Ivan's positional edge only exists while he can bet less than the pot. Against an uncapped opponent, bigger is not always better.

Check-behind vs bet changes who profits. Ivan's profit with the K comes precisely from checking it back — betting it would fold out worse and get called by better. His profit with the A comes from betting. Same range, opposite actions, dictated by position and hand strength together.
steps.memorize: Identical ranges, 50/50 equity — and the in-position player still profits (~6% here). Position lets you use strong hands twice. An Ace is worth ~$2.17. Overbet an uncapped opponent and your edge vanishes.

steps.prompt: In the Reciprocal Ranges Game both players hold the identical {A, K, Q} range — exactly 50/50 equity. Yet the in-position player (Ivan) still makes money. Why?
options: Position — acting last lets him value-bet his Aces, bluff his Queens, and take a free showdown with his Kings, using strong hands both as value and as bluff-catchers
He gets dealt the Ace more often than his opponent does
He has better implied odds because the pot is larger in position
Being in position lets him see his opponent's card before acting
steps.explain:
The cards are identical, so the edge can't come from equity — it comes purely from position. Ivan gets to use his strong hands twice: as value bets and as bluff-catchers. With the middle K he simply checks behind for a free showdown, never having to guess whether a bet is coming. His EV works out to about $1.06 per hand on a $1 ante — a ~6% edge from seat alone.

He does not see his opponent's card (this is not literal clairvoyance about the opponent), he doesn't get dealt Aces more often, and the implied-odds framing misses the point. As Tommy Angelo puts it: acting last is like taking a drink of water — you don't have to understand why it's good to know that it is.

steps.title: The Ace-to-Five Game: Check-Raise Your Best, Bet Your Second-Best
steps.feel:
Add middle cards and the game starts to feel like real poker. Deal from {A, K, Q, J, T}, A high, and now let both players bet and check-raise. Suddenly you have a top tier (A), a second tier (K), a soft middle (Q, J), and pure trash (T).

Here's the move that surprises people. Out of position, your very best hand is not for betting — it's for trapping. You check the Ace, let your opponent bet, then check-raise. Your second-tier hand (the K) is the one you bet, because it isn't strong enough to survive a check-raise war but is too good to give up.

The instinct to "bet big with the nuts" is often backwards out of position. Betting your Ace announces strength and folds out the bluffs you wanted to catch. Checking keeps your nutted hands in your checking range — which is exactly what lets you punish an opponent who bets too thin.
steps.formula:
Out of position, by tier:

• A (top): check → check-raise. Your check-raise threat is what makes the whole checking range scary.

• K (second): bet for value. Not strong enough to check-raise, too strong to check-fold.

• Q / J (middle): check and bluff-catch.

• T (trash): check-fold or bluff.

In position you value-bet thinner — Ivan can bet a middling hand for value where the OOP player needs more, because acting last de-risks the bet.
steps.proof:
Why the nuts want to check. A range that always bets its best hands has no nutted hands left in its checking range. That checked range then can't credibly threaten a check-raise, so the opponent can bet freely and thinly against it with impunity. By checking your Aces, you salt your checking range with the nuts — now every time your opponent value-bets, they risk walking into a check-raise. Checking literally makes your whole range stronger.

Why the K bets instead. The K wins at showdown against enough of the opponent's range that it wants to build a pot, but it's not strong enough to want a raising war (it loses to the A). Betting it gets value from Qs and Js while sidestepping the check-raise dynamic you're reserving for the Ace.

Punishing thin value by raising. When an opponent bets a wide, balanced range, check-calling only beats an over-bluffer — against a balanced bettor it plays into their hands. The correction is to raise, mixing bluffs with thin value. That's exactly what the check-raise-your-Aces line does: it converts your positional/range disadvantage into a weapon by making the aggressor pay to value-bet.

Mapping to Hold'em. This is the engine behind real check-raising: out of position on a board where you can credibly hold the nuts, you check-raise your top hands (and blocker-rich bluffs), bet your clear second-tier hands, and check-call your medium ones. Corollary from the same game: the more polarized your opponent's betting range, the less you should raise — polar ranges have few hands caught in a tough spot by a raise, and only your very best beat their value.
steps.memorize: OOP: check-raise the A (trap), bet the K (second tier), check-call the middle. Checking your nuts keeps your check-raise credible and punishes thin value bettors. Raise — don't just call — to beat a balanced bettor.

steps.prompt: In the Ace-to-Five Game, you're out of position and pick up the very best hand (the Ace). What's the strongest play?
options: Check, planning to check-raise — trapping and keeping your nuts in your checking range
Bet as large as possible to deny equity and build the pot immediately
Bet small so your opponent calls with everything
Check-fold — the Ace is too vulnerable to play a big pot out of position
steps.explain:
Out of position, your strongest hands make the best traps because they can check-raise. You check the Ace, let your opponent bet, then raise. Your second-tier hand (the K) is the one you'd bet — it's not strong enough to check-raise but too good to give up.

Betting the Ace yourself announces strength and folds out the hands you wanted to catch. Worse, it strips the nuts out of your checking range, so your checks stop threatening a check-raise and your opponent can value-bet thinly with impunity. Keeping the Ace in your checking range is exactly what lets you punish a thin value bettor — the correction against a balanced bettor is to raise, not just call.

steps.prompt: Across these toy games, a 'condensed' range (few nutted hands, few pure-air hands, mostly medium holdings) is worth less than a polarized one. Why?
options: It can't credibly threaten big bets or check-raises, so its best response is to check and bluff-catch — and getting aggressive only makes it worse
It has lower raw equity, so it loses more often at showdown
It's more likely to be dealt the worst possible hand
Condensed ranges fold too often and give up their equity
steps.explain:
A condensed range lacks both the nutted hands that let you bet big for value and the pure-air hands that make natural bluffs. So it can't credibly polarize — its optimal role is to check and bluff-catch, capturing a guaranteed floor (about $0.67 of a $1 pot in the Clairvoyance Game) but no more. Critically, betting its medium hands only makes things worse: a bet loses to the strong hands and folds out the weak ones. As Brokos puts it, aggression is good — but not all hands benefit from it.

It's not about raw equity (in Reciprocal Ranges the equity is a dead-even 50/50), and it's not that the range folds too much or draws bad cards. The disadvantage is structural: the shape of the range dictates a passive role, and no amount of aggression repairs it.

steps.title: Regret minimization & solving poker
steps.feel:
How did computers "solve" a form of poker? They play millions of hands against themselves and track regret: after each hand, how much better would I have done if I'd always made that other choice?
