The program leans harder into the choices it wishes it had made more, and drops the ones it regrets. Do this long enough and the self-taught strategy drifts toward un-exploitable — no human tuning required.

None of this changes how you beat a $1/$2 live table — that's pure exploitation of human leaks. This module is the "why the math works," not table strategy. Don't try to play a solver at $1/$2; play the humans.
steps.formula: Regret of an action = (payoff had you always taken it) − (payoff you actually got). Keep only positive regret and play each action in proportion to its accumulated positive regret (regret matching). Average regret shrinks at rate O(1/√t), so the average strategy over time converges to a Nash equilibrium. CFR (counterfactual regret) runs regret matching at every decision node, weighting each by how often that node is reached; CFR+ floors negative regret at 0 for faster convergence.
steps.proof: Regret matching is a no-regret online-learning algorithm: set action probabilities p(a) ∝ max(R(a), 0), where R(a) is cumulative regret; if all regrets ≤ 0, play uniformly. A standard result bounds average external regret by O(√(A)·L / √t) → 0 as iterations t → ∞ (the O(1/√t) rate). In a two-player zero-sum game, if both players use no-regret learning, the pair of time-average strategies converges to a Nash equilibrium (folk theorem via the minimax/duality argument). CFR decomposes total regret into per-information-set counterfactual regrets — each weighted by the counterfactual reach probability of arriving there — and minimizes each locally, which bounds the overall regret and yields Nash in the average. CFR+ replaces cumulative regret with regret that's reset-to-0 when negative, empirically converging much faster. Using CFR+, the Cepheus project solved heads-up limit Texas hold'em to within less than 1/1000 of a big blind per hand (about 900 CPU-years of computation) — "essentially unbeatable" over a lifetime of play, though the reported solution is that-close-to, not literally, perfect.
steps.memorize: Play in proportion to positive regret → average strategy → Nash; Cepheus solved HU limit hold'em to <1/1000 BB.

steps.prompt: In CFR / regret matching, which regrets do you act on when deciding future action frequencies?
options: All regrets, positive and negative
Only positive regret
Only the single largest regret
The average of all regrets, sign ignored
steps.explain: You set each action's probability in proportion to its accumulated positive regret (negative regrets are treated as 0; if none are positive you play uniformly). This is regret matching — it steers weight toward choices you wish you'd made more. CFR+ enforces this even harder by flooring negative regret at 0 each step.

steps.prompt: What did Cepheus solve, and how exploitable is its strategy?
options: No-limit hold'em, exactly 0 exploitability
Heads-up limit hold'em, less than 1/1000 of a big blind per hand
All of poker, provably perfect
6-max limit hold'em, about 1 big blind per hand
steps.explain: Cepheus solved heads-up (two-player) limit Texas hold'em to within less than 1/1000 of a big blind per hand — "essentially unbeatable," though not literally perfect. It required roughly 900 CPU-years using CFR+. No-limit and multiway games are vastly larger and were not solved this way.

steps.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Poker (and Chen's twist on it)
steps.feel:
David Sklansky's famous rule says: every time you play a hand differently than you would if you could see your opponent's cards, they gain — and every time they play differently than they would if they could see yours, you gain. In plain words: poker is a war over information. If you could always see your opponent's hole cards you would never make a mistake, so the whole game is about acting well while blind, and tricking the other person into acting badly while they are blind.

Chen and Ankenman accept the spirit of this but sharpen it. They point out that the theorem quietly assumes there are only two players and that a 'mistake' is obvious. Their bigger point is about the cost of mistakes, and it is lopsided: folding too much is usually a far worse error than betting too much. When you fold, you hand over the entire pot; when you throw in one extra aggressive bet that turns out wrong, you only lose that one bet. So a slightly-too-aggressive player leaks a little, while a too-timid player who loves 'big laydowns' hemorrhages. This is why they play aggressively on purpose.
steps.formula: Cost of folding-too-often ≈ the whole pot you surrender. Cost of one extra loose bet ≈ just that bet. Because the pot is usually much bigger than one bet, the penalty for being too tight > the penalty for being too loose. Chen's practical rule: when two lines feel EV-equal, pick the more aggressive one.
steps.proof: Chen & Ankenman reframe the theorem around one idea: an optimal strategy can be announced out loud and still not be exploitable. Imagine you had to tell your opponent your entire plan before every hand. To a normal player this sounds insane — of course knowing the plan helps them. But a truly balanced strategy is one where knowing the plan changes nothing they can profitably do, because every action you take contains the right mix of strong hands, medium hands, and bluffs. That is the real meaning of 'they gain when they play differently than if they saw your cards': against a balanced range, seeing your cards would help them, but seeing your strategy would not. The FTOP is therefore a statement about the value of hidden information, and balance is the tool that makes your information worthless to steal.
steps.memorize: Poker is a fight over information. Being too tight (folding) leaks more than being too loose (an extra bet).

steps.prompt: Chen & Ankenman's practical sharpening of the Fundamental Theorem of Poker is that the COSTS of the two opposite mistakes are lopsided. Which is the more expensive error?
options: Betting a bit too aggressively — you risk your whole stack
Folding too often — you surrender the entire pot rather than one extra bet
Both cost exactly the same in expectation
Calling too much on the river
steps.explain: Folding too much hands over the whole pot; one extra loose bet only loses that bet. Since the pot is usually far bigger than a single bet, over-tightness leaks more than over-aggression. This is why Chen & Ankenman break EV-ties toward the more aggressive line and warn against players obsessed with 'big laydowns.'

steps.title: Jam-or-fold: why shoving 16 chips to win 3 with 60%+ of hands is correct
steps.feel:
Picture a heads-up match where the stacks are tiny relative to the blinds — you only have a handful of big blinds left. Your realistic choices shrink to two: shove everything all-in, or fold. There is no room to make a small raise and then out-play someone; the money goes in now or not at all. This is the everyday endgame of online sit-and-go tournaments.

The counter-intuitive result Chen & Ankenman prove: at these short stacks you should shove a shockingly wide range. Their headline puzzle — two players, 16 chips each, blinds of 1 and 2 — has the button correctly jamming with about 61.7% of all hands. People recoil at this ('who risks 16 to win 3 with more than half their hands?!'). But it is right, because when you shove and get called you are not risking 16 to win 3 — the pot already has dead money in it, and folds happen often enough that most shoves just scoop the blinds uncontested.
steps.formula: The engine of every jam decision: when you jam, your hand's value is its equity against the range that CALLS you — never its equity against a random hand. A middling hand like 9-7 suited can be a fine shove because it plays okay against the big pairs and big aces that snap-call, even though it is an underdog to a random hand. Practical takeaway from their solved tables: play jam-or-fold whenever the smaller stack is roughly 10 big blinds or less (up to ~12-13 out of position).
steps.proof: In their toy version each player draws a number in [0,1] (lower = better). Both strategies are simple thresholds: the attacker jams with hands better than y, the defender calls with hands better than x. At those exact thresholds each player is indifferent between their two options, which lets you solve directly. For the game where the best hand always wins, they derive x = 3/(2+2S) and y = 3S/(1+S)² where S is the stack in blinds. Then comes the key upgrade: in real holdem even the worst hand has roughly 1/3 equity at showdown (it can suck out). Redo the algebra with the loser keeping 1/3 of the pot and the strategies get dramatically LOOSER — mathematically it is the same game with the stack replaced by S/3, its 'effective' size. That extra suck-out equity is exactly why real short-stack shoving is so wide.
steps.memorize: Short stack (≤10bb)? Jam or fold. Judge a shoving hand by its equity vs. the CALLING range, not vs. a random hand.

steps.prompt: Chen & Ankenman's opening puzzle: two equally-skilled players, heads-up, 16 chips each, blinds of 1 and 2. Playing optimally, with roughly what fraction of hands should the button move all-in?
options: About 15% — you only shove premium hands when risking 16 to win 3
About 35% — a standard tight-aggressive shoving range
About 62% — far wider than intuition suggests
100% — at these blinds any two cards is a profitable shove
steps.explain: Their solved jam-or-fold tables give roughly 61.7% of all hands. It startles people because it looks like risking 16 to win 3, but the pot already holds dead money and folds are frequent, so most shoves scoop the blinds uncontested. This is a signature result: short-stack shoving is much wider than intuition says.

steps.prompt: When you decide whether a given hand is a profitable all-in shove, which comparison actually matters?
options: Its equity against a completely random hand
Its equity against the range of hands that will CALL your shove
Whether it is in the top half of all starting hands
Its raw showdown strength ignoring position
steps.explain: A shove only sees a showdown when it gets called, so the relevant number is your equity against the CALLING range. That is why a hand like a middling suited connector can be a fine shove — it plays acceptably against the big pairs and big aces that snap-call — even though it is an underdog to a random hand.

steps.title: The 'golden mean of poker': bet about 41% of the pot
steps.feel:
No-limit gives you an infinite menu of bet sizes. Most books wave their hands ('bet pot', 'bet small with weak hands'). Chen & Ankenman actually solve for the best size in a clean model. The setup: sometimes you hold an unbeatable hand (the nuts), sometimes a pure bluff; when you bluff, your opponent has the nuts half the time and a hand that only beats a bluff the other half. What fraction of the pot should you bet?

The answer is a specific, memorable number: bet a little more than 41% of the pot. Bet too small and you leave value on the table; bet too big and you win less often because your opponent can fold more and still be fine. There is a sweet spot in between, and it is not the round 'half pot' or 'full pot' that intuition suggests.
steps.formula: Optimal bet size (fraction of pot): r = √2 − 1 ≈ 0.414, i.e. about 41% of the pot. Chen calls this constant the 'golden mean of poker' because it keeps reappearing in the solutions. You bet this amount with your nut hands and add bluffs so your bluff-to-value ratio matches the size, and your opponent calls with a total frequency of 1/√2 ≈ 71%.
steps.proof: Write your expected value as a function of the bet size s (measured as a multiple of the pot). Your bluffs break even (the opponent calls just often enough to make bluffing a wash), so all your profit comes from value bets getting paid off. Working out how often the opponent must call to stop you bluffing (they fold a fraction s/(1+s), the bluffing ratio α) and how much you gain when called, the value function turns out to be f(s) = s(1−s)/6(1+s). Set its derivative to zero: s² + 2s − 1 = 0, which gives (1+s)² = 2, so s = √2 − 1 ≈ 0.414. The general recipe is the real lesson: solve the game in terms of the bet size, get EV as a function of it, then let the bettor pick the size that maximizes that EV. That technique — 'solve in terms of the variable one player controls, then optimize it' — is how you attack bet sizing analytically instead of by feel.
steps.memorize: √2 − 1 ≈ 0.41 pot is the model-optimal bet. General method: write EV as a function of bet size, then maximize.

steps.prompt: In Chen & Ankenman's clairvoyance model (you hold the nuts or a bluff; when you bluff, opponent has the nuts half the time), what is the model-optimal bet size — the 'golden mean of poker'?
options: Exactly half the pot
√2 − 1 ≈ 41% of the pot
The full pot
Twice the pot to maximize fold equity
steps.explain: Maximizing the value function f(s) = s(1−s)/6(1+s) leads to s² + 2s − 1 = 0, so s = √2 − 1 ≈ 0.414, a little over 41% of the pot. Chen dubs this recurring constant the 'golden mean of poker.' Bet smaller and you leave value behind; bet bigger and you get called less often.

steps.title: Against a strong enough range, just fold — no matter how small the bet
steps.feel:
Here is a genuinely surprising result that shows how far the math can go past intuition. Suppose your opponent's range is very strong — say more than half of their hands are actual winners (a 'clairvoyant' or near-clairvoyant player who bets his good hands and protects them with a correctly-tuned dose of bluffs). Your intuition says: they're betting, sometimes they're bluffing, so I should call sometimes to catch the bluffs.

Chen & Ankenman show that against a sufficiently strong betting range your best response is to fold every single hand — even if they bet an absurdly tiny amount, like 1% of the pot. You do no worse throwing your hand away in the dark than trying to hero-call. The strong player can simply 'claim' the pot with everything because you lose money by calling at all.
steps.formula: When the bettor's distribution is strong enough (more winners than a threshold), the caller's optimal calling frequency drops to zero for ALL bet sizes. Lesson: bet size does not save you against a range you are crushed by — the strength of the range dominates. Conversely, when YOU hold that strong range, tiny bets can extract value your opponent literally cannot defend against.
steps.proof: Take the half-street clairvoyance game with the bettor holding 60% winners, betting the whole pot. You might think 's=1 pot means call with half my hands.' But if you call any positive fraction, the bettor exploits you: he bets his winners for value and shoves all his bluffs, and because his range is so strong the exploit is worth more to him than you can claw back by catching bluffs. Since he can always increase his edge against any calling frequency you choose, no calling frequency is stable — the only equilibrium is you folding everything. From his side, pushing all-in with every hand and 'claiming' the pot is optimal, and you do exactly as well folding blind as playing 'well.' Information hiding cuts both ways: when one player's range is lopsidedly strong, the other player's cards stop mattering.
steps.memorize: Vs. a range you're crushed by, small bets don't help — fold. When YOUR range is that strong, tiny bets can't be defended.

steps.prompt: Your opponent's betting range is very strong — more than half of it is genuine winners, balanced with correctly-tuned bluffs. He bets a tiny 1%-of-pot bet. Chen & Ankenman's optimal response is:
options: Call with about half your hands to catch the tiny-bet bluffs
Raise, since a tiny bet signals weakness
Fold every hand — you do no better calling than folding blind
Call only your strongest 10% of hands
steps.explain: Against a sufficiently strong range the caller's optimal calling frequency is zero at every bet size — even 1% of the pot. The bettor can 'claim' the pot with everything because you lose money by calling at all; you do exactly as well throwing your hand away in the dark. Range strength dominates bet size.

steps.title: Play a strategy, not a hand
steps.feel: You quit face-up autopilot and assign the whole class of hands a betting frequency.
steps.formula: Your EV to BET a hand is compared to its EV to CHECK — never judged in a vacuum. If bet > check → always. If indifferent → mix. If bet < check → never.
steps.proof:
The reason to bet at all is your informational edge: you know your hole cards, they only know your range. If you'd only bet strong and check weak, you're face-up and exploitable — so you must bet some weak hands (bluffs) alongside strong ones and check back some strong hands (traps) to protect the checking range. Whether a hand is bet 100%, checked 100%, or mixed comes straight from comparing bet-EV to check-EV, not from the hand "feeling strong." Solvers mix heavily; humans can collapse most mixes to one action with tiny EV loss — but the RANGE must stay balanced across future runouts (board coverage).
How solvers decide bet / check / mix per hand
Bet-EV > Check-EV → bet always
Bet-EV = Check-EV → mix (frequency)
Bet-EV < Check-EV → check always
Bet weak (bluff) + check strong (trap)
= protected, un-face-up range
steps.memorize: The EV of a hand is bet-vs-check, always. Balance the range, not the single hand. Bluffs exist to make your value un-face-up.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: MDF and Alpha are rough guides, not gospel — most flop hands retain equity, so they don't have to defend the full MDF. Compare EVs; don't worship the formula.

steps.title: Choose bluffs by what they block, not by "badness"
steps.feel: You stop bluffing your worst hand and start bluffing the hand that erases their calls.
steps.formula: Best bluff blocks their VALUE / continuing combos and unblocks their folds. Best bluff-catcher blocks their value and misses their bluffs.
steps.proof:
River, missed flush board: with the nut-flush blocker you remove villain's trap flushes, collapsing the spot into pure polarized-vs-bluff-catcher — go all-in, bluff only nut-blockers (bluffing non-nut blockers loses EV). Without the nut blocker, NO blocker beats a non-nut blocker: if you bluff the K-high blocker the solver just overfolds K-flushes, so bluff the dead low cards instead. On flop x/r: a bluff that blocks villain's continuing range (44 on 9♥8♥4♥) is a better raise than one that blocks his bluffs. Calling: block his value → call more; block his bluffs → fold more.
Card-removal rules for bluff & call selection
Bluff: block their VALUE (nut blocker)
Bluff: unblock their FOLDS
Call: block value → call more
Call: block bluffs → fold more
No nut blocker → bluff DEAD cards
steps.memorize: Bluffs want to hold cards that kill their calls. Bluff-catchers want to hold cards that kill their value.

callout.text: Acevedo / Modern Poker Theory: "second-nut blocker" feels clever but is often the WORST bluff — they simply overfold that flush and call the rest. No blocker > a partial blocker.

steps.prompt: River, flush completes. You want to bluff. Which holding makes the best bluff to represent the nut flush?
options: A hand with the A of the flush suit (nut blocker)
A hand with the K of the flush suit
Two off-suit blanks with no flush cards
A middle pair
steps.explain: Holding the A♥ (nut-flush blocker) removes villain's strongest flushes — his traps vanish and the spot becomes pure polarized-vs-bluff-catcher, letting you jam max size and get maximum folds. The K-blocker is worse than a random blank: bluff it and he just overfolds K-flushes and calls with the rest. Represent the nuts by blocking the nuts.

steps.prompt: MIT's Bill Chen: in PLO with a flush on board, why is holding the bare ace of that suit (no other value) a great bluff?
options: It makes a backdoor flush
Card removal — you block the nut flush, so villain is far more likely to fold his strong hands
It has the most raw equity
Aces are always the best bluff
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L7, Chen: the bare nut-flush blocker means "you're blocking him from having a great hand... a lot of his hands he's freezing himself with." Ignore card removal and a good opponent bluffs exactly the spots where you can't have the nuts — "a strategy that can be exploited pretty easily." Blockers pick your bluffs in cash too.

steps.prompt: MIT's Bill Chen (and the Rose/Colin toy game): the pot is p and villain bets 1. To stop him from profitably bluffing, how often should you call?
options: Always call
p/(p+1) of the time — the indifference frequency
1/(p+1) of the time
Half the time regardless of pot
steps.explain: MIT 15.S50 L7, Chen: "you want to call about p/(p+1) of the time." Pot 10, bet 1 → call 10/11; if you defend less, "he's going to bluff everything and take it." This is the defense side of alpha and the backbone of not-being-exploited in cash — call enough to make bluffing zero-EV.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: 'it's always a repeated game'
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8, Hawrilenko on the most common excuse for spew — "I'll never play this guy again, so I'll just bluff 100%." His answer: "it is a repeated game." Imagine playing the same spot against a thousand different opponents. "You can think of each opponent as a random sampling from the distribution of possible strategies." Some fold too much (you own them); some call too much (they own you). Bluff 100% and the callers punish you across the pool.

The cash takeaway: even your first hand against a stranger is one draw from a population. Play the balanced strategy that wins against the whole distribution. "Get that 'it's not a repeated game' notion out of your heads. It's bad for business."
steps.formula: One-off villain = one sample from the strategy population. Unbalanced play loses to the sub-pool that punishes it, even if you never see them again.
steps.proof: Against a distribution of opponents, a 100%-bluff strategy has negative EV versus every over-caller in the pool — and there are enough of them to eat your edge. A balanced (indifference) strategy is safe against the whole population. So novelty of opponent never licenses imbalance.
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: every hand is a repeated game — one sample from the opponent population; stay balanced.

steps.title: Matt Hawrilenko's MIT lecture: the toy games assume symmetric ranges — check before you trust them
steps.feel:
MIT 15.S50 Lecture 8, Hawrilenko names the big hidden assumption of the Ace-King-Queen and coin-flip toys: "distributions are symmetric." That fails exactly when ranges are lopsided: "if you raise under the gun at a ten-handed table and the big blind calls, your distribution is way, way stronger — it's not symmetric." There the 1/(1+s) call frequency doesn't map cleanly.

His reassurance for cash: "as you progress throughout the hand, distributions tend to become more and more symmetric," so the mapping "holds pretty well" by the river — but on early streets with a range-advantage spot, adjust.
steps.formula: Symmetric ranges → 1/(1+s) works. Range advantage (e.g., UTG open vs BB call) → the stronger side bets more, calls less; the toy underprices your edge.
steps.proof: The Ace-King-Queen game gives both players an identical distribution of value/bluff-catcher/bluff. When your range is genuinely stronger (position + preflop line), you hold more value hands than your opponent, so equilibrium frequencies skew in your favor — the naive toy calling number is too loose for the strong side.
steps.memorize: MIT/Hawrilenko: 1/(1+s) assumes symmetric ranges — override it in clear range-advantage spots.

steps.prompt: You fire a pot-sized bet on the flop planning to barrel all three streets with a polarized range. Roughly what share of your flop bets should be bluffs?
steps.explain: Janda / Applications of NLHE: with pot-sized bets and a polarized range, river is 2/3 value, turn (2/3)² = 4/9 value, flop (2/3)³ ≈ 30% value — so ~70% of your flop bets are bluffs. The same value hands fire every street; you just shed a layer of bluffs as streets run out. Counterintuitive but correct because two streets remain.

steps.prompt: River, pot is 100. With a polarized range, which sizing lets you have the HIGHEST proportion of bluffs while keeping villain indifferent?
options: Half-pot (50)
1.5x pot overbet (150)
Quarter-pot (25)
steps.explain: Janda / Applications of NLHE: value fraction = (X+1)/(2X+1) where X is bet size as a fraction of pot. Half-pot needs 3/4 value, pot 2/3, the 1.5x overbet only 5/8 (62.5%) value -- the biggest bet gives villain the worst price, so you get to add the most bluffs. Bigger bet = more bluffs supported per value hand.

steps.prompt: You've been barreling and get to the river with a busted nut-flush-draw type spot. Villain checks. Between two air hands, which makes the better river bluff?
options: The hand that blocks villain's calling combos (good removal)
The hand that blocks villain's folding combos
Whichever has more backdoor equity
It doesn't matter, both are 0 equity
steps.explain: Janda / Applications of NLHE: every river bluff has 0 equity when called, so removal is the whole game. Bluff the hand that blocks combos in villain's CALLING range (makes him fold more) and avoid hands that block his FOLDING range. A missed flush draw that blocks his folds is a bad bluff; a hand that unblocks his air and blocks his calls is a good one.

steps.prompt: You barreled flop and turn. On which runout is a big river overbet with your nutted hands MOST justified?
options: Wet turn (J♥T♥6♣5♣) that bricks to an offsuit deuce
Dry paired board Q♥Q♠7♣2♦
A river that completes the obvious flush
Dry K♣9♥5♠2♦ where villain can slowplay a set
steps.explain: Janda / Applications of NLHE: overbet when villain is capped. On a draw-heavy turn he can't afford to slowplay a monster (too likely to get outdrawn or lose value), so he raises strong hands earlier — a brick river leaves him with almost no nutted hands and you bomb it. On dry/paired boards slowplaying is cheap and safe, so his range isn't capped; bet smaller there.

steps.prompt: In position after villain checks, you consider betting KQ top-pair-good-kicker on Q♥8♣6♠. Why might checking be better?
options: Betting everything strong-ish leaves your checking range too weak and invites check-raises
KQ can never win at showdown
You must always bet top pair for value
Checking guarantees you win the pot
steps.explain: Janda / Applications of NLHE: if you bet all your strong-ish hands your flop bet frequency balloons (~80%) and your checks become trash villain can attack. Checking KQ protects the checking range — it can call turn bets or value-bet a river check — and dodges getting check-raised off top pair. Some value has to be checked on purpose.

steps.prompt: River in position, deep, villain won't raise and defends optimally. You're effectively beaten ~15% of the time. The optimal sizing is ~0.83 pot. What's the key takeaway about that size?
options: A well-sized river value bet should win the MAJORITY of the time when called
You should always jam when ahead
Bet tiny so villain always calls
Sizing doesn't affect EV on the river
steps.explain: Janda / Applications of NLHE: the optimal-river-size formula (solved via a quadratic) lands where you still win the majority when called. Bet too big and you only get called by better and fold out worse — barely beating a check; bet too small and you leave value on the table against the hands you already beat. Pick the size that keeps you a favorite when called (and remember: betting reopens the action, so a check-raising villain can flip that math).
